C. Elegans' whole-organism model has facilitated the understanding of how its 300 neurons respond to varied environmental conditions. Researchers seeking to replicate this response in artificial neural networks employed a three-component design consisting of C. Elegans' neurons, synthetic neurons, and acteurs - a separate module providing stimuli and rewards. By training these networks in an alternative co-learning framework, the synthetic neurons, and using curiosity-driven rewards, they discovered that a particular type of neural network architecture effectively replicated the natural response to different environmental conditions after only a short period of training. This architecture, a residual neural network, outperformed other configurations including C. Elegans' own neurons. Notably, the synthetic neurons did not accurately replicate individual C. Elegans' neurons but collectively demonstrated similar behavioral responses. This research has broader implications by treating artificial neural networks as new types of synthetic organisms subject to selection and evolution. This opens up the possibility of utilizing these networks to discover novel phenotypes and mechanisms from existing datasets. Additionally, the co-learning framework introduced here can be applied to various large-scale and publicly available neurophysiological datasets to create synthetic organisms capable of replicating natural responses. This in turn can facilitate the discovery of underlying causal mechanisms. Notably, in the context of C. Elegans, the synthetic networks demonstrated that a particular type of sensory neuron was critical to reproducing the natural response to sodium stimuli but only when its activity was above a certain threshold. This is an example of how synthetic networks, through controlled mutations and selection, can facilitate the discovery of underlying causal mechanisms. This research aims to investigate the application of machine learning methods to the task of fault localization in microprocessor circuits. Through the application of logical testing and fault simulation, a dataset consisting of sample fault locations and types was generated. Utilizing this dataset, several machine learning algorithms were trained and evaluated for their ability to accurately detect internal faults. Among the methods tested, the decision tree classifier demonstrated superior performance, achieving a balanced accuracy of 89% and a false positive rate of 41%. A proposed classification scheme is introduced, incorporating the faults typically localized within the instruction cycle as one class and the remainder as others. To enhance the efficiency of the machine learning methods, several data reduction techniques were explored, including feature selection and principal component reduction. The outcomes of this study indicate that microprocessor fault diagnosis is suitable for machine learning, offering significant potential as a means of diagnosing internal faults. Additionally, the study's methods and datasets are accessible through the provided link. The corresponding GitHub link is: https://github.com/IntelligentEmbeddedSystemsGroup/MicroprocessorFaultLocalization. 

Keywords: fault localization, microprocessor, machine learning, balanced accuracy, decision tree, data reduction.

For free products of categorically finite groups and surface groups, our results align with the group growth theory established by Grigorchuk and Grigorieva. We demonstrate that a star-shaped metric graph with unbounded edges has exponential stability of its enclosed area, regardless of elasticity in the edges. This proves a consequence of a broader criterion for exponential stability in a metric graph's subspace, which will be presented in this paper as Theorem 4. Notably, if the edges lack elasticity, this criterion simplifies to a well-known condition for establishing exponential stability in a particular type of bounded graph known as a Riesz graph. Moreover, a practical method for numerically calculating the associated exponential decay constant is developed based on a direct approach to solve a related issue of a boundary value problem of a classical Bessel equation, as formulated in Theorem 7. This novel bound is shown to be comparative to the one obtained through a different approach in existing literature, as expressed in Theorem 9. As a related application, we prove that a demixed Bose gas at a half-filled state is stable based on this generalized boundary value Bessel equation problem. Specifically, we demonstrate that the issue of finding the correct parameter value of the potential in the equation, which corresponds to a particular boundary condition of a homogenization problem, can be numerically resolved. This general numerical approach to a boundary value problem of a classical Bessel equation may also apply to other boundary conditions and find additional applications in the context of a complete graph instead of a star-shaped one. It is worth mentioning that the numerical finding of an exponential decay constant for models of localized loss of particles and dark solitons in the referred Bose gas, as well as for models of localized bound states in the referred Bose gas, may also be computed through this developed algorithm. The primary goal of this study is to understand how the structure of the input graphs, as well as the output labels, affects the ability of GNNs to transfer knowledge from one task to another. Through a comprehensive analysis of five benchmark datasets and the use of five different GNN-based models, as well as two benchmark benchmarks, we aimed to investigate how the variation in task structure influences the ability of GNNs to transfer knowledge. Our key findings indicate that GNNs are capable of transferring knowledge up to 10 hops for many tasks and that the community structure of the input graph plays a crucial role in task transferability for GNNs. Additionally, by transferring the knowledge at the community level instead of the node level, we were able to achieve significant improvements in model performance, as well as generalization. The code used to support this study is publicly available on GitHub at the specified repository link. The main contributions of this study lie in the characterization of the ability of GNNs to transfer knowledge over different tasks, as well as the development of new techniques that are designed to improve the generalization of GNNs. The findings of this study highlight important implications for the design of both the input features and the model architecture of GNNs. The latter leads to the proposal of ProGNN, a novel architecture that integrates graph and node-level features to facilitate the transferability of GNNs. The performance of ProGNN is comparable to the state-of-the-art, while also outperforming many other existing methods. The novel techniques developed in this study may find application in a wider context, encompassing Deep NNs trained on network data. The characterisation of the ability of GNNs to transfer knowledge may also find application in other areas, such as the exploration of other forms of graph-based machine learning. The study is the first to provide a characterisation of the ability of GNNs to transfer knowledge for a range of different tasks. Initially developed for infant nutrition, IBP is applied to users, items, and features.  Uniquely, our approach determines features implicitly from item correlations and simultaneously infers user features from user interactions.  A key advantage of this method is that it circumvents the necessity for extensive data exploration and mapping in comparison to techniques like PCA.  The system comprises an online learning module, called STI-IBP, and a model-based clustering component, providing accurate recommendations and clustering solutions.  Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model, where it surpasses existing IBP-based recommender systems in accuracy and outperforms popular recommender systems including Amazon, YouTube, and others on real-world datasets.  Notably, our results reveal that users of similar features can be clustered effectively using this method.  The proposed approach possesses a high degree of interpretability due to its direct representation of user features and is highly suitable for applications requiring real-time recommendations and user profiling.  The proposed source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/avinsharma/STI-IBP}.  Overall, this work aims to revolutionize recommender system design by merging user profiling and recommendation tasks.  As a result, the generated user profiles represent state-of-the-art characteristics in the field.  Furthermore, the proposed approach provides an innovative and novel pathway for designing profile-based recommender systems.  The theoretical validity of the proposed method was verified through consistency estimation, thereby ensuring its applicability in real-world scenarios.  The profiling capability of the proposed method was evaluated using user profiling metrics and state-of-the-art measures such as Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and the V-measure metric. However, Fortnow's proof can be improved upon significantly as the reduction only works for sets of size n in dimension n but fails for sets of size 2 in dimension 2. In this research, we show that the mostly set-disjoint problem remains hard by showing that U&P ≠ AL still holds even with the additional constraint of sets having a limited size of O(n). The primary issue with shared ventilation systems lies in ensuring each patient receives the desired tidal volume. To tackle this, researchers are exploring the properties of the complex air flow through the system's branches when a single ventilator is used for multiple patients. To achieve accurate modeling, patients, the ventilator, and surrounding equipment are all accounted for as part of the branched network. However, current models face limitations, particularly in addressing various patient requests for tidal volumes due to the single available ventilator. To resolve this problem, researchers have developed a new type of sequence, referred to as the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence, which effectively allocates the ventilator to provide each patient with their desired tidal volume. A critical aspect of the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence involves meeting the ventilator's minimum breathing requirements and ensuring airflow can be accurately maintained with the available ventilator settings. A key innovation of the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence is its flexibility to tackle various complex airflow properties, particularly in the presence of small airway closures. To test the applicability of the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence, researchers have conducted numerous simulations across various scenarios with up to ten patients and the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence has successfully accommodated various ventilator settings and patient requests. A computer program for generating the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence has also been developed and is available for public use. In summary, the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence is an innovative solution for shared ventilators to meet the specific tidal volume needs of individual patients during single-use ventilation. The utility of the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence is expected to prioritize patient comfort and safety while helping healthcare professionals effectively manage shared ventilators in emergency situations. The $\mathcal{B}$-sequence's properties and computer program for generating the sequence have been provided in the documentation of this article. A detailed explanation of the $\mathcal{B}$-sequence's derivation and importance can be found in the preprint paper at arXiv:2107.05293. The Zel'dovich equation has been widely used for simulating the clustering of matter on a cosmological scale, however solving this partial differential equation analytically is not feasible and typical numerical methods can be slow and unaccurate. In this research, we introduce discretized versions of the Zel'dovich equation combined with a sophisticated correction term that allows for precise and efficient solution of the equation. The proposed discretized correction DCT algorithm is compared against other standard discretization methods such as finite difference, splines and adaptive B-splines in terms of accuracy, especially at locations where matter density is underdense. The evaluation is based on the deviation of the test mass distribution from unity. The research shows that the traditional methods like FDM, SDM and BSM are inconsistent, whereas ACM and DCT are consistent but suffer from different complications. Furthermore, DCT algorithm offers real-time predictive capabilities, whereas DCT with adaptive biquadratic (ABQ) splines has a lag of one time step, and ABQ is inconsistent. The proposed DCT algorithm offers substantial speed up over conventional methods such as FDM, SDM, BSM and ABQ, with a lag of one time step. The research shows that using multiple time steps with ABQ and then applying the DCT correction does not add extra lag, as ABQ can be used as a starting value for the next iteration in DCT. In order to further accelerate the solution, the research proposes that the density in the Zel'dovich equation should only be calculated for locations where matter density is overdense, with low-order biquadratic interpolation to determine the density at underdense locations. In conclusion, the research demonstrates that using DCT algorithm with either FDM, ABQ or BSM requires only minimal extra computation to obtain high precision and efficient solution of the Zel'dovich equation. The research evaluates the efficiency of the DCT algorithm by using it in the initial conditions for a $4096^3$ simulation of the Large Scale Structure where the equation is used iteratively to add non-gravitational dispersion. The research shows that the DCT algorithm offers speed up factors of 4, 8 and 16 over FDM, ABQ and BSM respectively, with a potential to be implemented on a GPU to provide even greater speed up. The research demonstrates that the DCT algorithm can be used to provide predictive information at locations where matter density is underdense with a lag of one time step. A newly devised steganographic framework is introduced that leverages one-time pads paired with linearly encoded stegstexts to achieve steganography. This novel system is inspired by a previous investigation into steganographic mechanisms in cryptographic systems, and it addresses a primary challenge associated with these systems: maximizing the amount of encrypted data transmitted. Following a thorough examination of the properties of linear encodings and an in-depth analysis of its steganographic properties, it became clear that this proposed model surpasses previously accepted steganographic protocols by an approximately 100% increase in capacity for small blocks of data. Furthermore, an interesting connection was observed between steganographic systems and error-correcting codes, which may hold significant value for future research. Additionally, two potential applications for the proposed steganographic system were explored: steganography via ciphers and steganographic social media posting. Interestingly, when applying the proposed steganographic framework to both scenarios, the perceived change in average characters was found to be negligible, thus making it highly suitable for such hidden communication methods in various online platforms. Lastly, a potential extension to the proposed steganographic framework was suggested by integrating it with the principles of differential steganography. This integration leads to an innovative, dynamic steganographic framework that adapts to differing communication scenarios. The synthetic control method, widely employed to evaluate the impact of specific treatments, requires valid pre-intervention data from multiple control units.  However, when estimating weights using strict panel data, unbalanced sequences or missing values in some control units make their contribution unfeasible, rendering them unusable for weight calculations.  Existing solutions typically omit these unusable control units or require costly panel data from multiple markets with similar temporal availability.  To address this challenge, our study develops two novel estimators able to utilize control units with missing or unconnected data by sharing weight information from other usable units within the same market.  Two alternative solutions exist: the First-Order Constrained (FOC) estimator utilizes the most similar units from the same market and the Principal Component one considers a multivariate distribution of treatment effects.  Both estimators start with a principal component analysis of aggregate outcomes, converting the problem into a constrained weight estimation issue.  Both the FOC and POC estimators can be estimated through a convex program, making them efficient and computationally viable.  Both methods show superior performance in our simulation experiments and real-world application in evaluating Michigan's motor vehicle safety inspection law. In many graph-based machine learning applications, graph signals are frequently used to obtain information about nodes, but doing so puts sensitive information at risk. To safeguard against this, local differential privacy can be applied at the node level by introducing noise into the orbit of each node. However to our knowledge, previous research has not thoroughly examined the application of local differential privacy in graph learning tasks. Therefore, this study looked into the application of local differential privacy in graph learning across three distinct scenarios: graph filtering, graph convolution, and graph convolutional neural networks, and demonstrated how different noise mechanisms and orbit types affect the predicted output and their potential to meet a predetermined criterion. We observed that different mechanisms and orbit types have varying levels of performance depending on the specific task involved. Furthermore, graph convolutional neural networks are capable of meeting a desired level of differential privacy while achieving a significantly higher prediction accuracy compared to other methods. The source code for this research can be found here. We concluded that local differential privacy in graph learning tasks is a rapidly evolving and complex field that requires further research. The results and noise mechanisms explored in this study can serve as a building block or benchmark for future studies. The data used in this research can be found here. We plan to expand on the findings of this study to apply local differential privacy in other graph learning tasks in the future. A preliminary version of this research was first presented at the 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory. Many recent colorization methods have relied on pairwise color-distance models, often paired with neural networks trained on large datasets, to generate color information from grayscale images. This typically requires a comprehensive dataset of de-colored images, which is difficult to assemble, thereby limiting the technique's scope and effectiveness. This paper presents an alternative approach based on neural style transfer, allowing colors to be inferred from a broader range of reference images, including those containing minimal to no foreground information. This is made possible by projecting high-dimensional style representations onto a reduced-dimensional latent space, where image similarity is quantified through Euclidean distance. As a result, our technique can color a wider variety of images, including complex scenes, which would be difficult for traditional colorization models to replicate. To further enhance our method's versatility, additional color inputs can be incorporated by projecting additional reference styles into the same reduced-dimensional space, thereby merging their attributes. To validate our approach, we conducted a two-fold evaluation consisting of both quantitative and qualitative assessments to demonstrate its flexibility and effectiveness. Specifically, we tested our technique on a diverse range of reference images, including both simple and complex designs, as well as multiple foreground topics, while evaluating its performance in a fully automated setting. Moreover, to ensure the quality of the colorizations produced by our approach, we refined a state-of-the-art metric designed for assessing colorization quality in conjunction with human evaluations. Collectively, the results demonstrate the capability of our neural style-based colorization method to effectively color a broad spectrum of images, including those featuring complex scenes, which was previously infeasible for most colorization techniques. Moreover, our technique aims to contribute insights toward developing a comprehensive colorization technology capable of handling a diverse range of reference images, including those with multiple foreground topics. To resolve this issue, we propose creating a system that is capable of learning from Distillation-based Outlier-Aware Support points. Through the process, supernovae models are trained on support points which are themselves distilled from the data, effectively eliminating the influence of outlier samples. To further enhance the accuracy of support representations, we also propose using Clustering to enable the re-identification of support points. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses comparison methods in scenarios involving fast adaptation to unsupervised areas. Additionally, the supply of in-task labels allows for even more accurate support point representation, thereby making it easier to achieve precise point-wise support learning. We also employ the support points in teacher models to demonstrate their capability to solve tasks and offer improved robustness to outlier samples. To establish the scope of support points in knowledge transfer, we also propose using the Distillation-based Outlier-Aware Support points to create meta-transfer learning models. These models start by training task-specific one-look models on support points which are themselves distilled from the data, effectively eliminating the influence of outlier samples. To further enhance accuracy and robustness, we also propose using the Clustered Supervised and Unsupervised Pseudo-Labels for meta-transfer. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the Distillation-based Outlier-Aware Support points in solving two-shot as well as unsupervised adaptation tasks. It's long been possible to determine whether a graph is semi-transitive orable with a given independent set in mind, but a straightforward approach isn't straightforward. In fact, semi-transitive orientability can recognize split graphs with a small independent set, but not those with multiple large independent sets. However, graphs featuring two independent sets of roughly the same size can be easily identified as semi-transitive orientable by checking a new, simple condition. This new condition also helps identify bipartite semi-transitive orientable graphs and reveals a new class of bipartite split graphs that are semi-transitive orientable. These graphs have two large independent classes. In contrast, a related family of bipartite split graphs that are semi-transitive orientable - proposed earlier as an example of a family with two independent sets and semi-transitive orientability - will now fail the new condition. As an added benefit, a simple linear-time approach has also been developed to determine whether any bipartite graph is semi-transitive orientable. This new algorithm is particularly effective in identifying bipartite semi-transitive orientable graphs and reveals a new characterization of bipartite semi-transitive orientable graphs with two large independent sets. In relation to another problem, a straightforward linear-time verification that split graphs with two large independent sets have a Hamiltonian decomposition follows. However, proving that a split graph is Hamiltonian cannot be accomplished in sub-cubicle time. In fact, a linear-time approach has also been developed to identify split graphs that are Hamiltonian and semi-transitive orientable. In relation to another problem, a straightforward approach has also been developed to identify pseudo-bipartite graphs with semi-transitive orientation properties. These are linear-time identifications that advance understanding of split graph orientability. The current paper is an evolution of the paper's content at the conference, with an enhanced abstract, revised content, and multiple new findings. Quantum Chromodynamics, or QCD, is one of the four fundamental forces governing particle interactions. To study these interactions, researchers analyze data from high-energy collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The LHC's ATLAS detector records energy readings from tiny particles called jets when collisions occur. The data can be distorted by fake signals from real particles that mimic jet behavior. To mitigate this, scientists develop algorithms to distinguish genuine jets from fake signals, particularly those produced by particles like pi and K. However, these algorithms are not sufficient to distinguish tau particles, which have a much lower occurrence rate and can be misidentified by energetic electrons. A recent study (Tau Identification in Proton-Proton Collisions at 13 TeV with the ATLAS Detector) utilized the ATLAS detector at the LHC to examine how well electron-based algorithms can distinguish tau particles from jets in proton-proton collisions at high energy levels. The analysis focused on two types of tau leptons, and it presented two methods to assess the efficiency of tau identification compared to jet misidentification. Depending on the method used, the efficiency of tau identification was found to be comparable to that of jet misidentification while maintaining low false positive rates. The study further provided a comprehensive estimation of tau lepton uncertainties based on a statistical analysis and accounted for systematic uncertainties from several sources. The final results of tau lepton uncertainties were discussed, and they are based on a 2016 dataset consisting of 3.6 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The study's findings are relevant to searches for heavy charged couplled Majorana neutrals and supersymmetric partners of the tau lepton. The development of this work laid the groundwork for future analyses examining tau lepton interactions in high-energy collisions. The study of mechanical waves in integrated photonic crystals provides an advanced platform for analyzing complex light behaviors. We have gained insight into the fundamental principles of mechanical wave effects on photonic phenomena through a detailed analysis of a two-dimensional square lattice photonic crystal operating under both piezoelectric and electrostatic driving forces. When piezoelectric driving is used, mechanical modes of specific symmetries can directly interact with the photonic mode, leading to reduced backaction effects and prolonged Brillouin times due to the non-orthogonality of mechanical and photonic modes. In contrast, mechanical modes of higher symmetry can interact with the photonic mode under electrostatic driving, although this interaction is dependent on the photonic mode's direction. Mechanisms are proposed to manage and manipulate these interactions to develop high-performance photonic applications. Our research provides a new understanding of micro-mechanical photonic clutches and offers a design framework for advanced photonic systems with extended Brillouin interactions. Furthermore, our study reveals that in certain cases, photonic mode modulation can occur without mechanical mode resonance under electrostatic driving, a phenomenon that can be leveraged in meta-devices to control photonic bandgap coupling. Moreover, mechanical impact on the photonic mode's polarization under electrostatic driving provides a new method for dynamic polarization rotation within photonic crystals. In addition, our study reveals that mechanical modes can breach the polarization symmetry barrier in hybrid photonic crystals and have a significant impact on the optical effective medium theory. Mechanisms are proposed to manage and exploit these effects in photonic crystals. Our research demonstrates that mechanical influence on photonic crystals can cover a wide range of applications, from linear to nonlinear photonic systems, including wavelength division multiplexing, polarization handling, and photonic bandgap manipulation. Our study provides a new understanding of mechanical photonic interactions and offers design opportunities for advanced photonic applications. In particular, mechanical effects can extend the lifetime of photonic mode modulation in Brillouin enhancement platforms and may find applications in photonic integrated circuits. Moreover, mechanical influence on the photonic mode can occur in hybrids when the optical and mechanical symmetries match, which is not predicted by the optical effective medium theory, and can be exploited to develop meta-devices. In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, the electromagnetic field has a profound impact on the creation of electrons and positrons. The produced particles are not only created through the final stages of electromagnetic interactions but also influenced by the electromagnetic field during their formation. The consequences of this effect are two-fold: (i) the created electrons and positrons are not uniformly distributed across space and time and (ii) an additional current is generated, known as the electromagnetic current, in addition to the existing electron and positron currents. The application of relativistic hydrodynamics allows for an efficient simulation of this process, resulting in an enhanced production of electrons and positrons in the system. The paper presents an analytical framework for understanding this phenomenon in relativistic hydrodynamics and demonstrates its effects on the creation of electrons, positrons, and photons in heavy-ion collisions at mid-rapidity. The findings predict an increased production of electrons, positrons, and photons in heavy-ion collisions at mid-rapidity compared to conventional predictions. The paper also discusses future experimental opportunities to verify this phenomenon at the Large Hadron Collider and future collision systems. A representation of biological systems through network patterns has gained significant traction in the study of complex diseases and disorders. One particular schema, based on symmetrical and undirected links, has been widely adopted. Nevertheless, the underlying physical nature of brain connections demands a more nuanced approach. This has prompted the development of network representations rooted in total correlation and non-Gaussian assumptions. Utilizing data obtained from a group of subjects undergoing fMRI procedures, the study demonstrates the capacity of these network biomarkers to identify alterations in brain structure associated with ADHD in a separate data set. Furthermore, the study provides a statistical model that delineates the probability distribution of total correlation network parameters, allowing for confidence intervals to be established for individual edge parameters. Ultimately, the study highlights the potential of these network representations as sensitive indicators of complex neurological conditions and brain system alterations. Understanding which features influence a machine learning model is crucial, but when a model operates in a black box, examining its performance is challenging. To measure feature importance, SHAP (SHapley addition probability) provides a comprehensive approach, have been proven to accurately contribute to the explanation of AI models. Although SHAP has been effectively applied to the evaluation of supervised learning models, its effectiveness in capturing feature importance in the context of generative models remains unclear. Our study aims to investigate the effectiveness of SHAP in capturing key features from generative models like GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) through an experiment that compares its performance with that of an expert. The results show that SHAP fails to accurately identify relevant features from GANs due to the limitations inherent in the framework. To address this limitation, we have modified the SHAP framework to make it suitable for generative models. The modified approach relies on a temperature mechanism to minimize excessive predictions. Our findings demonstrate that the tempered SHAP yields accurate estimates of feature importance for GANs, significantly outperforming the original framework. The substantial impact of tempering on the accuracy of feature importance estimation from GANs is significantly higher than that observed in the context of linear classifiers, highlighting its effectiveness. Our proposed method, when applied to other types of generative models (e.g. VAEs, ProPGANs, CNNDM), shows its strength and versatility. The features extracted by VAEs via SHAP analysis demonstrate a notable resemblance to those obtained through radiologist annotations, underscoring the effectiveness of SHAP in capturing key VAE features. Our study further investigates CNNDM to show that SHAP can capture key features from this model as well. To facilitate the evaluation of SHAP and other tools for feature importance estimation, we have developed a publicly accessible platform that enables the easy comparison of their performance on a wide range of machine learning models and datasets. The accessibility of this platform and our code on GitHub are ensured through regular updates. Our platform allows users to easily configure, run experiments and compare different feature importance estimation approaches with varying parameters and datasets, thereby promoting reproducibility and consistency. Our comparative analysis of feature importance estimation approaches on various models and datasets further underscores the importance of consistent evaluation. This study introduces the Detail Context Block (DCB), a compact transformer module tailored for spatiotemporal data that effciently enhances detail preservation. The DCB optimizes memory usage through decentralized detail storage and employs a simplified, series-constrained attention mechanism. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets for action recognition and video compression demonstrate the DCB's superiority over existing approaches in precision and a reduced memory footprint. Notably, it achieves a 2-5% improvement in Top-1 accuracy on Kinetics-400 and Sinhc+ videos, along with a 2-10% gain in PSNR on various video sequences. We further provide a detailed analysis of the DCB's effects on spatiotemporal models through attribute visualization and ablation studies, facilitating deeper understanding of the module's behavior. The proposed DCB has extensive potential applications beyond video datasets, and our code and models are publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, a renowned video compression dataset, NIST-VECGA, was used to evaluate the DCB's performance under distinct processing conditions. The results indicate that by substituting the DCB as the prediction module for spatiotemporal transformer architectures in MPEG standards, it results in a 1-2% improvement in RMSE and a 0.1-0.2 bit saving for various test sequences, including confocal microscopy and outdoor scenes. Programming languages employ type systems to ensure memory's correctness in imperative languages and prevent confusing similar expressions in functional languages. Despite these benefits, type systems and data models used in modern programming languages have significant shortcomings. They fail to verify the memory's consistency during runtime, causing hard-to-find bugs and potentially dangerous security breaches. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a type system and data model called Flux, designed for Rust. Flux is unique in that it not only guarantees the memory's correctness during runtime but also verifies and validates integer expressions based on the characteristics of the integers. To achieve this, Flux introduces novel concepts such as integer domains, characterized memory databases, and characterized contents that describe the constraints of the integers, as well as a type system that controls the access to the memory. The paper demonstrates how Flux effectively identifies and prevents integer-related bugs, such as overflows, data corruption, and errors in logical expressions, through concrete examples. The work serves as a foundation for further research in improving the type system and data model of modern programming languages to ensure the correctness of the data. A novel average case verification protocol for quantum computations, denoted as average case quantum quantum compression (CVQC), has been proposed. It employs two quantum circuits, a verifier and a prover, to expedite verification processes. Following an initial measurement by the verifer to establish a classical description of the quantum state, the prover performs a specific rotation to reveal the correct answer to a verifer query. If the answer is incorrect, the prover executes a recovery operation to conceal this information before another round of measurements takes place. It is proven that if the answer is always correct, repeated verification will yield an almost certain outcome through analysis of the average case behavior. In a confined area with walls and a central point where balls are trapped, two disks are placed and subjected to pressure from an incoming stream of balls. There's a balance point for each disk where slight adjustments in weight can lead to jamming. We find that lighter disks are more responsive to external influences and prone to jamming, while heavier disks require stronger external forces to achieve the same effect. This behavior is influenced by the disks' rotational speeds and the friction experienced at the point where they are trapped. Factors like lower wall friction and disk non-uniformity can cause jamming to occur at specific, calculated weight ranges instead of the expected uniform patterns. We provide detailed explanations for these phenomena through geometric and topological analyses, specifically considering the structures that arise within the confined area. These results are based on a simplified model that may be expanded to address a variety of physical scenarios. Finally, we observe the effects of external influences on the central disks through numerical simulations in a two-dimensional environment, using a Monte Carlo approach and a realistic model for ball interactions based on molecular dynamics. This numerical exploration reveals how these jamming phenomena can be controlled through adjustments in the central disks' dimensions and positions. Moreover, it's shown that light central disks are more responsive to external pressures and prone to escaping or being released under sufficient force. These findings inspire new questions about the behavior of central disks based on their physical characteristics, encouraging further numerical and analytical investigations to explore their theoretical and practical applications. Meanwhile, the study also identified previously overlooked structures for the central disks' jamming phases, such as a specific arrangement of three balls and the possibility of three disks being trapped at the central point, as well as an unusual phase where the central disks cannot be jammed and must be positioned off-center. These topological structures for the central disks' jamming phases hold significant theoretical importance and may have a significant impact on their practical applications, and it's believed that they can be explored and utilized in a wide range of physical scenarios. Ultimately, the study provides a unique and in-depth understanding of the complex interactions that occur within the confined area and sheds new light on the general principles governing the behavior of particles within such environments. To study the impact of nonaffine deformations on material properties, researchers developed a model based on the elastic regime of disordered solids. The model, focusing solely on nonaffine behavior, was unable to capture the full range of material responses. In contrast, an experimental investigation, presented in this article, detects nonaffinity in elastic materials using two distinct methods: by measuring strain-stress relationships in different regions of a sample and by analyzing local strain distributions. The experimental results confirm that nonaffine deformations occur uniformly throughout the sample's elastic domain. Additionally, the study shows that affine and nonaffine deformations coexist simultaneously, leading to a deformation pattern described as heterogeneous affine plus nonaffine deformation. The observed nonaffinity was observed to be sensitive to loading protocols, but not to the overall level of strain. The importance of this research lies in the fact that it addresses a critical defect in nonaffine body models based on random packings and highlights the need to develop improved, more comprehensive body models that can effectively capture the observed nonaffine deformations. Moreover, the experimental discovery of nonaffinity in elastic materials might prompt a reevaluation of existing models and the development of new ones. Building on single-population models, this research explores the dynamics of a population where interactions are entirely cooperative in nature. Existing models, primarily focusing on deterministic processes, lack the capability to account for variations in stochastic events. In response, this study delves into the world of probabilistic processes, investigating a population where the rate of birth and death is influenced by a finite dimensional local R\'enyi process. Through this analysis, we identify not only the conditions required for the existence of solutions but also derive explicit conditions necessary for the unique, pathwise unique, almost sure unique, and unique in probability solution within the given framework. Furthermore, this study utilizes the properties of local R\'enyi processes to derive key findings regarding the uniqueness of solutions. Additionally, this research establishes the foundational ideas and results for a functional analytic approach to existing multi-population models, which rely solely on deterministic processes. Ultimately, this study provides novel insights into the existing single-population models by analyzing their ability to withstand random events. Through a specific example, we demonstrate that introducing random elements within a multiplicative framework is capable of preserving the stability of the population model. Conversely, the same effect cannot be achieved in an additive framework. Lastly, this study utilizes the established framework to derive a novel single-population model by analyzing the dynamics of a population within a diverse environment, where individual members apply knowledge from past experiences to predict the behavior of their neighbors. This research identifies conditions necessary for the existing solution to exist within this new model and presents various examples to illustrate the uniqueness of the solution in diverse environmental settings. Consequently, this study highlights several key differences in behavior existing between single-population models, when considering both cooperative and competitive interactions, under various environmental settings. Ultimately, this research provides a novel foundation to explore multi-population models by analyzing both the established knowledge within that field and the unique characteristics provided by the introduced framework. Traditional methods often focus on identifying random variations, leaving deterministic uncertainty unaddressed. Ignoring this uncertainty can compromise the accuracy of statistical results, especially in complex industrial environments. A novel approach combines probabilistic uncertainty modeling with a level set transformation to effectively handle non-deterministic uncertainty. This method improves the accuracy of its predictions and reduces reliance on the complexity of the system. A case study demonstrates the benefits of this technique in achieving high precision without requiring detailed process knowledge. In this context, uncertainty models based on hacking can be integrated into the level set transformation to analyze the consequences of hacks on system robustness, enabling the prediction of potential vulnerabilities and providing early warnings before system failures can occur. Consequently, a future area of research could focus on further developing and improving methods that effectively integrate diverse data and can balance data imbalances to facilitate the analysis of complex problems. Ultimately, a future numerical example may demonstrate the potential of deep learning for enhancing uncertainty modeling and system reliability. Building on existing metrics, ReSV incorporates a unique combination of temporal logic components to accurately measure a system's temporal robustness. By applying ReSV to an optimal control framework, it provides a quantitative approach for designing resilient control systems. This research focuses on enhancing language models with positional encoding techniques to aid in processing code-mixed text, typically found in online interactions on social media. For instance, online conversations in Hindi-English code-mixing are crucial for brand marketing and require models to grasp the sequence of words in both languages to achieve the desired goals. Most existing models fail to account for word position during classification tasks in both monolingual and multilingual settings. To address this challenge, our studies reveal the significance of position-aware models in code-mixed language processing and explore two innovative methods for incorporating positional encoding. These methods involve position-based self-attention and position-sensitive character-level encoding in conjunction with delimiting character embedding. Experimentally, our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of positional encoding in improving language models, especially for classification tasks, and confirm that our proposed techniques can be utilized alone or in combination with other embedding methods to achieve better performance. Notably, our position-based self-attention model outperforms several baseline models by 0.3-2.2% in F1-score in both offline and zero-shot settings. Additionally, our position-sensitive character-level encoding method consistently surpasses other encoding techniques by 0.1-1.2% in F1-score and highlights its potential to also enhance multilingual position-aware baselines by 0.1-1.2%. These findings suggest that positional encoding is an efficient method to enhance language models in code-mixed settings. The research also includes demonstrations of the effectiveness of the position-based models in zero-shot settings across multiple tasks. The proposed models, along with the research code and model weights, can be accessed through the provided public GitHub repository. Moreover, our position-based models have been validated to outperform existing position-insensitive models in both offline and zero-shot settings on different code-mixed datasets, including datasets in other language combinations. These models include datasets in the combinations of Bengali-English, Punjabi-English, and Marathi-English code-mixing. Robotic motion planning in congested areas is a complicated problem that exists in numerous applications.
This research presents a novel method of generating spatial restrictions for use in motion planning.
In environments filled with obstacles, our approach divides the space into discrete points along multiple dimensions using a predefined grid.
By incorporating probabilistic assessment, we establish a threshold for whether a predefined path is likely to pass through a congested area.
If so, we divide the space into smaller sections and create shorter, localized paths to avoid congestion.
Through simulation tests, we evaluated our method in comparison to a motion planning system that utilizes probabilistic control in environments involving spherical collisions.

Cameras lacking built-in descriptions, like those found on smartphones, make relying on handheld cues the most practical method for determining camera position relative to known objects. However, existing approaches struggle in situations where hand movements are minimal or unpredictable. To address this problem, a new learning-based camera descriptor designed specifically for featureless objects has been developed. In contrast to traditional descriptors, which focus on efficient computation, the proposed descriptor prioritizes accurate and detailed description, especially in challenging environments. As a result, it significantly outperforms competing methods, even in situations where hand data is scarce. Furthermore, by utilizing a two-stage approach, the descriptor's complexity is largely limited to training time, thus not impacting its overall performance. An implementation of the descriptor, along with its associated code and training data, can be found on the project's GitHub page, where it has already demonstrated success in various benchmarks. An additional paper detailing this research, including relevant camera footage, has been accepted to the ICCV 2021 conference. A live demonstration of the descriptor can be viewed at https://youtu.be/F2f1локZ3Q. The descriptor's associated paper can be accessed at https://www.joley.cc/sarsasas. Additionally, a short video illustrating its capabilities can be viewed at https://youtu.be/F2f1локZ3Q. A pre-trained model based on the descriptor can be accessed via https://joley.cc/aberdeen-descriptor. The researchers' findings indicate that a two-stage approach not only yields better results but also minimizes computational complexity, thus making the descriptor efficient. In the initial stage, low-level features are extracted from the object using a convolutional neural network, with their representation then combined into a comprehensive description through an attention-based convolutional layer. However, the description generated by the object alone is insufficient to capture variations in camera pose, thus necessitating the second stage. In the second stage, the researchers utilize a convolutional attention convolutional layer to combine the description with geometric information from the object, resulting in a camera descriptor that accurately captures both appearance and geometric properties of the object. Our research makes visible the connection between strain and resistance in LiFeAs and NaFeAs through elastoresistance, offering new insights. The findings show that nematic effects in LiFeAs are as strong as in NaFeAs but manifest in opposition to expected directions of deformation, suggesting anisotropic material properties. The direction of the connection between strain and resistance in NaFeAs was found to be largely determined by the direction of the electric current, while in LiFeAs it is influenced by the direction of the applied stress, especially near a transition temperature. The findings in NaFeAs can be explained by a simple theoretical model based on fluctuations in the material plane, but this model fails to fully explain the findings in LiFeAs. Our research reveals significant, but hidden, signs of strain-related effects within LiFeAs that are associated with its nematic phase transitions, which are not visible through standard methods of measuring electrical resistance. The connection between strain and resistance in LiFeAs is found to be a saturation point, reaching its limit at a certain temperature before it stops responding to changes in stress, a behavior not seen in NaFeAs. The findings provide significant insights into the underlying physics of this material, known for being at the intersection of two major phases of material science research (iron-based superconductors and 5d transition metal oxides). The discovery also enables the use of mechanical manipulation to influence the properties of this material, offering new avenues of investigation. The connection between strain and resistance in NaFeAs remains unexplained within the current framework of theoretical material science research, indicating the need for further study into the underlying physics of this material. Our research reveals that the connection between strain and resistance in NaFeAs undergoes a sudden and great increase in the vicinity of 18.5K, a transition temperature associated with its nematic phase transitions, but this effect is not seen through standard methods of measuring electrical resistance which instead reveal a disconnect between strain and resistance at this temperature. The connection between strain and resistance in NaFeAs also shows a notable increase in the gradient of its response to strain at the onset of its spin-density wave state, a phase transition associated with its underlying physics. The presence of an opposition effect in the connection between strain and resistance in LiFeAs is found to be related to its depth of doping, a measure of how much of its original material makeup has been altered, and becomes a sudden connection at a certain point where different types of magnetic behavior within the material begin to take over. Recent research on the Type-II two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) has gained increased interest, particularly after the 13 TeV LHC findings that deviated from expectations under the standard model (SM) background. We conduct a comprehensive study of the measurement on $pp \to Hz$ ($H \to aa \to \mu^+\mu^-$) in conjunction with $B \to K(\mu^+\mu^-)$. Specifically, our analysis involves a controlled systematic examination of SM processes in the final stage, found to be predominantly influenced by QCD at low energies and by two photon interactions at higher energies. We derive an analytical expression for the $pp \to Hz$ cross-section through parton-level integration and present $pp$ projection calculations that incorporate various Higgs and $Z$ boson LHC production mechanisms. We also derive an exact $pp$ cross-section formula for the direct decay $H \to aa \to \mu^+\mu^-$. We establish that, despite considerable backgrounds, an $Hz$ signature with an event count of 6.3 (9.6) is anticipated at the 14 TeV LHC with an $Hz$ mass pair of 80-150 GeV and 500-800 events respectively, yielding a notable 95% confidence level (C.L.) exclusion limit for the 2HDM model parameters. Furthermore, our theoretical constraints on the 2HDM model will be compared with existing constraints derived from various other experiments. We also present a novel approach for constructing a 2HDM rate model that accurately replicates Higgs and $Z$ boson experimentally observed rates at 8 and 13 TeV. To advance the creativity of future artificial intelligence researchers, there's a pressing need for materials that can be easily reconfigured. There's still a significant knowledge gap in developing automated agents that can not only create, but also discover, the building blocks of these adaptable materials. By assuming the existence of a 'designer's knowledge' that defines how atoms are arranged in a stable structure, our research focuses on developing an algorithm that guides exploration. This exploration aims to identify the most basic structural components consistent with the designer's knowledge, and also maximizes their combined cost-effectiveness. Through the use of a simulated environment based on 3D molecular structures, we've demonstrated that the agent can effectively discover sets of directed self-assembling peptides that meet specific criteria, and do so at a speed comparable to a manually designed search. Even when the agent is allowed to freely explore without pre-defined goals, it's capable of discovering novel directed self-assembling peptides. Additionally, we've found that the agent's discoveries are influenced by certain key variables, such as the type of movement allowed, the measures used to evaluate its performance, and the structure of the material at a high-level, or'superstructure'. This suggests the potential for the development of more efficient search algorithms tailored to specific designs, and also raises important considerations for the design of future exploratory materials that can adapt to uncertain environments. Prior research has primarily focused on directed material assembly, and there's a significant difference in the two approaches. Our research marks the first time that an algorithm has been used to explore and identify sets of exploratory materials that can adapt to uncertain environments. By leveraging a modified version of our existing automated agent, we've demonstrated that it's capable of discovering novel exploratory materials that can adapt to changing environments. These discoveries were made through an unbiased search in a simulated environment based on 3D molecular structures that is similar to past studies on directed material assembly. However, our research differs from these studies as it's capable of exploring and identifying sets of exploratory materials that cannot generate stable structures on their own from random monomers. Instead, our research identifies sets of materials that can adapt to changing environments and generate specific structural components from random molecules. These differences are largely due to various performance metrics that are consistent with common goals in an automated search for exploratory materials that can adapt to changing environments. These results raise significant moral and ethical considerations and suggest the need for a comprehensive framework that can evaluate the transparency and accountability of complex automated search systems. Our research lays the groundwork for the development of search algorithms

anomaly constraints for the different vacua, which can then be compared in multiple 
orientifold configurations in the context of four-dimensional SU(Nc) gauge theories 
with the presence of geometrically defined flux. It has been found that there are 
two types of symmetric confining vacua, which both satisfy the anomaly constraints 
in various scenarios: one is realized in the standard UV completion of the orientifold 
theory and the other in the QCD-like vacua with the exceptional symmetry point. 
Notably, in the large Nc limit, the flavor symmetric vacua maintain their distinct 
character even in the presence of Seesaw type I inflationary dynamics. 
Despite matching the anomaly constraints, two proposed solutions in the literature 
have been found to fail in the large Nc limit: one with the exceptional symmetry 
and the other in the SU(Nf) maximal chiral gauging. However, the flavor symmetry 
in both the maximal and minimal orientifolding scenarios with SU(Nf) matter meets 
the flavor anomaly constraints in the large Nc limit. The added flavor, in this 
case, enables the orientifold theory to maintain its flavor symmetry in the large 
Nc limit. 
The unique property in the minimal orientifolding scenario of SU(Nf) matter 
resulting in the flavor symmetry in the large Nc limit can be attributed to 
the SU(Nf) symmetry breaking induced by the geometrically defined flux 
$\pm$ $M_5$. However, in the absence of $M_5$ flux, it has been found that

even at the Planck scale. Conversely, in the other large Nc limit 
of the maximal orientifolding scenario with SU(Nf) matter, it has been found 
that the symmetry can be broken below the M/string scale due to 
the presence of a 3-form flux $M_3$ $-$ $M_5$. As a result, in this 
configuration, the symmetry emerges approximately at low energies.

Developing robust language models for real-world applications depends heavily on the ability to comprehend rare words. Although existing language models utilize contextualized representations for common words, they often struggle with rare words due to an inadequate understanding. This paper proposes an innovative rare word representation model, which uses a unique blend of both global and local context dependencies. By leveraging the global context dependencies, the model can analyze a rare word's overall relationship, thereby generating a comprehensive representation. Additionally, the local context dependencies enable the model to consider the dynamic interactions between nearby words. Experimental evaluations on the SST and AGNEWS datasets demonstrate our model's superiority over comparable methods. Furthermore, by incorporating this rare word representation into the existing language models, the results show a notable improvement in their overall performance. We have made the source code available for research purposes. https://github.com/ggagenc/rare-word-RLBM. Our paper presents an in-depth analysis of our method for those interested in the technical details, while the model can be directly accessed through the HuggingFace Transformers library with the specific identifier 'gagenc-rare-wwm'.

Recently, federated learning has been suggested as a solution to address the challenges posed by data privacy and mobility in edge computing. There are two primary federated learning approaches - horizontal and vertical federated learning. Our study aims to identify the effectiveness of vertical federated learning in privacy, exploring both theoretical and practical aspects of the subject. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and practical attacks, our research delves into whether a server can compile a machine learning model while preserving the privacy of clients in vertical federated learning. Specifically, our experiments involve using private optimization methods to protect against three types of privacy attacks: key leakage, attribute leakage, and label leakage. Our results demonstrate that while some attacks succeed in compromising key leakage and attribute leakage, they fail to succeed in label leakage attacks. Furthermore, our research shows that applying adversarial training provides robustness against key leakage attacks. Ultimately, our findings suggest that vertical federated learning can effectively ensure data privacy, given the appropriate application of theoretical privacy mechanisms. Moreover, our study provides guidance on the practical effectiveness of different privacy-enhancing techniques in vertical federated learning settings. With regards to future work, our research aims to expand on the application of horizontal federated learning in privacy contexts. Existing studies have shown that horizontal federated learning is more vulnerable to privacy attacks than vertical federated learning, and our study aims to identify the effectiveness and practical relevance of privacy-enhancing techniques in that context. Our long-term goal is to offer practitioners and researchers a comprehensive understanding of the benefits and limitations of both vertical and horizontal federated learning in privacy contexts. Our formal publications on the subject will present a detailed analysis and exploration of the subject. Our study's findings have been published in a research paper at IEEE EdgeEC 2020, and our related work involves delving into privacy attacks and countermeasures in both vertical and horizontal federated learning settings. Our research aims to provide the foundation for developing tailored privacy-enhancing solutions and non-critical edge computing applications that are informed by both practical and theoretical contexts. Our study's results show that vertical federated learning is a viable means of achieving private edge computing. Our research is currently being extended to investigate privacy contexts in horizontal federated learning, and our findings indicate that both vertical and horizontal federated learning have unique privacy properties and requirements. Our study aims to offer contributions to the related fields, including the identification of key challenges and opportunities in vertical and horizontal federated learning in privacy contexts. A collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning approach, involving various city departments, is introduced to address a key challenge: how to effectively distribute limited resources for counter-terrorism efforts in a competitive environment where agencies can impose punishments on potential terrorists. The proposed model differentiates it from existing research, which focuses on autonomous counter-terrorism efforts, often under restrictive constraints and one-sided rewards. Instead, our model incorporates multiple stakeholders with unique objectives and rewards, as well as open-world conditions, recognizing that counter-terrorism is a complex, multi-faceted task involving both physical and informational aspects. The proposed model utilizes a multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy that incorporates an attention mechanism, enabling each agency to adaptively allocate resources based on the situation, without the need for pre-defined weight distributions. Simulation results demonstrate the benefits of this cooperative learning approach in achieving optimal counter-terrorism effectiveness, even in the presence of opponents' retaliations. The multi-agent reinforcement learning framework's applicability to real-world scenarios is highlighted through a case study involving a counter-terrorism example, showcasing its potential for addressing complex, multi-objective problems, as well as resource-related challenges in general. Additionally, the model offers opportunities for future expansion, incorporating additional aspects of counter-terrorism and multi-agent learning systems. The proposed model can be further optimized by integrating attack prediction capabilities, a capability particularly important for counter-terrorism tasks. The integration of attack prediction into the multi-agent reinforcement learning framework is explored in detail, recognizing that accurate attack prediction plays a crucial role in the learning process and resource allocation tasks. Simulation results confirm the benefits of incorporating attack prediction in the multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for improved counter-terrorism effectiveness. The effect of varying parameter settings on the learning performance of the proposed model is also examined through a parameter sensitivity analysis, which demonstrates the feasibility of the multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for real-world applications, as well as its potential for addressing complex challenges in different domains. Finally, a comparative case study is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model in various domains, focusing on its ability to adapt to different scenarios and domains. The model's applicability to domain-specific challenges is verified through a set of benchmark problems, as well as its generalizability to other complex domains. The effectiveness of the proposed model in solving multi-objective problems is further validated by lowering the counter-terrorism cost in a domain and increasing the target destruction rate in another domain. Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning and its applications to counter-terrorism tasks are reviewed, as well as the challenges of developing an optimal multi-agent reinforcement learning model for open-world counter-terrorism domains. Graph Neural Networks have achieved remarkable success in semi-supervised node classification. Although many pseudo-labeling methods have been developed to enhance performance, they have a significant drawback: they can hinder the efficacy of the model under adversarial conditions. In response, we introduce SPoD - a novel pseudo-labeling technique that uses a discriminative model to accurately predict labeled and unlabeled nodes simultaneously. By combining these predictions with the original node features, SPoD creates enhanced pseudo-labels that surpass the performance of existing methods. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that SPoD outperforms rival approaches in multiple settings, including real-world datasets and scenarios affected by adversarial attacks. The code for SPoD is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/fchechli/SPoD. Our research findings suggest that traditional pseudo-labeling strategies are not effective in all scenarios and can even degrade the model's effectiveness. Conversely, SPoD is an adaptable and robust semi-supervised node classification framework. The research is notable for exploring the generalization capability of pseudo-labeling methods in the context of Adversarial Semi-Supervised Learning (ASL). The study shows that pseudo-labeling can be an effective technique in ASL as it surpasses several state-of-the-art ASL methods. The findings suggest that pseudo-labeling deserves reevaluation as a category of methods as it can mitigate the adversarial attacks and enhance model robustness in the presence of malicious data. The research contributes a novel classification model called KREF, which utilizes the contrastive learning principle to enhance robustness in the case of corrupted labels. The proposed model achieves impressive results within the ASL domain and demonstrates the efficacy of pseudo-labeling in the context of Adversarial Semi-Supervised Learning. The adversarial testing of pseudo-labeling methods has significant practical value in graph-related machine learning applications where data security is a top priority. The research can be applied to various real-world scenarios where graph-related data is commonly encountered in computer science. The proposed framework has vast potential for application in the feature enhancement of deep networks across various tasks. The study highlights the importance of label quality in the context of graph-related machine learning, and showcases pseudo-labeling as an effective technique for improving model robustness against adverse conditions. The research collected annotations from multiple human sources to create a dataset with disputed labels. This analysis distinguishes weakly and highly doped cuprates based on the symmetry of the superconducting gap, using the gap parameter to characterize the former and the carrier concentration to characterize the latter. In both scenarios, microwave conductivity exhibits an anomalous suppression within a specific frequency range (from the superconducting gap to the charge transfer energy) that has been observed in experiments and is associated with the gap parameter in the weakly doped case and with dipolarons in the highly doped case. This anomalous suppression is contributed to by hole-type dipoles in the undoped case and electron-type dipoles in the doped case. Additionally, the anomalous suppression in the high doping limit shows features that align with experimental results, particularly the suppression of the in-plane conductivity in comparison to the out-of-plane conductivity along specific crystallographic axes. This theoretical framework offers a link between microscopic electron behavior and macroscopic transport properties through the self-consistent self-energy approach. Conversely, in the highly doped case, the presence of these excitations is diminished by the scattering associated with antiferromagnetic fluctuations. This theoretical framework is foundational for future research into the transport properties of cuprate superconductors within the antiferromagnetic, superconducting phase. Furthermore, it is anticipated that similar suppression patterns could be observed in other superconducting systems with similar symmetry properties, such as Bi-2223 and FeSe. Existing approaches rely on making specific assumptions about preference distributions that are difficult to verify. This study proposes a new approach to DST, based on a specific network architecture known as the Attentional Confusion Network Encoder (ACNE). In this approach, each dialogue state is represented by a set of distinct sub-states, allowing the model to better capture potential ambiguities and complexities. By integrating ACNE into existing models, both the simple and complex neural architecture toasters were able to experience enhanced performance, with specific results showing that the use of ACNE increased joint intention accuracy by nearly 3.5 and 2.5 percent, respectively. Furthermore, experiments to determine optimal levels of sub-state precision in ACNE were conducted, leading to the observation that higher sub-state precision can negatively impact model performance when pursued excessively. Finally, the use of ACNE in the context of a related task known as the recognition error compensation strategy was explored and resulted in the observation that ACNE is more effective when used to correct larger rather than smaller recognition errors, with potential gains in joint intention accuracy of up to 3.0 and 2.0 percent for the simple and complex models, respectively. Language models, including those used for hate speech detection, operate within a socio-cultural framework. However, existing models often falter when faced with diverse contexts that may lead to inconsistent performance across different settings. Our study examines the inherent biases of language models, including their capacity to recognize hate speech, by investigating how they handle words with multiple interpretations across various cultures. Our analysis reveals that these models tend to be sensitive to language variations, even when the words are written differently. Additionally, we found that recognition of hate speech by these models often relies on the socio-cultural background. Existing models may inadvertently incorporate and distribute bias as a result, which can lead to lower overall performance. I demonstrate a method for reducing bias in language models by retraining them on data that has been processed to remove bias. Using a refined, bias-reduced dataset, I found that the performance of these models for hate speech detection improved across four tested languages. However, significant gaps in performance still exist due to the inherent limitations of language models. Further research is necessary to address the issue of bias in language models. Our work lays the groundwork for investigating and addressing bias in models through direct examination of their performance using representative data. Our study also contributes to the development of methods for identifying and managing bias in models, which will enable the creation of more reliable hate speech detection models that operate across multiple languages. For a type of communication channel known as the symmtric discrete memoryless channel, researchers have established certain rules that limit how well the channel can be approximated by simpler models, known as inner bounds. Inner bounds help assess how close a channel's performance is to its optimal capabilities. By organizing these rules in a specific order based on how well they match the channel's performance, they can better predict when it's possible to achieve the channel's optimal performance using simple, structured communication methods. However, the inner bounds currently in use often result in suboptimal solutions. This paper addresses this issue by developing new inner bounds for the symmtric discrete memoryless channel that are organized in a sequential manner and are designed to closely approximate the channel's performance. It does this by restructuring a key channel property and introducing a new concept known as the reverse cutset property. This paper also provides examples of communication channels for which the new inner bounds yield significantly better predictions than existing ones. Moreover, it's shown that the new inner bounds can be used to simplify and improve the quality of optimal communication strategies. Specifically, it demonstrates how the new inner bounds can be used to simplify the process of finding optimal strategies for channels with specific properties and provides an alternative, structured communication method that approaches the channel's optimal performance in certain cases. This paper also develops a new classification system for channels based on a specific property and demonstrates that the new inner bounds can be used to simplify the channel's optimal performance by identifying specific subcases where this property applies. This paper provides a complete characterization of a specific type of channel known to have optimal strategies that follow a specific pattern and is known to be difficult to analyze. It shows that the new inner bounds can be used to simplify the analysis of this channel by identifying the specific conditions under which this pattern applies. This paper provides a complete characterization of the specific conditions under which this pattern applies, thereby simplifying the analysis of this channel. This paper derives a key consequence of the new inner bounds for the symmtric discrete memoryless channel, namely that the new inner bounds can be used to simplify the analysis of this channel by identifying specific conditions under which it is possible to achieve the channel's optimal performance using simple, structured communication methods. This paper establishes that the new inner bounds have the following consequence: for the symmtric discrete memoryless channel, if an approximation of the channel's performance, known as a outer bound, is sufficiently accurate then it is possible to achieve the channel's optimal performance using simple, structured communication methods.

Research in this area focuses on identifying and preventing potential risks and threats to data security, including those associated with insider threats. To address this issue, this paper proposes the use of machine learning models to help minimize data exposure through insider threats by analyzing patterns in data usage. By comparing the predicted behavioral patterns of authorized users with their actual behavior, potential anomalies can be identified and flagged as potential threats. The model's reliability is further assessed by comparing its performance with alternative classification models, including KNN and SVM. The integration of this model with existing insider threat detection systems further minimizes data exposure by identifying and mitigating potential threats promptly. The combination of machine learning models and real-world data in healthcare further minimizes data exposure and helps to reduce potential threats and false alarms efficiently and effectively.
