In recent years, research on electronic discovery channels has gained momentum. In this context, a novel discrete-time channel model has been introduced that comprises only two output states. Our analysis demonstrates that the model's accuracy is directly influenced by the characteristics of unamplified communication links, specifically amplification gain and noise variance. A thorough, exhaustive investigation was conducted to thoroughly examine all possible relationships between these factors. A step-by-step mathematical approach was employed to precisely determine the probability distribution of the model, a crucial aspect that has been largely overlooked in the analysis of conventional Gaussian channels. As a result, a precise formula for calculating channel accuracy has been developed, while existing methods often rely on approximate noise statistics. Furthermore, a direct comparison of our proposed model's accuracy with the conventional Gaussian channel has been made under various amplification conditions. Our findings indicate that the model's performance may be insufficient in certain scenarios, specifically when high gain and low noise variance are present. Consequently, a novel iteration method for refining the model's output distribution has been proposed. The process involves finding the most likely distribution that places a high probability on a predefined reference channel. A step-by-step general method for calculating the optimal distribution's parameters has been introduced, while the proposed scheme can be easily extended to model channels with more than two output states. Multiple examples have been used to demonstrate that the proposed method is valid in all cases. A direct comparison of our proposed model's accuracy with the conventional Gaussian channel has been made, revealing that the new method significantly reduces the model estimation error by 72.95%, 85.31%, 87.43%, 89.75%, and 87.59% for signal-to-noise ratios ranging from 0 to 20, respectively. Furthermore, the proposed scheme has been successfully applied to a real-world scenario, specifically, electronic discovery channels where the output voltage is affected by a fault. In this context, a novel iterative algorithm for finding the optimal distribution's parameters has been proposed. The proposed method has been shown to outperform conventional Gaussian-based approaches in this specific application. The research findings and methods have been thoroughly validated through practical experiments. Multi-task learning has a long history in deep learning but remains a major challenge in knowledge-based learning. A significant obstacle is making efficient use of the knowledge to avoid negative effects on performance when inappropriate knowledge is used. A varying amount of knowledge can significantly impact multi-modal learning capabilities, prompting the question of how to utilize knowledge effectively. This study addresses this issue by introducing a method to adaptively regulate the usage of knowledge in a two-stage process involving transforming knowledge into complementary modalities and selecting the most relevant to incorporate into a unified model. Comprehensive experiments on ICDAR2013-15 and PASCAL-11 have confirmed the proposed approach yields better results than existing methods for diverse tasks. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/nthse/ERMQ/tree/main/ermq. Additionally, pre-trained models are available on https://github.com/nthse/ERMQ/tree/main/ermq_models/pretrained. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the role of knowledge modalities in multi-modal learning and suggests considering knowledge modalities as essential components of complex systems to enhance the robustness of multi-modal learning systems. They propose that one achievable goal is achieving robustness by incorporating multiple knowledge modalities, which is a key unexplored area in the field. They posit that one potential outcome of this is removing unnecessary knowledge modalities to realize more efficient learning. A hypothetical learning curve illustrating this concept is provided in Figure 1. According to this hypothesis, one feasible means of achieving robustness is through the removal of unnecessary knowledge modalities, which is supported by experimental evidence demonstrating the eradicability of one knowledge modality in Figure 2. We further suggest that one significant benefit of this is the facilitation of more efficient learning processes. To validate this, we present statistical analysis indicating a positive correlation between the specificities of individual models and the number of knowledge modalities in use, which is visualized in Figure 3. Ultimately, we are confident that one significant potential benefit of this is the induction of more efficient learning processes and we believe that one significant potential outcome of this is the removal of unnecessary multi-task learning complexities, which is an area worthy of further exploration. Our proposed approach utilizes unsupervised machine learning and deep learning to forecast the progression of mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, as assessed by annual cognitive scores from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset. We tested three scenarios, comparing two different types of models: self-organizing maps and convolutional neural networks. The former was developed in the 1990s, while the latter was paired with a digital label to serve as a reference point. Our results indicate that the unsupervised models we developed exhibited comparable performance to the supervised convolutional neural network, with accurate predictions from around 85% to 87% for different timeframes and model configurations. However, the unsupervised models' ability to identify Alzheimer's disease was significantly more challenging, accounting for around 51% to 54% of cases in contrast to the 61% rate of the supervised network. To address this challenge, we developed a second convolutional neural network, trained in a semi-supervised manner using data from ADNI, as well as patients from China's Alzheimer's Disease Project. Ultimately, integrating the unsupervised and semi-supervised models through simple voting resulted in a high overall accuracy of 85%, as well as improved forecasting capabilities from around 80 to 87%, based on different timeframes and model variants. Our study's success offers significant practical implications for the development of personalized Alzheimer's disease treatment plans. This method looks beyond immediate context for clues to determine what constitutes
noise, thus enabling it to capture and mitigate complex, long-term patterns within

underlying patterns, making it suitable for use in scenarios where linear trends

Our research focuses on how spin-orbit coupling influences the point of a Mott transition in two-dimensional systems with d electrons, taking into account the interplay between doping and spin-orital effects. We delved into the impact of SO coupling on the resistivity and Seebeck coefficient within the vicinity of a Mott transition in two-dimensional metals with d electrons, taking into account the limits of small and large SO coupling, slightly understating the strength of SO coupling in real-world scenarios. We observed that within the relevant SO coupling range, the turning points of SO-induced effects occur near the point of a Mott transition that is modified by carrier doping. Moreover, the carrier doping modifies the effective SO coupling in comparison to its intrinsic value, specifically increasing SO coupling when doping electrons but decreasing it when doping holes. Our key conclusion arises from comprehensive numerical calculations via a SO extended one-dimensional model through a finite-dimensionally deformed Clauser-Reatto-Mattis-Rashba Hamiltonian. We derived a set of renormalized effective model parameters in two states - a metallic state near the point of a Mott transition and a metallic state with high SO coupling, thereby leveraging the scaling of the t' t t' coupling in the latter. We ultimately derived the temperature-dependent Seebeck coefficient in both states, thereby constraining the SO coupling in 2D materials with high accuracy. Our findings also demonstrate that the principle of Flouquet et al. for describing the trend of SO coupling in the vicinity of a Mott transition may be altered based on whether we consider particle or hole doping, with the former requiring a larger doping level to occur than the latter. Our key contributions comprise i) a revised summary of the many-body effects of SO coupling in the limit of weak to moderate SO coupling in 2D systems with a two-dimensional representation of SO coupling in the free Fermion model; ii) a new three-dimensional scaling of the interlayer SO coupling in the free Fermion model, thereby extending the theory to two-dimensional systems with a two-dimensional representation of SO coupling in the free Fermion model; iii) a novel extension of the theory to two-dimensional systems with a two-dimensional representation of SO coupling in the free Fermion model; and iv) a novel extension of the theory to two-dimensional systems with a two-dimensional representation of SO coupling in the free Fermion model. A novel approach for assessing the performance of black-box models in medical imaging is being developed, with a key component being conformal prediction theory's output - conformal intervals. This method's usefulness in imaging is hindered due to its high computational requirements. To overcome this limitation, we have created the conformal net, a neural network that generates conformal intervals, with the ability to be trained alongside other models for prediction purposes. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of the conformal net in estimating prediction intervals for 1) automatic segmentation of brain tumors and 2) brain lesion detection tasks using imaging datasets. Results show that the computational time for computing conformal intervals on large datasets is significantly reduced with the conformal net's implementation, enabling more accurate uncertainty analysis and performance evaluation of white-box segmentation models. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexrichter21/conformal-net. This project highlights the utility of conformal prediction for future assessment and evaluation tasks in medical imaging. To this end, we suggest an evaluation framework similar to the Q-score to quantify the quality of a model's prediction capability, especially useful for noisy inputs where reliable prediction is not feasible. Additionally, we have demonstrated the potential application of conformal prediction and the Q-score in estimating the uncertainty of clinical models, such as those used for calculating 95% marginal expected frequency scores in computer-aided diagnosis systems. The proposed scores - conformal Q and operator Q - outperform existing marginal expected frequency estimation methods, showcasing the utility of conformal prediction in the evaluation of operational models. The ongoing search for extraterrestrial life centers on identifying DNA and RNA structures that are both widespread on our planet. There's a growing need to apply bioinformatics tools to analyze these complex molecular patterns. The majority of existing software, including the well-known Nick program, utilizes an energy-driven approach to investigate DNA and RNA configurations. However, this traditional method is limited in its ability to account for nucleic acid deformations, making it less effective for certain types of structures. In contrast, our proposed algorithm, the RBB-NA method, takes a unique, efficient approach to accounting for these deformations. The RBB-NA method takes as input a sequence, a stem-loop structure, and a set of constraints to determine the most favorable configuration, considering both energy and geometric constraints. To test the performance of the RBB-NA algorithm, we compared it to Nick for four different scenarios. The results showed that the RBB-NA algorithm consistently yielded equivalent or better outcomes than Nick for a variety of DNA and RNA structures. Given its efficient approach, our algorithm allows for the in-depth study of complex nucleic acid deformations. We have demonstrated this capability by using the RBB-NA algorithm to investigate a range of DNA and RNA types. The findings from these experiments are presented in detail. Previous approaches, however, have failed to yield bit-counts directly correlated with the precision requirements, necessitating, extra calculations for determining output bit-length. A recent variant of range ANS achieved some degree of correlation but still incurred additional steps. In this work, a revised ANS variant is presented for performing integer divisions with fixed accuracy in binary strings, closely related to the \lceil y/2^{k+1}\rceil, where parameters $k$ and $y$ can be adjusted. For any given value of $y$, the revised method facilitates efficient division with minimal extra bits, thus enhancing overall efficiency. We demonstrate that our approach compares favorably to related techniques previously proposed for division operations. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of the revised ANS variant in minimizing output bit-length for integer division operations. These outcomes illustrate that minimal extra bits are saved during the process, which in turn leads to the reduction of bit-counts required for encoding in comparison to earlier methods. In addition to the revised method, the output bit-length in the revised ANS variant is found to be directly related to the precision requirements. The dielectric property is frequently utilized as a indicator to monitor concrete structures' state, as it is closely linked to moisture content, which is closely associated with the performance of the structure. For instance, detecting delaminations in composite materials is a significant application of dielectric property monitoring. In this paper, the dielectric property measurement technique is analyzed and categorized. Subsequently, an experimental investigation comparing various time-domain and frequency-domain techniques is conducted, utilizing a Material Measurement Center Dielectric Property Characterization System. The experiment's findings demonstrate that dielectric property models can be accurately represented using various analysis methods. Nonetheless, utilizing a model-based analysis approach tends to yield more accurate results in comparison to time-domain or frequency-domain representations alone. Consequently, utilizing a model-based analysis approach leads to more accurate retrievals of material parameters as compared to time-domain or frequency-domain approaches alone. The findings of this experiment demonstrate that utilizing a correct dielectric property representation results in a more accurate estimation of material parameters. The most effective extraction method among those evaluated is found to be utilizing a model-based approach as it yields either the lowest or a low RMSE in comparison to other extraction methods investigated. The outcomes of this research also demonstrate that almost identical material parameter extraction can be achieved regardless of whether analysis is performed in the time domain, frequency domain, or a combination of both. An important finding is observed in which utilizing a model-based approach as compared to utilizing either time-domain or frequency-domain representations alone results in approximately $3.53\times10^{-11}$ as a bound on the difference in extracted parameters. Furthermore, among the compared methods, analyzing the dielectric property in the time domain is shown to yield results that are either equivalent to or slightly better than frequency-domain analyses in terms of accuracy. An observed trend suggests that analyzing the dielectric property in the time domain is slightly more sensitive than frequency-domain analysis. This research aims to contribute towards improving the understanding and development of dielectric property analysis and extraction methods. The extracted material parameter time-series data is made publicly accessible to facilitate future research in this area. The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules is considered natural due to their underlying principles, which are widely recognized and well-established. The potential existence of various types of these molecules, such as $TX-Q\bar{Q}N$ (featuring a tetraquark component $TX$ and a diquark $Q\bar{Q}$ with color triplet and quartet properties, respectively), is being explored. Notably, a composite hexaquark molecule formed by three quarks and one antiquark is also being investigated in theoretical studies. In particular, certain composite hexaquarks, such as $S U c \bar{D} c$, are found to be stable up to a few hundred MeV when analyzed within the context of the relativistic quasipotential method and considered within the approach of heavy quarks. The properties of these composite hexaquarks can be categorized into various types, such as hexaquarks with two dibaryons combined and those featuring symmetrical quark distributions in space. The diversity of composition for these molecules may result in diverse properties, such as masses, spacings, and decay behaviors. The existence of composite hexaquarks is anticipated to be confirmed through future high-energy hadron colliders, which are expected to operate at a lower energy compared to those required for heavy-heavy meson-meson molecules. The study of these composite hexaquarks can provide insights into their unique formation processes and contribute to our understanding of their structural characteristics at the quark-gluon level. The potential for new physics can be explored by analyzing the decays of these composite hexaquarks, which may occur more rarely in nature compared to other types of hadronic systems. The theoretical approach for studying heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, which includes both experimental and theoretical aspects, is expected to be applicable to the study of composite hexaquarks, thus enhancing our understanding of these complex systems. The study of composite hexaquarks in particular can facilitate a deeper understanding of the internal structure of hadrons and the development of new theoretical methods to describe these complex systems. The exploration of composite hexaquarks can also lead to new avenues in the investigation of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at the limits of its applicability, which may reveal novel properties and phenomena unique to these systems at the quantum level. The theoretical description of composite hexaquarks can be refined through approaches such as QCD sum rules and relativistic quasipotential method, which are both expected to provide valuable insights into the properties of these complex systems

A Boltzmann machine's dynamics and parameters significantly influence its system complexity. We investigated the time evolution of system complexity in a Boltzmann machine using the mutual information between its hidden and visible units, which increases initially and then decreases as the network adjusts. By examining the time derivative of this information, we analyzed the phase space of a Boltzmann machine to understand the complex adaptation process. Our results provide insight into the optimal parameter range that maximizes information flow and minimizes energy function changes. Furthermore, we found that this information peaks within the symmetric parameter range and then declines as the network adjusts, which aligns with previous observations of information flow in Boltzmann machines. By applying our information measure to a simple vision task, we observed that it identifies the robust learning phase where the network accurately represents key features. Overall, our information analysis offers valuable insights into the complex behavior of Boltzmann machines during their initial learning stages. As information theory is a powerful tool for analyzing and understanding complex systems, we discuss its potential to improve Boltzmann machine training and provide systematic insights into the complex dynamics leading to its stable configuration. Moreover, we identify future research directions that could utilize information theory to correct current drawbacks in many-body methods. Lastly, we make the source code available to study other machine learning models through open-source analysis. We hope that this information will pave the way for future research in the field. This research investigates a multi-variable extension to the series of Carlsson and Johansson's 'algebraic semi-groups'. We find that certain infinite series resulting in $C^\infty$ functions can converge under a Holder condition when the common denominator and numerator share a uniform bound, which can be illustrated by providing an example with a bounded Holder coefficient. Similarly, we identify a condition under which the series yields a $C^\infty$ function that meets a Lipschitz condition. Furthermore, we examine C*-algebras generated by these infinite series and establish isomorphism with Crosbie and Kachuk's cross products of C*-algebras. We also demonstrate that these cross products can be created through the infinite series, providing a direct, initial representation of certain C*-algebras. Additionally, this study converges to an earlier result linking $\mathbb{C}^2$-valued functions and matrix C*-algebras, initially explored by Brion and Spector. As a starting point in a broader study, the following research is positioned as a prelude to a larger investigation, specifically as a precursor to the 'polynomial version'. Specifically, it examines how the performance of a speech recognition system decreases when its training and testing environments become more dissimilar. This environmental shift is comparable to a topic shift, which is defined as a change in the distribution of training transcripts. Our findings also reveal that the system's ability to handle speaker variation is comparable to its ability to handle topic variation. Moreover, it is observed that the system's diversity can be either a benefit or a hindrance, depending on the context. Finally, the paper suggests that modeling individual core ideas within a topic could enhance the system's ability to adapt to new topics and maintain consistency even in the face of significant changes in language. Compared to models trained solely with in-domain data, our results show significant improvements in performance for text classification tasks on out-of-domain datasets. Specifically, our method achieved a 9.5% absolute F1-score increase over traditional methods when applied to the SST-2 dataset. Additionally, our results show that using task-specific data augmentation strategies greatly impacts the iterative training process, enabling it to successfully generalize to out-of-domain data, whereas task-agnostic methods fail to achieve this breakthrough. We provide theoretical analysis and supporting evidence from our experiments. We also introduce a task-specific permutation technique known as Balancing Permutation that particularly benefits the SST-2 dataset, providing the current state-of-the-art with F1 = 87.8% when applied to the SST-2 test set. Hastie and Tibshirani argued that neural networks with multiple hidden layers are capable of representing kernel machines of higher order, such as polynomial and rational kernels. They suggested adding an extra layer to replicate these kernels would enhance interpretability. In a surprising move, Liao and Paulsen took this idea further by showing a single hidden layer in a neural network is enough to express any kernel type. Nonetheless, implementing these kernels using a traditional neural network is often impractical, which is why researchers proposed using neural tangent kernels (NTKs) as an alternative. NTKs can effectively express kernels based on a closed-form solution, making them trainable. In our study, we leveraged the concept of NTKs to develop an algorithm for determining and training linear NTKs over R^n. The method we established extends the concept to determining and training multi-layer perceptrons. The key takeaway from this research is that NTKs offer a level of interpretability not found with other deep learning models, and we have provided an innovative approach to handling the challenge. Additionally, we demonstrated that NTKs can be applied successfully in classification and regression problems, as shown through synthetic and real-world data experiments. In these tests, our model achieved results on par with standard deep learning techniques, opening up the possibility of incorporating NTKs in feature mapping to boost the overall performance of machine learning tasks. The accompanying code for this research can be found at https://github.com/teigonn/ntk-kernel-learning. Overall, our study marks the first successful implementation of kernel learning using NTKs and provides insights that can contribute to understanding the capabilities of deep neural networks. As an added benefit, our research revealed a connection between neural networks and Kiefer's uniform distribution, explored in depth in the appendices of the study. The findings regarding gradient descent on polynomial NTKs over R^n are presented in the preprint paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10237, while a companion paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.15475 delves into the application of NTKs to graph data. In the final section, we outlined future areas of investigation related to these problems. This effect varies based on specific trait combinations and is influenced by how much each trait contributes to the overall competence perception. Previous research found Stress, Loudness, and Jitter have a significant impact on competence perception but their interactions remain unclear. This study investigated how mixing levels of these traits within optimal values for each alone affects competence perception in a female voice and revealed that convex combinations significantly influence how competent a generated voice is perceived. Through a listening test, it was discovered that averaging the optimal values for each individual trait results in a voice deemed less competent compared to optimizing the combination of those traits. Furthermore, our results suggest that there is an upper limit to how competent a female voice can be perceived to be, which is beyond what can be achieved by adjusting the level of Stress, Loudness, and Jitter within optimal ranges for each trait alone. This women's voice synthesis system, designed for maximized competence, differs significantly from systems optimized for friendliness or neutrality. The distribution of stress, loudness, and jitter levels in this competence-optimized system are outside the typical range found in human speech, underscoring challenges in simultaneously achieving multiple perception goals. Recent research has highlighted the importance of change detection in various fields like agriculture and risk analysis, where it helps identify subtle changes in the environment. Most existing methods fall into two main categories: supervised and unsupervised techniques. Supervised methods tend to detect changes more accurately, but they demand a substantial amount of labeled data which can be costly to obtain. On the other hand, unsupervised methods are often less effective and rely solely on intrinsic characteristics of data, limiting their performance across diverse scenarios. In an effort to bridge this gap, a new approach is proposed which integrates concepts from pixel embedding and normalizing flows to automatically detect changes. This approach utilizes two distinct processes, each handling a different type of data, and employs a deep normalizing flow to map images from one domain to another. Experiment results indicate that the proposed method outperforms normal unsupervised approaches and approaches that rely on limited supervised data. Additionally, it offers a unique visual analysis tool to study the dynamics of scenes. This method has promising applications in diverse fields and can be used to analyze multiple modalities of data. A public demonstration of the project can be found at https://s-faez.github.io/ChangeFlow/. The project's source code is also publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/S-Faez/ChangeFlow. Our research suggests that normalizing flows may be utilized for a broader range of applications beyond change detection. Furthermore, the proposed method opens up possibilities for decision-making tasks in multi-domain scenarios. Ultimately, the goal is to develop advanced techniques for change detection and analysis using machine learning. The research was made possible through funding from the NASA grant number 80HQSGW051. Quantum Theory, the current standard for describing physical phenomena, is known for exhibiting nonlocal properties. This nonlocality has been primarily studied through the principles of counter-factual measurements and measurement independence. This research examines nonlocality in all classical theories without assuming measurement independence and introduces a new concept - the nonlocality of counter-factual measurements. This new concept redefines the nonlocality of classical theories and offers a more comprehensive understanding. In exploring theories that are classical in their input states, we demonstrate that most existing nonlocality arguments against them are invalid. This research also provides a comprehensive set of criteria that distinguish the quantum realm from the classical realm based on nonlocality principles alone. This research addresses an open question in the field by showing that classical theories can be formulated to prevent nonlocality derived from the principles of counter-factual measurements, while a collective disturbance theory is formulated to prevent nonlocality derived from the principles of measurement independence. This research further provides a new set of criteria that differentiate the quantum realm from the classical realm through the application of a quantum-like disturbance theory. This research ultimately implies that nonlocality derived from the principles of counter-factual measurements cannot distinguish the quantum realm from the classical realm, and a theory of quantum mechanics without nonlocality, in principle, is theoretically possible. The ever-growing complexity and capabilities of neural networks increasingly compromise latency and resource consumption, making them impractical for deployment on devices such as smart speakers, tablets, and wearable devices. This research explores how memory usage, computational demands, and architectural design elements including pruning, quantization, and dimensionality reduction impact neural network deployment on devices with limited capabilities. By integrating these narrative reviews with experimental findings, this study investigates the trade-offs among memory, computation, latency, and accuracy in neural networks and discusses the feasibility of modern neural networks on platforms like speakers and head-mounted displays. Crucially, this research identifies potential hurdles in implementing deep neural networks on low-resource devices and outlines necessary advancements for their successful deployment. Based on these insights, this study proposes novel low-resource efficient neural networks combining dimensionality reduction, pruning, and few-parameter approaches, which demonstrate exceptional performance under strict resource constraints: fewer parameters than recent network designs with comparable accuracy while reducing computational complexity and achieving competitive accuracy on platforms with limited resources. The proposed methods are implemented using the Tensorflow framework, and our findings demonstrate that AlexNet dimensionality reduction and pruning yields 0.73 bits per parameter, 33% fewer FLOPs, 1.16% lower top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet dataset than the recently designed SuperNet with 1 million parameters. The new network design produced on average 58% fewer parameters (0.56 MP), 80% fewer FLOPs, and 4.64% lower top-1 accuracy than the efficient recently-proposed PNRNet with 0.56 million parameters. Notably, this study demonstrates that pruning followed by dimensionality reduction outperforms the reverse order, and some interesting insights and patterns are highlighted in the accompanying results section. The proposed models are available online at https://github.com/guennaki/efficientnn. Moreover, this research contributes a comprehensive survey of recent advances in neural network efficientization by applying dimension reduction techniques. The results are shared at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U8rws1Zj_D8. Last but not least, this research proposes a new taxonomy and terminology joining both system architects and machine learning engineers' perspectives and opinions on the topic of model efficiency. Notably, the conditions for chimeras to exist become similar to those found in Kurvaish and Barahona's original study when comparing systems with a small vs. large number of coupled oscillators. Quantum shadow tomography is a novel, efficient method to reconstruct a complex quantum system's properties using an adaptive measurement strategy. This strategy allows for optimal estimation of a specific target property without a prior understanding of the system's state. We examine shadow tomography for a collection of identically prepared quantum systems and develop maximum likelihood estimators to track the average shift in the target property as multiple measurements are taken. Unlike traditional state tomography which often requires measuring all systems, shadow tomography can skip or utilize only a subset of the ensemble, depending on the measurements taken. Our analysis makes shadow tomography more practical for utilizing weak, low-count measurements typical of near-term devices. We find in the scenario where each system contains a single photon in a multi-mode Gaussian state, the performance gains from utilizing the full ensemble are modest, but we expect the benefits to be greater for more complex quantum circuits producing fewer photons. Shadow tomography may be particularly beneficial for measurements constrained by these near-term resources. The method we introduced can also be applied to other quantum systems. 

Keywords: shadow tomography, quantum state estimation, Gaussian quantum states, near-term quantum devices.

Endofullerenes, situated at the core of both cyborg and artificial bacteria, are unique in being enclosed by inorganic shells on biosystems. By substituting these with metal shells, researchers strive to comprehend how these inorganic compositions affect the inherent properties of the internal carbon nanostructures. In our theoretical investigation, we examined how specific surface metals influence the conformation, magnetic behaviour, and electrical properties of the carbon framework within a silicate empty fullerenelike structure. Our results show that the shape of the carbon framework is heavily influenced by the shape of the enclosing shell and external surface metals, while also exhibiting some variability due to molecular spin systems. An in-depth, atom-specific investigation revealed direct correlations between the conformation, magnetic and electrical properties of the carbon framework and the metals surrounding it. Specifically, our findings suggest that carbon framework properties can be directly modified through the introduction of additional metal shells. Ultimately, our research highlights that controlling the arrangement of external surface metals can a effective means of tailoring the inherent carbon framework properties. The inherent connections between the conformation, magnetic and electrical properties of the carbon framework and the metals surrounding it may open up the possibility of precision engineering these unique carbon structures. Precision engineering may be applied to various practical uses including the manipulation of magnetic and electrical signals, the modification of carbon framework properties through the introduction of a second metal shell, or the control of carbon framework shape via the arrangement of multiple metal shells. Our investigation lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the inherent properties of carbon nanostructures within metal shell fullerenes and their potential uses.

We apply this technique to both a low-fidelity qubit and a two-qubit system, comparing its performance to two other search strategies - a heuristic adaptive approach and a random design protocol. The simulation reveals that the Bayesian design strategy achieves significant improvements over the heuristic adaptive strategy, particularly for the two-qubit case where it also outperforms the random design protocol. However, for the low-fidelity qubit, the random design protocol exhibits comparable performance to the Bayesian design. The reasons for these trends are discussed through sensitivity analysis and examination of the posterior uncertainty. Additionally, we investigate how the Bayesian design's gain in performance varies with the accuracy of the low-fidelity Hamiltonian. Ultimately, the results suggest that the Bayesian design strategy is beneficial for optimizing two-qubit interferometry but may not be necessary for precise measurements of low-fidelity qubits. This work offers a promising approach for improving the efficiency of high-fidelity qubit operations and may have potential in driving up conversion efficiency in quantum fourier transforms. Furthermore, potential sources of underperformance in the Bayesian design are discussed and possible methods for mitigating these issues are explored. These potential drawbacks include model inaccuracies in the Bayesian method and incomplete exploration of the search space. Future work could focus on addressing these limitations and applying the Bayesian design strategy to more complex scenarios such as multi-mode interferometry.

Using the jet dual of the Faber Theorem, we establish a Griffiths positivity conjecture for forms of positive characteristic by linking it to the positivity of polynomials in specific Chern forms, a phenomenon previously observed over complex number fields by Griffiths. We derive various polynomials expressing Chern forms, having distinct degrees, which ultimately leads to multiple instances of polynomial positivity. Subsequently, by linking these polynomials to the positivity of Chern forms, specifically the second Chern form $c_2$, we conclude that $c_2$ is positive for minimal projective surfaces in positive characteristic, thereby resolving a long-standing open problem posed by Griffiths. Furthermore, our approach also enables us to prove the positivity of the Beauville-Wei Chern forms for surfaces, as well as establish an analog of Narasimhan's conjecture for minimal curves in positive characteristic. The proof relies heavily on the construction of a non-degenerate meromorphic function, an approach originally proposed by Griffiths, along with an application of classical polynomial theory results from the works of Polya-Szegö and others. We are proud to offer the first direct proof of several characteristic-dependent results known to be true, while also addressing some previously unproclaimed conjectures. We are confident that our approach can be utilized in the positive characteristic complex setting to address several open problems there as well. We analyzed the prevalence of tidal features in tidal disruption events affecting early-type galaxies. This analysis is based on a dataset of quasi-solar tidal features found within a subset of galaxies from the Galaxy Zoo project. Our research focuses on 220,000 galaxies from the General Catalogue of Galactic Structures. We utilized tidal features' geometry to recognize and extract tidal disruption events and then quantified the prevalence of these features in galaxies of different stellar masses. Our results show a clear relationship between tidal features' prevalence and galaxy mass: a notable 25% of low-mass galaxies contain these features, but this number drops to around 3% for high-mass galaxies. Additionally, a study on galaxy pairs shows that features resulting from tidal interactions are more extensive compared to those observed in single galaxies or as part of larger galaxy systems. These findings support a model where tidal features' persistence decreases as the mass of the galaxy increases. This contrasts with the idea that tidal features' persistence is tied to their original size. Neither theory fully explains the features' observed persistence in low-mass galaxies. This discrepancy may be due to the complexity of how tidal features interact with their surroundings or the relatively small current understanding of how these features' original characteristics influence their persistence. It is possible that low-mass galaxies' relatively small tidal features lead to fewer issues with their surroundings, resulting in their observed persistence. An investigation into the timeframes in which tidal features fade could provide more significant insights into this phenomenon's underlying nature. An accompanying catalogue containing information on 2,811 tidal features can be accessed through the Catalogue of Nearest Galaxies platform. Our research contributes to a broader understanding of how tidal features interact with their surroundings once their original structure has faded. Potential volunteers can sign up at https://zoo.mastervisionuah.edu.mx/volunteer/. In this revised interpretation, the radiation difficulty, typically encountered by massive celestial bodies during their formation phase, is resolved. Additionally, specific mathematical equations governing the behavior of massive objects are derived and analyzed, confirming that their behavior conforms with established observational criteria. Furthermore, the computational methods developed for use in GR can also be applied in the ASTG context. As such, the results obtained are comparable to those generated by other modified radiation problem studies within the ASTG framework. We observe that the constant and linearly increasing mass sources, commonly applied in similar analyses, do not exert uniform influence on the radiation zone characteristics. Specifically, when using a mass source with constant properties, the radiation zone dimensions are found to be in direct proportion to both the source parameters and the radial distance from the source, whereas a linearly changing mass source is found to impact the radiation zone properties in a manner analogous to a static electric dipole. It is worth noting that within the ASTG framework, the radiation difficulty is resolved and the radiation zones are found to be uniformly filled with radiation. We derive the general equation governing massive object motion under radiation field influence in terms of the ASTG theory and analyze specific motion modes, including rectilinear and elliptical paths. To simulate laser pulses with specific characteristics, it's crucial to accurately model laser systems used for various applications, including those employing CPA (Chirped Pulse Amplification) technology. Due to the complex interaction of multiple components (amplifiers, crystals, waveguides, and others) in CPA systems, traditional models often fall short. To overcome this limitation, a unified model has been developed that combines the descriptions of individual components with a unique numerical scheme. This new model has been successfully applied to an experimental setup and has greatly improved predictive accuracy compared to previous models. Specifically, the modified model achieved a level of accuracy equivalent to measuring experimental outcomes, resulting in precise agreements in multiple metrics. Building upon established individual component models, the enhanced numerical scheme allows for accurate simulations of laser systems employing nonlinear optical amplification, an important advancement in modeling applications. To facilitate confidence in its results, the model's various assumptions and complexity were evaluated, confirming its effectiveness in modeling nonlinear processes. This two-wave representation of complex laser pulses was shown to be an efficient and precise method for simulating nonlinear interactions, an important discovery in theoretical modeling. To expand its scope, the model has also been applied to a laser system used for generating few-cycle laser pulses and achieved agreements with experimental measurements of pulse metrics, further affirming its usefulness in modeling specialized laser systems. Consequently, the precision of simulated photonic processes has also been substantially improved. We introduce Delegated RingCT, a RingCT upgrade with significant scalability benefits. Delegated RingCT assigns a publicly chosen "delegate" to create and distribute TXs for users, enhancing transaction speed. This upgrade also promotes user engagement through simple TX creation processes and publicly disseminated rewards. Our experiments demonstrate Delegated RingCT's ability to conceal TX values while maintaining an average transaction time of 0.22 seconds, at a cost of 0.44 BCH. This upgrade is compatible with Bitcoin Private and can be seamlessly integrated into its ecosystem. Our analysis confirms that Delegated RingCT does not violate Bitcoin's rules and can coexist with existing nodes. Additionally, we conducted a community vote using a BP token to determine the delegate in a decentralized manner. Our results show that the Delegated RingCT model can effectively determine the delegate in a timely and efficient manner. Furthermore, we compare Delegated RingCT's revenue with Synergies' simple RingCT solution, revealing that the former generates approximately 185% more revenue in a year. To promote mainstream adoption, Delegated RingCT was presented to the Bitcoin Private Development team and successfully implemented on the Bitcoin Private Mainnet on June 1, 2019. Upon its implementation, the first delegate was chosen through a community vote using SYRN tokens. As of July 2019, the current delegate is chosen via BP token vote, providing users with the option to vote for their desired delegate using Bitcoin Private. Our analysis showcases the effectiveness of Delegated RingCT and its potential to accelerate Bitcoin Private transactions. As the Delegated RingCT upgrade has already been integrated into Bitcoin Private, it can now be used to enhance transaction speed and scalability for both the network and its users. To promote an even smoother user experience, we suggest introducing a TX confirmation timer to balance TX processing speed with network congestion. Our results demonstrate the trade-off between TX speed and network congestion during Delegated RingCT's implementation on Bitcoin Private. As of August 2019, the average block time on Bitcoin Private is 1 minute, with an estimated 420 blocks per hour and 25,200 blocks per hour, resulting in an estimated 4,800 transactions per hour. Combining Delegated RingCT's capabilities with a TX confirmation timer may help mitigate network congestion issues and provide users with faster transaction processing. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an estimated 3-month breakeven period for Delegated RingCT. To accelerate mainstream adoption, we suggest offering discounts to early adopt

Utilizing generative models in medical imaging is becoming a widespread practice. Nonetheless, making use of such models in a clinical setting is hindered by the requirement for extensive annotations, particularly in cases where deep learning techniques struggle to provide accurate results. We have therefore developed a novel, annotation-free framework that enables the generation of realistic training data from unlabelled medical images. Our framework begins with a supervised task of generating image pairs, and then employs a novel method of dissimilarity measurement to fine-tune the generative model through self-supervision. This leads to a significant improvement in the model's performance, as evidenced by our experiments conducted on a dataset of chest X-rays. The results suggest that our approach outperforms standard generative pre-trained models and achieves comparable performance to models trained with annotations. Furthermore, our framework's supravision pathway can be adapted for various generative tasks without requiring annotated data. We believe that our innovative framework contributes importantly to the growing trend of using generative models in medical imaging. Our code and dataset are publicly available. A fault-tolerant distance label is a vertex label that indicates the shortest distance between two vertices in a graph, with the ability to withstand the occurrence of one edge or vertex failure. We have investigated the existence of such labels in trees and other graph structures, with the goal of achieving an efficient size requirement that does not scale with the square of the number of vertices. A significant contribution of this research is the confirmation that label existence in trees is feasible, with a requirement that is logarithmic in size. In addition, this research highlights that label efficiency in a graph is closely related to its combinatorial properties, including the presence or absence of cycles. Specifically, this is demonstrated by the identification of a family of bipartite trees with no cycles that lack label existence, thereby exhibiting a minimum label efficiency of at least n^2 for all feasible implementations. Furthermore, this research has also explored the existence of fault-tolerant distance labels in a generalized graph structure known as a quasi-tree, with the conclusion that label existence in a quasi-tree is dependent on cycle existence. A comprehensive finding from this research is the presentation of a fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme in a graph that has the specific characteristic of having no cycles, with a requirement that is logarithmic in size. We believe that this research contributes significantly to the field, with a particular emphasis on advancing our understanding of fault-tolerant distance labeling in trees. A full version of this research, with additional details and analysis, is available in a companion paper. We're examining the phenomenon of Floquet heating in a one-dimensional Bose gas that's coupled to a bath. The target is to map out the gas's behavior as parameters change, with a specific focus on how interplay between dissipation and inter-player interactions impacts the gas's thermal properties. To understand the system's response, we start by describing the open system using a quadratic Hamiltonian whose dynamics is normal. The results reveal a new region on the phase diagram characterized by regular Floquet heating that's distinct from both thermal and nonthermal behaviors. The findings also indicate that Floquet heating can lead to remarkable effects such as strong cooling, anomalous thermal properties, and the formation of Bose condensation in places where dissipation is minimal. The system's regular Floquet heating may be leveraged to create novel many-particle quantum states and manipulate the system's ground and thermal states through the injection of energy. The produced states could be challenging to replicate using traditional quench techniques. The system's stability against dissipation implies that Floquet heating can persist even in the presence of dissipation, with the condition that the interactions between particles are not too strong relative to the properties of the bath. The system's behavior could be replicated in experiments with two-mode Bose-Josephson junctions that interact with environments comprising a mix of superconducting qubits and cavities. This distinction dictates $\alpha$'s position relative to 1 as follows: if $\alpha > 1$, the function is in $W^{1,p}$, but if $\alpha \leq 1$, it is not. A specific condition involving $\alpha$ and $p$ serves as the boundary that separates these two scenarios. A later part of the talk explores a particular scenario within Muckenhoupt theory where $\alpha$ is close to 0. Here, the condition it satisfies can be seen as an alternative to the $\beta$ condition first introduced by Muckenhoupt. This particular class of functions is linked to convex functions, specifically those in $W^{1,p}$, and in a larger class known as $A_p$ when $p > 1$. This property stems from the functions being log-concave and was initially explored by Almgren in 1988, but was later revisited by Fu and Kennedy who removed the restriction to convex functions. A comprehensive review of the results will be presented in this talk. A particular question remains open and may be resolved by the application of an additional geometric condition first identified by Chau, Chen, and Zhang. When considering only the system's state evolution, these detectors act as instruments that can either enhance or diminish precision. However, taking into account the full measurement process reveals precise, non-zero minimum uncertainties in the clock signals, which are consistently below their corresponding deterministic limits. To determine the optimal detector operation, we establish the maximum achievable precision as an objective to be optimized through the identification of an effective optimal gain for the photon counter. This gain surpasses the square root of 1/2 as the optimal value, surpassing previous findings. Ultimately, our analysis involves examining the relationship between the clock's precision and its inherent, quantum-based characteristics as well as its inherent, non-conservative dynamics. Moreover, our investigation delves into the connection between the photon counter's measured rate in the number of photons and the system's quantum state purity, providing additional insight into quantum dynamics. Additionally, we develop a metric to quantify nonclassality in the clock signals based on the quantum purity and develop a method to extract the nonclassical aspect from the measured distributions. This paper presents a novel online energy-efficient multi-path routing strategy known as OFES. By combining energy efficiency and packet delivery ratio, a new cost function is designed to optimize the parameter alpha. Following this optimization, the parameters alpha and beta are dynamically updated to facilitate online optimization of the cost function through the application of the Multipath Single-path Opportunistic Routing (MOR) algorithm. Consequently, a heuristic version of OFES, termed HFES, is developed to maximize the number of packets delivered to the destination. A comparison between the simulated results of OFES and HFES with those of MOR, as well as Sequential Path Selection (SPS), shows that HFES significantly enhances packet delivery ratio while online variants of OFES outperform SPS in achieving better energy consumption and reliability ratios. Notably, the time required by HFES to achieve its optimal performance is approximately 130 seconds for 20 nodes, 140 seconds for 25 nodes, 155 seconds for 30 nodes, 170 seconds for 35 nodes, 190 seconds for 40 nodes, 210 seconds for 45 nodes, 230 seconds for 50 nodes, 240 seconds for 55 nodes. In this research, we delve into the image retrieval task using deep metrics learning, where a significant drawback is the inefficient use of pair-wise loss gradient decomposition. Therefore, we have developed a novel strategy, referred to as the gradient decomposition distribution strategy (GDDS), with two primary objectives. Firstly, to enhance the precision of pair-wise loss gradient decomposition for speed up convergence. Secondly, to explore a more efficient direction for loss optimization, leading to improved image retrieval accuracy. The proposed GDDS approach integrates a unique distribution mechanism coupled with a segmentation method to accurately identify and interpret the significance of individual loss gradient components. Consequently, this enables the precise identification of primary contribution parameters, thereby reducing the time taken for convergence by as much as three times. Moreover, the distribution of loss gradient values facilitates further refinement of the deep network, resulting in better generalization and performance on the fine-tuning task. To evaluate the performance of the proposed strategy, we have conducted comprehensive experiments using various datasets such as Columbia University Images of Animals, Stanford University Animal, UsAirForce-100, MARS, NIST-300, and MS-COCO, among others. The results obtained are superior to those achieved by prior art, including SoftLoss, PartLoss, PairLoss, CircleLoss, Circle-Assisted Loss, Identity Mixture Loss, Age Mixture Loss, Gender Mixture Loss, and Age Identity Mixture Loss. Moreover, the proposed strategy has been successfully applied to a wide range of real-world applications including age, gender, and vehicle category classification, demonstrating its versatility and generalization capabilities. The code and dataset used in this research are available for public access at https://github.com/FlyingTang/GDDS. The experimental findings indicate that the proposed strategy outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin, with a significant improvement of 6.9%, 9.1%, 9.6%, 2.1%, and 2.6% on Columbia, SU-A, UsAirForce-100, NIST-300, and MS-COCO respectively. Even at a distance of ten thousand epochs, the proposed strategy successfully matches or surpasses existing techniques. Furthermore, the time taken for convergence is significantly lower than the best existing technique by a margin of two to four times. The research findings presented are significantly more generalizable and reliable than existing methods. The novel strategy developed as a result of this research contributes significantly to the image retrieval field in terms of its generalization capabilities and performance. The experimental findings presented in this research provide valuable insights to engineers

New findings from Chandra and XMM-Newton observations of magnetized radio filaments in the edge of the Veil Nebula offer significant insights into their complex structure and magnetic properties. A systematic analysis of their optical counterparts and X-ray emissions reveals two types of filaments: those powered by supernovae and cloud interactions, and an additional set of filaments in radio starburst complexes, for which a new hypothesis is proposed to explain their magnetization. It is suggested that when a cloud encounters a strong magnetic field, it causes a shift in the magnetic field lines, leading to the formation of filamentous shapes. This cloud-magnetic interaction hypothesis is applicable to magnetized radio filaments in other locations as well, such as the Cygnus Cubes. It's discovered that filaments not hosting PDRs have harder X-ray spectra, indicating an interaction between cosmic rays and the Veil's matter. For filaments hosting PDRs, a connection between their X-ray and H-alpha emissions is observed, suggesting that both are influenced by the filaments' magnetic fields. It's concluded that filaments are complex, elongated structures that exist at the intersection of cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and interstellar materials, thereby revealing their pivotal role in understanding the relationship between magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and gas in the galaxy's interstellar medium. Furthermore, this research is part of a broader project aimed at creating a comprehensive X-ray map of the Veil Nebula using a combination of archival and planned observations. A detailed paper on radio starburst complex filaments is currently in preparation. 

A crucial finding from these observations is that the Veil's southernmost edge, marked by radio starburst complexes, has the strongest magnetic fields among all the filaments examined so far, with estimated surface magnetic field strength of approximately 100 micro-Gauss. To date, filings associated with star formation, supernovae, and cloud interactions have been found to share the same filamentary structure, with their magnetic fields aligned in the same direction. It's hypothesized that a cosmic ray flood in the Veil is triggered by the interaction between magnetic fields and clouds, with the cosmic ray flux in the region potentially reaching 10% of the standard galactic value. Under the condition that all sequences have similar properties and the longest sequence experiences relatively low loss rates, we derive tight limits for the regret of the optimal arm choice. For practical purposes, text-generation in dialogue is typically approached as a task of producing the next sentence given the current dialogue context, which is established at the beginning of each dialogue. However, this context is highly dependent on previous conversations, making it difficult to reproduce exactly as needed. We propose a novel method to circumvent these complexities by treating dialogue contexts as complex functions involving multiple interactive inputs. By training these functions simultaneously for all dialogue participants, we develop a unified model capable of generating subsequent contributions from any participant. Our model is trained using existing datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art models on two essential tasks: preserving the existing dialogue context and producing logical, contextually relevant responses. You can view our model's source code on GitHub at https://.github/AToken-Shared-State. Additionally, we release a series of theoretical papers, each covering essential aspects of our model's formulation. Since its inception in the early 1970s, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has been the foundation for understanding strong-interaction matter. Despite being formulated nearly five decades ago, a robust numerical platform for solving QCD did not materialize until the 1990s. Lately, advancements in massive computing capabilities, cutting-edge algorithms, and cutting tools have made it possible to trustingly achieve precise numerical solutions for QCD. Contemporary computer simulations primarily rely on the lattice QCD method, paving the way for exploring this in vivo medium. Researchers have leveraged lattice QCD to investigate an array of topics, including properties of light hadrons, heavy-quark behavior, and the intricate dynamics of baryons, as well as the melting of heavy quarks within simulated environments. Moreover, simulations on more complex matter have been conducted to investigate phase transitions to quark-gluon plasmas and observe novel forms of strongly interacting material. Our review delves into cutting-edge advancements in state-of-the-art quantum computing hardware, the emerging quantum algorithms for simulating QCD, and the first experiments featuring quantum computers in strong-interaction physics. Furthermore, we examine the growing potential of a global collaborative quantum computer network, known as the quantum internet, in support of these simulations. Our project also contemplates the role of quantum computing in contemporary theoretical physics, observing that quantum algorithms are predominantly being developed without consideration of their underlying implications on fundamental theory. In place of conventional standard model simulations, researchers are employing quantum computers on machines bearing little resemblance to the standard models themselves. This paradox prompts an exploration of the prevailing attitude towards the quantum computer as a multifaceted tool, the significance of simulations in general, and the growing reliance on the quantum computer as a novel analytical instrument in the study of fundamental theory and its converse--the prediction of unknowns. Our review offers an examination of the present state in the quantum computer community and the emerging quantum algorithms for simulating QCD in the context of their potential impact on the quantum computer's broader scientific implications. Our project concludes by discussing LQCD's involvement in the simulation of quantum field theories and the potential future role of quantum computers in the development of novel theories in the context of their potential future role in the LHC's successor research. Our review concludes by discussing LQCD's involvement in the quantum computer's core research. Our review concludes with a call for greater awareness among fundamental theory researchers of the potential future role of quantum computers in fundamental theory research. The movement of turbulence and waves in the ocean is unpredictable and causes variations in the forces exerted on offshore wind turbines, leading to greater and more variable loads. To mitigate the risk of damaging these turbines, accurate predictions of their loads are essential, but the uncertainty of the turbulence and wave patterns poses a significant challenge. We propose a novel approach that separates the turbulence and wave effects from the turbines' response to get a more precise understanding of the stress. In this method, data from wind turbines in different places is used along with wave and turbulence data to make predictions of the turbines' response. We test this idea using simulated data from the NREL C3Tx models and find it gives very similar results to the dynamic state equation model that considers all the variables at the same time, especially for the axial forces of the blades. We also find that just using measurements of the turbines' vibrations and movements in real-time allows us to make reasonably accurate predictions of the stress. Overall, this new technique shows the importance of wave and turbulence data in determining the stress on offshore wind turbines in the ocean. It has potential to be used to make predictions of the stress on offshore wind turbines in the ocean based on real-time measurements of their vibrations and movements. However, for optimal results a combination of wave forecasting models, turbine monitoring systems, and sophisticated simulation software is needed. We suggest that this technique be developed further to be used in the design and optimization of future offshore wind turbines. We also find that this technique is not limited to calculating the axial forces of the blades and can be applied to predicting the stress in other parts of the turbine. In the future, this technique could be used to predict fatigue and damage in offshore wind turbines by calculating the stress in specific areas. We are working on improving the accuracy of the turbulence and wave models used in this study and exploring new applications of this technique. Additionally, this technique could be used to predict the stress in offshore cybersystems by calculating the time it takes for data and signals to travel through the digital environment. We are currently investigating this possibility and hope to make the source code of our model available in the future. In summary, this novel approach shows the significance of wave and turbulence data in determining the stress on offshore wind turbines in the ocean and highlights the potential of real-time measurements and data integration to enhance our understanding of the relationship between the ocean's atmosphere and offshore wind turbines. We hope that this study provides valuable information and a methodological framework for predicting the stress on offshore wind turbines in the ocean and encourages future research.

If a given subgroup, is R-for-nilpotent in G, then its (G : H)-th power results in a subgroup, G[H^(G : H)], which is the largest possible R-for-nilpotent subgroup of G, contained within H. Given the significant influence of R-for-nilpotent subgroups in both theoretical and computational aspects of group properties, there is a pressing need to establish a deeper understanding of the R-for-nilpotency degree. Our investigation focuses on the R-for-nilpotency degree of finite p-groups and aims to establish a relationship between this degree and the exponent of p, as well as explore the analytical and computational implications of this finding. Our study reveals that a comprehensive analysis of R-for-nilpotent degrees is essential in both theoretical and computational group structures. Furthermore, our investigation demonstrates that calculating the R-for-nilpotency degree of any finite p-group is achievable through a polynomial-time algorithm, after first determining the group's order and isomorphism with a given p-group, using an approximate method. Our algorithm, in turn, utilizes a modified version of the group-schreier, as an essential component to establish the group's base and ascending series, resulting in a novel, time-efficient approach to identifying p-group homomorphisms towards finite groups. In accordance with our findings, p-groups exhibiting an R-for-nilpotency degree minimally associated with p will exhibit an abundance of such p-group homomorphisms towards finite groups. Our practical computational examination based on our results clearly indicates a direct correlation between the R-for-nilpotency degree and the p, as well as the group order and class for the p-groups examined. Our study has provided significant insights and findings of general significance applicable to any finite group, in addition to p-groups. Our work has successfully implemented an innovative approach to approximating finite group representations towards achieving a precise R-for-nilpotency degree for any given group. Our findings have further revealed the significant influence of the prime, p, on the R-for-nilpotency degree, as well as the group's order and properties towards achieving such degrees. We re-examine the projective measurement process in quantum mechanics by addressing indirect measurements. We develop an alternative measurement process, which does not involve projecting to energy eigenstates, and is characterized by a set of hermitian operators chosen a priori. The non-projective measurement process is defined in terms of a transition probability between initial and final states, and is calculated by applying the constraints of detailed balance and the conservation of probability. The non-projective measurement process is evaluated for a system described by a two-dimensional Hilbert space and subject to thermal fluctuations. When certain conditions are met, the results from the non-projective and projective measurement processes yield equivalent outcomes in terms of their associated mean energies. However, when these conditions are not met, the non-projective measurement process can exhibit behaviors such as dynamic phase fluctuations and history-dependent responses that are not found in the projective measurement process. When a non-projective measurement process is optimized, it converges to an ideal projective measurement process. The distinctions between projective and non-projective measurement processes are also studied in terms of their influence on the linear response theory and the onset of dynamic phase transitions and history effects in the context of quantum parametric oscillators that exhibit either symmetric or anti-symmetric resonances. When projective measurement is employed, the onset of quantum oscillations is as would be anticipated from classical physics, with projective measurement describing a quadratic relationship between mean energy and either displacement or coupling parameters. However, when non-projective measurement is used, the measured mean energy during strong resonances is observed to deviate from classical prediction. The measured mean energy is found to exhibit random fluctuations following a type IV Lorentzian frequency distribution. The type of measurement employed is found to impact the onset of dynamic phase transitions in parametric oscillators. When projective measurement is used, the transition is observed to occur at the classical DQPC, as would be anticipated. However, when the non-projective measurement is used, the transition occurs at a stronger coupling strength, as the calculated critical coupling is found to be 1.25 times greater than the classical value. The measured history effects in the context of quantum oscillators are found to be influenced by both temperature and coupling strength, with colder or stronger coupling leading to the emergence of larger history effects. The measured history effects are found to be in agreement with classical prediction for its form. We draw a connection between special G2 instantons and abelian instantons on a 7-dimensional sphere to study the rigidity of G2 instantons, finding evidence that non-renormalizability implies rigidity. A comprehensive analysis of the moduli space of G2 instantons is provided, informed by its intersection with the sphere's tangent bundle, much like in the case of CP2 instantons. However, our findings diverge from CP2 instantons in two key ways: the G2 instanton's moduli space has boundaries and intersects with singular loci where certain calibrations fail, but surprisingly, these failures do not occur inside the instanton moduli space itself, and a specific ratio of areas between holomorphic curves on CP2 describes the G2 instanton moduli space's volume. This approach, drawing from the G2 instanton moduli space's boundaries and singularities, yields a distinct outcome, proving that virtually all G2 instantons are rigid, especially those in the reference background. Consequently, we propose that the moduli space of any G2 instanton is a compact, smooth manifold. Lastly, we identify a new U(1) connection on the sphere, generalizing a CP2 instanton rigidity result to G2 instantons. In the process, we establish relationships with the sphere's tangent bundle and a modified Green's function for the Yang-Mills equation, making further analysis of G2 instantons in the vicinity of singular G2 structures possible. Additionally, our findings hint at a possible connection between G2 and special Sp(2)-instantons, which could be the subject of a future research paper, and provide an explanation for the absence of bound states in the G2 instanton moduli space, much like in the case of CP2 instantons. In the extreme low-calibre limit, we discover that G2 instantons are indistinguishable from abelian instantons at a renormalized level, which is a surprising outcome. Consequently, we propose that the G2 instanton moduli space's volume, described using a ratio of areas for holomorphic curves on CP2, undergoes a transition as it evolves towards a smooth, rigid, and Landau-Ginzburg model surface, much like in the case of CP2 instantons. In an effort to understand this process, we identify a singular connection on the G2 instanton moduli space's boundary, generalizing a CP2 instanton connection rigidity result. In conclusion, we outline several future research objectives

A typical approach to decoherence involves a noisy environment model where the measurement process is unclear. In contrast, we propose an alternative interpretation. Decoherence is primarily a consequence of physical interactions that can lead to entanglement between subsystems. When subsystems have limited capacity to become entangled, measurement-like effects can occur. Physically, this entanglement capacity is often limited by the fundamental properties of the subsystems involved. This perspective is demonstrated using the Landau diagram method to illustrate how interactions between the system and environment can create the illusion of spontaneous localization. As a case study, we examine spontaneous emission from an excited atom, highlighting how the entanglement capacity between the atom and electromagnetic field affects the collapse of the system wave function. This research offers a fresh understanding of decoherence and suggests potential strategies to control and manipulate quantum states. Moreover, it may facilitate the development of thermodynamic devices operating in the quantum regime. In the context of current research, our focus on the atom-emission process enables an examination of the principles underlying the QO QUEP proposal. Finally, our analysis contributes to the ongoing discussion on the role of projection operators in quantum mechanics and entangled subsystems. To develop practical applications based on the atom-emission system, we propose a protocol to store quantum states using a coherent superposition of ground and excited states, thereby achieving near-future prospects for quantum processing. Near-term experimental verification of quantum phenomena is also more likely with an optical setup using a coherent superposition of optical modes. In general, our findings indicate that the quantum entanglement between the atom and electromagnetic field can be maximized to facilitate measurement-free decoherence, and this idea may be applied to other systems to achieve similar effects. Ultimately, our research provides a flexible approach to analyzing quantum processes and identifies potential applications for controlling quantum interactions and developing novel quantum technologies. To facilitate further research, an open-source program is provided to calculate the Landau diagram for specific scenarios, offering an accessible tool for analyzing interaction processes. The program is compatible with Linux and Windows operating systems and is available for download from online repositories, accompanied by a user manual detailing implementation instructions. The program's calculation results can be utilized directly in future research, as exemplified by its application in the present study.
