The combination of acoustic waves and rheological measurements has emerged as a 
promising approach to learning how mechanical energy affects gelation processes.
Rheological tests often reveal hidden patterns in sample dynamics, buried 
within torque signals of little apparent significance. Through the application 
of ultrasonic hydroacoustics, this study uncovers substantial harmonic 
oscillations within the torque transferred by the lower platens of our rheometer, 
indicating that ultrasound waves profoundly interact with material particles 
during acoustic gelation. A theoretical framework for fluidization in gel phases 
has also been developed, showing that particles are suspended in phases with 
low acoustic intensity, according to a detailed model. Moreover, this model 
predicts that particles will be held stationary only if acoustic waves are 
truncated at a specific cutoff frequency, corresponding to the lower order of 
the gel's module of rigidity. As a result, this frequency can be determined 
by identifying the corresponding harmonic oscillations within the torque 
signals. Moreover, this principle has enabled the precise calculation of the 
module of rigidity for a particular gel system. The convergence of ultrasonic 
mechanics, material modeling, and rheological analysis presents an innovative 
way to study acoustic gelation, offering a previously overlooked route to 
modulating gelation dynamics via acoustic wave intensity. The findings of 
this study support a new generation of micro-acoustic approaches for creating 
micro-gelations. Ultimately, this research suggests that interactions 
between acoustic waves and elastic networks can produce reversible gelations, 
potentially enabling a novel method for tuning gelation dynamics via 
acoustic wave intensity. The developed concept of rheo-acoustic gelations 
paves the way for the creation of micro-gelations through acoustic waves, 
and could yield a new way to study interactions between elastic networks and 
acoustic waves at the micro-scale. 

This published paper developed a comprehensive theoretical framework for 
understanding ultrasound-assisted gelation dynamics and developed a new 
method for determining the module of rigidity for polymerizable gelations. The 
funding and acknowledgments for this work were supported by an NSF grant. The 
primary author of this research is to be contacted for any further discussion 
or collaboration opportunities.

As a result, the BEVFusion framework integrates point cloud-based object detectors employed in parallel, each operating with an artificially restricted range, and an ensemble-based detector combining multiple outputs. Critically, the latter can function without access to point cloud data via adaptation of the beamformer operation in radar technology. Ensemble-based method outperforms alternatives in object detection on synthetic data across diverse scenarios and is shown to utilize effectively only the relevant range in which each bias is corrected. Experimental findings on synthetic data, along with detection performance metrics, loss plots, and visualization of false positives, indicate that the beamformer-based approach outperforms alternative solutions. This note examines the fluctuating hydrodynamics equations and its relation to the Navier-Stokes equations, particularly focusing on the Navier-Stokes terms' impact on energy dissipation in turbulent flows and their representation in the fluctuating hydrodynamics model. It argues that the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation fails to accurately capture the Navier-Stokes terms' behavior, leading to minimal energy dissipation in turbulent flows as observed in direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equation, whereas the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation predicts a non-zero, constant level of energy dissipation. It then discusses the potential consequences of this discrepancy for the simulation of atmospheric turbulence flows. Additionally, the energy spectrum and associated coefficients of the fluctuating hydrodynamics model for wave number spectra are compared with those of the stochastic Navier-Stokes model and direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equation. Lastly, the absence of a stochastic term in the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation for temperature transport has significant implications for the modeling of heat transfer in turbulent flows, as it is critical for the correct simulation of an inertial range in temperature spectra, a range not influenced by boundaries in turbulent flows. Although other stochastic models, such as the one developed by Leslie, correct this oversight, they are also subject to the aforementioned energy dissipation discrepancy. A further investigation reveals that a similar issue arises in Leslie's stochastic model, where the Navier-Stokes terms' impact on temperature transport are not accurately captured. A new stochastic model for temperature transport is proposed, which not only addresses the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation's and Leslie's model's limitations, but also provides a more general, applicable solution to the modeling of wave number spectra of temperature, where an inertial range is present. This model achieves this goal by utilizing the Navier-Stokes equation's exact energy dissipation, while maintaining a linear relationship between the velocity gradient tensor and the Navier-Stokes terms. As a result, the new model ensures that the velocity structure function and energy spectrum are unaffected. Furthermore, a local incoherence in energy spectrum models by Yvonne Pouquet and colleagues and the present work allows for a straightforward extension of the work to magnetohydrodynamics, where an incoherent model for the Lorentz force is adopted. Lastly, a direct numerical simulation of the incompressible MHD equation reveals that the new model for temperature transport, when combined with the stochastic model by Leslie, yields a realistic description of the fluctuating magnetic field through comparison to experimental data. The binary system CR Dra, composed of two M dwarfs with a highly eccentric orbit, has been observed to exhibit radio flares. These flares, similar to those observed on Jupiter, feature radiated and induced emission components. Based on 16 observed flare events, a two-component radio spectrum was detected, comprising low-frequency and high-frequency emissions. These two emissions were found to be closely linked, sharing the same center latitude and rotation symmetry. Our findings suggest that the induced emission may be stronger than the radiated emission. Furthermore, the flare emissions did not extend to the expected light cylinder, causing the emissions to be confined to the plane containing the Earth and the star's rotation axis. Neural radiance fields, 'NRFs', are highly accurate 3D models that have been limited in use due to high computational demands. Articulation Neural Rendering, 'ANR', is a new framework proposed to enable efficient 3D modeling of dynamically moving objects by simplifying NRF inference. It achieves this by estimating a fixed number of 3D poses for each object, overcoming challenges from data distribution and object structure uncertainties. The approach addresses pose estimation uncertainties through data conditioning and object interaction boundaries are accurately maintained through a novel approach called style tokens. The results show that ANR is capable of efficiently handling complex 3D models of articulated objects, while demonstrating robust 3D modeling capabilities for objects in various poses, such as human clothing, furniture and vehicle models, which was previously difficult with NRFs. The method also allows for the creation of efficient view synthesis using a minimal number of 3D models and poses, even for very complex objects, enabling applications on machines without high-end graphics processing units. To resolve this issue, we present a novel framework that leverages large, recently generated datasets without manual annotations to boost few-shot parsing performance. To achieve this, we combine the capabilities of a lightweight parser and a pre-existing zero-shot or few-shot named entity recognition model. Next, we describe a set of data and parsing performance metrics tailored to short utterances with variable structures. Our framework's efficacy is demonstrated through improved few-shot parsing performance on Uswitch data, surpassing current state-of-the-art results by 9% using a 1024-type vocabulary. We attribute the success of this approach to two main factors: the ability to derive semantic parsing guidance from a lightweight parser, and the opportunity to augment limited parsing data with correct labels from a pre-existing model. To comprehend the atmospheric dynamics of rapidly rotating B-type magnetic stars, it is essential to analyze their magnetosphere and disc formation in relation to their rotation rate, magnetic field intensity, and age. These parameters influence the size of their magnetosphere and can result in the depletion of their inner atmosphere if strong magnetic fields dominate. To investigate disc formation around these stars, we employed a 1D model for the atmosphere of a slowly rotating, non-magnetic B2V star, observing both a model with a smooth wind and one with a dense wind, driven by metal-line variability. These models were then modified with a treatment of ambipolar diffusion in the surrounding space, simulating the effects of a magnetic field. These rates are then compared to those derived from H30α emissions, which were collected as part of a separate study, across ten metal-poor galaxies. This comparison shows that the SFR derived from total infrared flux is consistently lower than that from H30α emissions by around 0.2-0.5 dex. To address this discrepancy, we explored two possible factors – underestimation of total infrared flux due to a specific observing frequency, and SFR undersampling by H30α emissions. Our observations suggest an inverse correlation between the SFR and metallicity when using total infrared flux, but this trend is not seen when using H30α emissions. This implies that the SFR derived from these two different methods may have varying levels of accuracy. To account for a possible bias in total infrared flux powered stars towards lower metallicity galaxies with lower SFRs, we modified the Calzetti et al. (2000) conversion equation. This resulted in SFRs derived from total infrared flux that are around 0.1-0.5 dex lower than those from H30α emissions, which were previously observed to be lower. To further reduce uncertainties, we combined the corrected total infrared flux SFRs with those from H30α emissions, yielding an average star formation rate of around 2-3 solar masses per year. This rate is consistent with a separate study, which reported a combined star formation rate of around 1.5-2.5 solar masses per year based on FIR flux and H30α emissions, respectively. The objective is to find approximate solutions of integral equations involving operators that are applied to signals or functions in spaces like $L^2(-1,1)$. We examine the convergence and convergence rates of classical projection methods like the Galerkin method in comparison to more modern kernel-based techniques. These kernel methods can be further categorized into two submethods: the first involves projecting the unknown solution onto spaces with basis functions that are the product of a kernel with a fixed element, and the second involves projecting the kernel itself with respect to the unknown solution. It is found that the first approach leads to higher approximation errors, whereas the second method is more effective but also more complex. To simplify the computations, an approximation algorithm is introduced for the second method that involves replacing the kernel by a piecewise constant approximation on a finite partition of the interval $[-1,1]$. We demonstrate that this approximation is equivalent to the method of replacing the kernel with a polynomial of a pre-existing degree $n$ within a Galerkin framework. Consequently, it achieves the same approximation error as the original second method, specifically $\frac{\mathsf{M}^2}{n}$ where $\mathsf{M}$ is a measure of the maximum value of the error of the piecewise constant approximation. Furthermore, it is found that replacing the kernel with a polynomial of a pre-existing degree $n$ within a first method is also effective in achieving the same approximation error, specifically $\frac{\mathsf{M}^2}{n}$. It is then shown that kernel-based techniques are effective in achieving faster convergence rates than classical methods when the approximation error is too large for the application of the original second method to be computationally feasible. Specifically, it is shown that when the approximation error is greater than a certain value, it is more computationally efficient to first project the unknown solution onto spaces with basis functions that are the product of a kernel with a fixed element, and then to use the original second method to project the resulting approximation. Advancements in nonlinear optical processes at the nanoscale hold great potential for enhancing quantum photonics and nonlinear metrology. We investigate the generation of short-pulse lasers at the nanoscale by analyzing two types of optical microresonators: one containing Kerr nonlinearity and the other exhibiting nonlinear absorption. We find that Kerr-lens mode-locking in the former requires nanosecond pump pulses and high ionized density to establish a gap in the laser cavity, whereas Kerr modulation in the latter produces soliton pulses at room temperature. However, the nonlinear absorption in this system is vulnerable to ionized dopants that can disrupt the laser operation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new technique called space-time four-wave mixing, which produces isolated soliton pulses at room temperature without relying on ionized dopants. Notably, soliton pulses with exceptionally low peak powers of 0.23 mW are achieved, along with a record-breaking threshold for nonlinear effects exceeding 2600 W/cm^2. This breakthrough demonstrates stable soliton generation in a nonlinear microcavity, opening up opportunities for novel nanophotonics applications. Furthermore, we theoretically investigate soliton generation in quantum systems, revealing new insights into the nonlinear effects of ionized dopants in this context. Ultimately, our study contributes significantly to the development of innovative nanophotonics platforms for quantum information technologies. Furthermore, it lays the groundwork for enabling new quantum effects like Dyson solitons, spin-drag effects, and anti-soliton formation in a quantum nonlinear microcavity. Moreover, it advances quantum state-controlled soliton generation essential for optical metrology, quantum information, and high-power applications by leveraging the unique properties of ionized dopants. Lastly, it offers a unique vision for scaling nanophotonics at the quantum level by leveraging the effects of ionized dopants in microcavity lasers. With its vast potential for groundbreaking applications, it is anticipated that the integration of soliton generation in quantum nonlinear microcavities will yield numerous avenues of further research and analysis. In the context of asynchronous online federated learning (OFCL), where models are continuously updated and trained in an online manner, recent research has focused on reducing communication costs for reduced-SI (Server-Initiated) scenarios. A key challenge arises when the model and server aim to quantify their respective losses, due to partial data sharing and limited computational resources. To address this issue, a novel partial-sharing-based communication (PSC) method is proposed in this study, reducing dependence on data sharing and requiring only minimal computational capability at the server. The proposed PSC approach utilizes a stochastic process to make informed estimates of model loss, with theoretical analysis demonstrating a bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$ on loss estimation accuracy, where $n$ denotes the number of samples. To verify its efficacy, a reduced-SI OFCL system is implemented, and both theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that PSC significantly decreases communication costs while maintaining scalability at both the model and server levels. Furthermore, when compared to prior OFCL systems, PSC has been found to achieve an almost $60.57\%$ decrease in communication costs under certain server computation constraints. The empirical results also indicate that PSC is robust to varying model accuracy and server computation capabilities, and it is compatible with different federated learning optimization algorithms. Overall, the PSC approach presents a pioneering solution for reduced-SI OFCL under partial data sharing and limited server resources, thereby advancing the understanding and efficiency of asynchronous online federated learning processes. To enhance quantum effects, we analyze the optical absorption within a thin Si film using the transfer matrix method, considering a specific design with a Si-photonic crystal back reflector. By coupling a Si layer with a photonic crystal back reflector, we find that its optical absorption shows a periodic pattern depending on its thickness. This behavior can be harnessed to identify the superlattices within the Si photonic crystal. Our study focuses on a Si photonics context that enables efficient integration with quantum systems, enabling control over atomic interactions through light-matter coupling. Utilizing a compact Si-photonic structure, we simulate a 3D quantum system where multiple quantum wells are arranged in a microresonator, enabling us to tune the light-matter interaction and quantum interaction between atoms. For a quantum system without a photonic structure, the quantum correlation between atoms is restricted by the critical coupling threshold. However, the atoms within a microresonator exhibit enhanced light-matter coupling and long-range quantum correlation. This increased coupling between atoms can be attributed to the localized light within the microresonator, forming a quasi-mode that interacts with the quantum system. Additionally, the position of the microresonator's mode can be adjusted by modifying its photonic crystal gap layer to leverage the system's properties for detection and manipulation of quantum effects. Using a specific design, we identify a compact structure comprising 5 quantum wells in a microresonator that provides an efficient detection environment for long-range quantum correlation and light-matter coupling. Conversely, the thin Si film employed in our simulations exhibits a 2D quantum system characterized by minimal thickness. Through simulations, we identify the critical coupling threshold for this system as being influenced by the application of a thin Si film. As a result, the correlation between atoms can achieve a maximum value when the system couples strongly with light. Moreover, the application of a thin Si film can increase this correlation, making long-range quantum correlation detection through Si-photonic structures efficient and independent of the microresonator's design. This correlation can be further optimized by adjusting the photonic crystal gap layer to modify the microresonator's properties. These models, based on a primary nonlinear phenomenon in optical fibers and including factors that cause data loss and distortion, are applied to complex, multiplexed signals with multiple states. Studies of these models in optical networks with four polymers highlight the importance of their nonlinear properties, and related research using a simplified, two-state signal demonstrates a method to estimate the rate of data transfer. This research investigates the evaluation and development of image fusion methods to address fire detection issues. Initially, we assess the performance of a deep learning-based image fusion technique, along with other relevant methods, through fire detection experiments using MODIS satellite images. We introduce a new performance metric, false positive rate, to quantify fire detection accuracy and find that pixel-wise assessment offers superior evaluation criteria compared to existing metrics. Based on these findings, we develop a novel fire detection image fusion architecture, integrating multi-spectral and panchromatic images, which significantly enhances the overall performance in comparison to previous versions. Notably, this optimized model exhibits an average 3% lower false positive rate and an average 21% lower false negative rate compared to the previous iteration. Moreover, we demonstrate that combining fire maps with image fusion approaches yields better performance in comparison to standalone fire detection or image fusion techniques. The proposed architecture, which integrates fire maps and image fusion, has the potential to be further improved by leveraging additional data such as active fire data to produce more accurate fire detection and geometric correction results. Active fire data may also enable the generation of higher quality panchromatic images, which in turn can improve the overall performance. Therefore, a framework that simultaneously utilizes fire information, image fusion, and active fire data is envisioned for future development. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, most hospitals and health care facilities worldwide have taken several steps to adapt to the challenge. This study aims to evaluate the impact of a range of measures taken by hospitals and health care providers, as well as the responses by infected individuals and society, on the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. A mathematical model is employed to incorporate the effects of various actions, some of which mimic standard in models as quarantine, contact tracing, and comprehensive sanitation, but others do not, such as increased testing due to multiple testing requirements for suspected cases and the possibility of asymptomatic infections. In addition to hospital and health care actions, the model also considers individual actions, including the decision to report suspected cases and stay in isolation, and societal actions, such as the implementation of lockdowns and testing programs. Optimality principles are then used to determine the optimal testing and lockdown strategies. Numerical results indicate that the actions taken by hospitals and health care providers can supplement lockdown measures, but may also accelerate transmission if individual precautions are not observed. In contrast, the action of comprehensive sanitation can lead to the within-hospital peak occurring before the community peak, thereby reducing transmission to outside individuals. Optimal testing policies suggest that hospitals and health care providers should prioritize testing if the probability of an asymptotic infection is high, whereas they should prioritize a multiple testing requirement if the probability is low. In the long run, the effects of some actions are found to be comparable to standard model actions, but others exhibit distinct behaviors. Furthermore, the account of individual actions involves a variable representing non-compliance with hospital and health care measures. A proposed model assumes that the individual actions can be effectively combined with the actions taken by hospitals and health care providers, but this assumption may not hold in cases where the model parameters indicate a high degree of non-compliance with health measures. In particular, the model finds that the action of individual isolation is less effective when individuals do not comply with health measures and hospitals provide a limited level of care. Ultimately, the study highlights that while the actions taken by hospitals and health care providers can play a significant role in mitigating the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, they are not sufficient on their own and that the cooperation of individual actions and societal actions are essential for effectively controlling the epidemic. In real-world applications, the study's findings suggest that hospitals and health care providers can effectively supplement lockdown measures but may accelerate transmission if individual precautions are not observed, which is consistent with the experience of China. We show that systems with classical boundary states of fractional type can exist in the absence of specific lattice symmetries. This phenomenon occurs when a boundary condition falls within a gap in the spectrum of the corresponding bulk system. A mathematical proof of this principle is provided for a model based on the restricted solid on a sphere, specifically the ones corresponding to the minimal models of Kondo physics with (C_(2)*, Z_2) and (Z_2, Z_2) symmetries. We reinterpolate the boundary modes of these models in order to understand their physics, revealing that they can be associated with charged particles under (Z_2) rotations, similar to the thermal double of topological insulators. Additionally, we propose that the boundary states of certain E8-related models may have a higher-order generalization of this classical form. This idea aligns with a broader theory suggesting that boundary states of fractional type can also appear in quantum systems without certain symmetry principles. Moreover, our results for the restricted solid on a sphere model match the current experimental conditions for an ultracold gas in a optical trap, allowing for a possible realization of the boundary states as a quantum Hall system through the application of a synthetic magnetic field to the gas. Ultimately, our findings for the boundary states of classical boundary states of fractional type may lead to an innovative approach in the replication of quantum systems through the use of classical systems. Furthermore, this knowledge could enable the creation of instructions for realizing these quantum states through the use of the quantum annealing process. However, it is worth noting that the boundary states of fractional type may not be usable for information storage in the same way that topological states cannot be accessed through local operations. This step is inspired by the Adaptive LMS algorithm's method of protecting against excessive learning within a specified bounds. To evaluate the protection efficacy of Bass' algorithm, we examine its performance on a network controlled by a sample data-driven algorithm known as the real-time homotopy algorithm (RTHA). By analyzing Bass' algorithm's performance on both an unsecured and secured network driven by RTHA, it is shown that the algorithm remains stable and efficient even in the face of disruptions. Additionally, the controller's stability and resilience were confirmed through various simulations. To further validate its performance, the secured network driven by RTHA using Bass' algorithm was compared against other conventional controllers such as the Adaptive LMS and the regular LMS algorithms. It is demonstrated that RTHA-Bass provides rapid convergence in a variety of chaotic systems, while also ensuring controller stability and preserving its ability to adapt and learn under normal and extreme conditions. Using three distinct chaotic systems - the Duffing vibration, the view dynamic, and the MIMO, in the presence of noise and random disturbances - it is shown that RTHA-Bass enables efficient learning and maintains a stable and resilient controller. This robustness is a significant advantage as it allows RTHA-Bass to handle a wide range of applications, while other conventional controllers are often limited by their lack of adaptive and robust properties under extreme conditions. As such, the secure learning offered by RTHA-Bass provides a foundation for synergistic learning across various real-world applications, where data-driven approaches are often complicated by noise and hardware limitations. Moreover, the algorithm has potential for generalization and can be applied to other synergistic learning problems, while its use of safe learning provides a significant advancement in the field of control engineering and learning algorithms. Furthermore, the computational feasibility of RTHA-Bass was evaluated and it was shown that the algorithm is computationally efficient, processing data 100 times faster than its conventional counterparts, in a time of approximately 0.0006 seconds. This rapid learning capability of RTHA-Bass makes it an ideal choice for a variety of real-time control and learning applications, where speed and efficiency are critical factors. This work presents an unsupervised domain adaptation framework called UoO-DAA that tackles ovarian cancer cell image classification. Ovarian cancer cells are typically classified into three categories: confluent, scattered, and mixed-cell patterns. The proposed framework transforms conventional ovarian cancer cell images into a suitable format for classification by removing the unwanted background, thus preventing feature distortion. To achieve this, the framework utilizes semantic segmentation to identify and separate ovarian cancer cells from the background using the Brier score metric. Following this step, the confluent, scattered, and mixed-cell pattern categories are identified using a classifier. Next, the background-separated ovarian cancer cell images are fed into a classifier to extract vital features. Subsequently, the features obtained from the confluent, scattered, and mixed-cell pattern categories are used to train three supervised classifiers. To enhance the robustness of the framework, the confluent, scattered, and mixed-cell pattern categories were combined into two domains with varying levels of feature extraction difficulty. The framework achieved a classification performance of 71% on the validation dataset and 64% on the test dataset, utilizing the combined training data of the Anacon, Confluent, Scattered, and Mixed-cell patterns. We develop a continuous model that represents asset prices, liquidity, and APM pricing. We calculate the optimal asset transfer for APMs and derive the corresponding liquidity demand. The demand is driven by arbitrage opportunities and price variations, leading to a naturally curved liquidity demand. The APM pricing becomes more unpredictable as its curve becomes more shallow, increasing chances of overfunding. We show that a balanced liquidity demand can reduce overfunding, thereby decreasing overfunding risks and the likelihood of price collapses. When overfunding occurs, a mechanism is proposed to address the issue. This mechanism involves redistributing funds to APMs with high liquidity demands, ensuring the stability of the APM pricing. In our new APM model, this mechanism reduces the probability of price collapses and increases overall surplus by adjusting the APM pricing and the likelihood of underfunding. These outcomes demonstrate that a balanced liquidity demand can reduce arbitrage risks, and our mechanism is an efficient way to eliminate overfunding risks. A cryogenic detector platform is being developed with the objective of reducing experimental volumes to centimeter scales for dark matter, neutrino, and double beta decay research.  Key facilities and technologies that are being incorporated to meet this objective include a cryogenic tank, electronics, and processing systems, as well as cryogenic detectors and low-temperature electronics.  In this presentation, recent advancements in a laboratory effort supporting the ICEC cryogenic platform are shared, focusing particularly on design and fabrication of specialized equipment to serve experimental campaigns.  In addition, the platform's proposed dimensions are presented as 20 x 20 x 30 cm, with an estimated 632 liters volume, although design flexibility allows for other dimensions to be explored.  This includes possibilities such as a cylindrical design, the details of which are discussed.  Final considerations are offered regarding a laboratory's role in supporting a cryogenic platform in accordance with its own scientific objectives and capacity for low-temperature operations.  In the context of this platform and relevant research, it is estimated that a single-room facility is sufficient for typical scales, although a larger volume of around 50 m³ might be necessary for larger experiments such as those for dark matter searches.  This work reports initial findings from a laboratory's involvement in the ICEC platform's development.  Specifically, the importance of contributing to the technology and platform evolution at an early stage is emphasized, as well as the benefits of collaboration between laboratories and platforms in general.  In addition, the platform's first experimental campaign is presented, involving a single-room experiment for dark matter and double beta decay research at a 20 kg scale.  This work also includes a proposal for a data analysis collaboration, the goals of which are outlined in detail.  In conclusion, the platform's potential to become a global reference for low-temperature cryogenic detector research is considered.  In the long term, the platform's concept could be used as a model for future underground physics facilities with larger volumes and a wider range of research focus.  In addition, the platform's potential to become an incubator for new technologies and a center for training and education is identified as an important consideration for its future development.  In the context of its first experimental campaign and a proposed collaboration, the platform's name "ICEC" is understood to refer to itself as well as its goal to serve as an "Inclusive Center for Cryogenic research".  In the context of its initial work presented here, the platform's name is understood to represent its mission to "Include" itself

The potential for future research lies in the development of an automated cryptographic function usability tester. The long-term goal is to create an automated tool to enhance the quality of existing cryptographic libraries, influencing the behavior of which users in critical situations. In smart cities, effective monitoring systems guarantee a high-quality delivery of essential services like law enforcement, transportation, healthcare, and entertainment. These systems typically emerge from private and public initiatives, combining varied technologies such as IoT, IP-based networks, and edge computing. As they become increasingly complex, specifications and guidelines govern data processing and management, ensuring user privacy and minimizing computational errors. However, these technical specifications differ from the original human-specified requirements, which lead to a gap between existing monitoring systems and actual user needs. Landmark Gabor Filters, with their carefully selected rotation values, ensure dense yet distinct coverage of the Gabor space, leading to a more efficient use of resources and image representations that can withstand orientation fluctuations. In this research, we identify the specific rotation values that define these landmark filters and explain how they are consistently represented across various image examples within each angle. Based on this understanding, we suggest a novel strategy to further integrate multiple Gabor filters with existing deep convolutional neural networks, unlike existing methods that merely replace the original filters. In trials on ImageNet, our approach demonstrated enhanced classification precision and more robust performance against image orientation variations. The source code for our proposed method is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/gemssilva/LGF-for-CNNs}. Additionally, our project is also hosted on: \url{https://github.com/gemssilva/LGFPipeline}. This research is a refinement of a previously published conference paper, further investigating the insights and benefits associated with the strategic placement of Gabor filters within deep neural networks. Specifically, we are premiering the LGS, a curated set of Gabor spaces tailored for analyzing various image characteristics. In order to facilitate a comprehensive evaluation, we also developed a benchmark framework, referred to as the Gabor-Eval, which assesses the impact of multiple Gabor filter integration on image representation robustness and classification precision across diverse network architectures, leading to notable insights and performance enhancements. Ultimately, our results validate the strategic integration of carefully selected Gabor filters at specific network layers as a viable strategy to further enhance deep neural network capabilities. In particular, we identify that filters added to early layers are ideal for capturing low-level image characteristics, whereas those integrated at late stages are more effective at analyzing higher-level image properties. This research introduces a comprehensive COVID-19 diagnosis model that utilizes clinical data and computational microscopy images of cells. The model is trained on converged convergent K-means (c-Kmeans) clusters derived from the images and relevant clinical data, utilizing supervised learning techniques. Specifically, the method employs Jaccard similarity index for binary clinical data and a modified Cosine similarity index for non-binary data. To generate optimal clusters, the value of K is determined using the C-index in conjunction with the c-Kmeans algorithm. Notably, the model is capable of operating in an unsupervised learning framework, automatically determining the value of K and generating relevant clusters. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed model, experiments were conducted on a unique dataset containing 1,624 samples of computational microscopy images and 774 binary clinical data points. However, these datasets were insufficient for thorough analysis and replication. The recent approval of satellite constellations by the FCC has sparked the need for significant changes in satellite design to accommodate the newly established guidelines. Before the regulatory change, a general rule of thumb was to keep the elevation angle of satellites above 45 degrees to prevent interference with optical devices, which impacted the design of mega-constellations. To analyze the impact on satellite design, we investigated the minimum orbital space required for non-interfering satellites, which we term as minimum space occupancy orbits. Using an iterative close loop algorithm and the Fourier transform, we determined the minimum orbital spacing required for non-interfering Rev 1 and Rev 2 satellite configurations. Furthermore, we analyzed the feasibility of increasing the coverage area of a single satellite to reduce the need for overlapping satellites in mega-constellations, which we term as minimum space occupancy orbits. To evaluate the impact of this modification on mega-constellations, we calculated the effect on coverage probability and satellite density, which showed that increasing the coverage area can significantly reduce the need for overlapping satellites in mega-constellations. Additionally, we calculated the impact on satellite number and density under both the MiSO and MSO orbits and found that MiSO orbits can reduce the need for overlapping satellites by as much as 50% while maintaining the same coverage area as traditional orbits. Finally, we calculated the impact on satellite number and density in mega-constellations with an inclination of 24.5.5 degrees and found that increasing the coverage area can reduce the number of satellites in mega-constellations with an inclination of 24.5.5 degrees by as much as 13% if compared to traditional orbits. These findings indicate that changing the coverage area of satellites can significantly reduce the number of satellites required in mega-constellations. The algorithm used in this dissertation can be further improved to determine the minimum number of satellites required for a given coverage area. The results presented in this dissertation can be applied to various satellite configurations and are not limited to specific parameters. When conducting statistical analysis, it's frequently necessary to identify how two variables are correlated. Rectangular areas in which two variables fall are often utilized as a basic statistic, leading to the occurrence of certain nonparametric tests. These tests can estimate p-values by comparing obtained statistics to a reference distribution of possible outcomes from independent samples that follow a bivariate normal distribution. However, in cases where this reference distribution doesn't accurately represent the data, a robust method has been developed that provides p-values by comparing the observed statistics to a combination of several reference distributions with varying correlation. The robust approach can be applied to various nonparametric tests, such as the Hogg rank, t2, and Wilcoxon tests used for bivariate data analysis. The robust method has been demonstrated to be resilient in simulations involving normally distributed and non-normally distributed data. The method is explained in detail, including how it can easily be extended to test hypotheses, and its capabilities are compared to other robust techniques in terms of controlling Type I errors and detecting real differences. The p-values provided are accurate up to the fourth moment, as demonstrated by simulations involving normally distributed data. However, in cases of non-normal data, the robust method exhibits greater sensitivity to data outliers, which may result in higher Type I errors occurring. The choice of correlation for reference distributions is a trade-off between accurately capturing the data and introducing negative consequences such as conservatism. The problem is explored using various examples, including data analysis involving stress-strength applications, where stress and strength do not follow a normal distribution, and conclusions are drawn about the bivariate normal distribution's limitations. The method and concepts discussed are considered straightforward, making them easily implementable in practical settings. The proposed method can be applied using available R packages such as the robustbiv and robustncbiv packages. The robust method has been incorporated into a novel package specifically designed to handle data with non-normal distributions, which can be downloaded from the GitHub platform using the citation command https://github.com/yspark/robustpivots. The package provides functionality for data analysis, including the estimation of p-values and comparison of obtained statistics, and can be used for various types of data, including circular and non-circular data. We believe that this resource will be a valuable tool for education and learning, as well as a useful reference for biomedical professionals and individuals looking to expand their vocabulary. Recommendation systems play a vital role in surfacing relevant content to users, and their reliance on implicit feedback methods like click-through data means their underlying decision-making processes are opaque to end-users and developers alike. To address this, post-hoc explanation techniques have become popular for gaining insights into recommendation models. Nevertheless, recent studies show that models relying heavily on post-hoc explanations are more susceptible to adversarial attacks from potential manipulators. In this research, we focus on how users' curiosity is stimulated by queries for post-hoc explanations and how this increases the risk of contamination of recommendation models through adversarial attacks. Subsequently, we present a novel theoretical framework called EXPLANATION ATTACKS DEFENSE (E2D) that considers the interplay between users, explainer queries, and defender measures in a game-theoretic context. Here, the goal of attackers is to deviate predicted item rankings towards adverse results by submitting cursed explainer queries, whereas defenders strive to minimize such adverse deviations. We propose and apply a robust threshold-based strategy to counter these explanation-based attacks, demonstrating its effectiveness in a real-world scenario involving a movie recommendation dataset. Additionally, we propose a new type of adverse input aimed at misclassifying media content, as well as a method for automatically generating cursed explainer queries with only limited manual labeling. Overall, our findings suggest that models derived without post-hoc explanations are more resilient to adverse attacks compared to those that heavily rely on them, highlighting an argument for deploying post-hoc explanations only when necessary. In contrast to traditional oversampling methods, GenBalance does not involve increasing a class by duplication but instead generates new data points from a deficient class to match the distribution of the overrepresented class. This work presents a new geometric approach inspired by the work of Vlasov and Nekhoroshev to study how Hamiltonian dynamics are affected by certain perturbations. Focusing on Lagrangian mean field games and dynamics, we develop a new summary statistic that captures key features of these systems, independent of specific reference frames. This leads to the identification of a key property: the statistical geometry in Lagrangian coordinates appears flat when compared to its Eulerian counterpart. As a result, we are able to formulate a new, more streamlined equation of motion that incorporates an influence function, providing a significant new perspective on this type of system. This new formulation enables us to investigate a range of intricate problems related to phase space localization and the development of stochastic models, all within the framework of a new theory of Lagrangian dynamics. This approach offers a significant amount of new insight into the characteristics of these systems across various dimensions. To conclude, we use our theory to derive new, more practical models for near-equilibrium states in a complex system characterized by a symplectic manifold across dimensions 1 through 3. These models take the form of a new, Lagrangian-based mean field games dynamic that closely mirrors the behavior of the underlying, truly Hamiltonian dynamics. This new dynamic is particularly notable for its departure from conventional mean field assumptions. Instead of the influence function representing a Lagrangian multiplier, it actually serves a more substantial role as a derivative-based function. This new dynamic is the first to directly characterize the curvature of the system's statistical geometry, effectively reducing it to a flat, influence function-based shape. This result holds considerable promise for the improvement of a range of models and simulations in various fields. To further expand our understanding of the theoretical implications of this new dynamic, we leveraged the connection between the Vlasov-Nekhoroshev equation and the Eulerian representation to derive an influence function-based estimate of the Vlasov equation. This approach represents a significant extension into the realm of more general transport equations. In the interest of preserving brevity, the remaining topics and implications of this new dynamic will be explored in greater depth in an accompanying document. A publicly accessible implementation of the theory can be found at the GitHub repository https://github.com/mjnewton/lagrangian-mfg. In this context, a regualr simplex within $Q_n$ with $s+1$ vertices is defined as the intersection of $Q_n$ and a hypersphere with radius $\sqrt{n}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$. If $s = n+1$, the interpolation nodes can be any subset of the vertices of the $Q_n$. It has further been shown that the interpolated function can be expressed as a polynomial of degree at most $r = \frac{s-1}{2}$. Consequently, a non-degenerate regular simplex within $Q_n$ with $s+1$ vertices allows for interpolation by polynomials of maximum degree $r$, with $s = 2r+1$. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a correlated random walk (CRW) on a lattice with the goal of obtaining the eigenvalues of its transition probability matrix. By applying a Kronecker equation and utilizing an expression based on the Laplace operator, we obtain the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix. From this, we determine the eigenvalues and analyze their density distribution, employing a Waleffe method. Consequently, we establish a representation series for the spectral measure, utilizing a representation theorem. This research serves as an expansion to a previously published study (arXiv:2103.14548) where we initially explored this topic, focusing specifically on diagonal elements associated with the transition probability matrix of a CRW. Notably, the approach in this research is versatile, enabling its application to various models, including the Ising model and Fisher's mean-field model. Furthermore, as an additional contribution to this research, we investigate the physical limitations of a variant of the CRW under a specific parameter constraint and leverage the main findings to analyze the Ising model, establishing a connection to its spectral properties via a representation series. Using this connection, we yield several identity series, one of which is a reiteration of Thomson's reciprocity identity. Finally, we investigate the Spectral Theorem for the transition probability matrix of a CRW under a particular parameter constraint, providing crucial insights into its behavior in this specific context. The research provides an open invitation for discussion on related topics, specifically the development of general theories for the approximation of eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and spectral measures, as well as the exploration of physical limitations of various models. In addition, we have written and compiled a newly created Julia package, CorrelatedRandomWalk, which not only facilitates the computation of eigenvalues but also enables the calculation of transition probability matrix elements, variance estimates, and time-series generation according to custom-specified parameters. The findings in this research have been accepted at the International Conference on Monte Carlo methods in 2019. The research is separated into seven sections, with Section 1 serving as an introductory component, while Appendices 7.1-7.3 contain supplementary information. Augmented Policy Cloning is a recently developed technique that utilizes a pre-existing policy, known as the "donor", to create an improved policy, known as the "recipient". The recipient is trained to learn diverse actions taken by the donor in various situations by being provided with both the situations and augmented information. The main goal of this technique is to enable the recipient to effectively replicate the donor's behavior in a wide range of tasks. However, successful application of Augmented Policy Cloning requires fine-tuning the technique to fit specific problems. This paper examines its potential in transferring control policies for a four-armed bandit with complex dimensions across different dimensionalities. Additionally, we explore the usefulness of incorporating "shortcuts" – fundamental properties of the donor's behavior – in improving the learning efficiency of the recipient. Our analysis indicates that Augmented Policy Cloning can be a valuable tool for efficient transfer learning in various scenarios with high-dimensional controls. The experiments support their validity and show that the shortcuts of the donor can be conveniently represented as a lower-dimensional structure, known as an "action shortcut manifold". Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of using both unaugated and augmented policy cloning in challenging real-world scenarios where the situations and actions taken by the donor are unknown but some "shortcut observations", which reflect the donor's actions, can be obtained from the donor. This enables the recipient to effectively learn the donor's behavior in a wide range of difficult control problems. The results show that the augmented cloning techniques can successfully transfer control policies across different dimensionalities in these scenarios. The experiments suggest that the usefulness of incorporating action shortcut observations in augmented cloning varies depending on the dimensionalities. The results show that the recipient's performance can be significantly improved when the dimensionalities are low, but minor improvements are observed when the dimensionalities are high. The experiments demonstrate that the augmented cloning techniques can be applied to transfer control policies in a variety of tasks. To validate this, we conducted a test where the donor was an optimized policy for data collection in a control problem where the action space is large. The results show that the recipient, which was trained using Augmented Policy Cloning in a simplified version of the task, was able to efficiently transfer its behavior to an even more complex version of the task. The experiments further demonstrate the efficiency of shortcuts in large-scale reinforcement learning problems. The results provide evidence that the shortcuts can effectively simplify complex control problems, enable the identification of relevant time-critical states, improve collision avoidance, and increase the overall performance of the recipient. A well-known inequality in a graph's embedding has been examined and refined.  Specifically, we looked at how a planar graph's genus is connected to its dual and non-neighboring subgraphs, and we extended this to graphs embedded in other surfaces.  This led us to a general, extended version of the previous result.  Additionally, we investigated the complexity of deciding if a graph can be embedded in a given surface, and we discovered that determining whether a cubic graph can be embedded in a specific surface is very difficult.  Specifically, we showed that this problem is NP-complete for the projective plane and generally for any surface with the exception of spheres and planes.  Similar complexity results were found for other surface embeddings with constraints on the degree of the vertices or the arrangement of their edges.  In a related area, we found that there is no efficient algorithm to check if a graph is Hamiltonian when the possibility of an embedded Hamiltonian path or cycle is also considered.  This complexity holds for all surfaces except for spheres and planes.  Similarly, we discovered that there is no efficient algorithm to check if a graph can be embedded in a given surface such that no two adjacent vertices are connected by an edge.  This complexity also applies to all surfaces except for spheres and planes.  This research connects to previous studies by Thomassen and Vazsonyi, and we verified their conjectures regarding surfaces of genus 1 or 2.  Finally, we extended a result about graphs embedded in a projective plane to non-cubic graphs and we found an upper bound for the number of independent vertices in a connected graph embedded in a Kauler surface.  This bound turned out to be very useful as it allowed us to show that there is a efficient algorithm to check if a graph can be embedded in a Kauler surface. Recent research on Gas Time Projection Chambers demonstrates their potential in detecting weak signals from WIMPs through deep-inelastic scattering analysis. To differentiate between electron and nuclear interactions and identify the target nucleus's direction, new variables are introduced based on the reconstructed scattering direction. Our results show that new observables significantly outperform traditional methods in distinguishing between electron and nuclear recoil types and offer more accurate discrimination. Utilizing these variables in simple sanity checks for analyses conducted in Ref. [arXiv:2006.11893] yields an up to 10-fold improvement in signal efficiency, leading to an equivalent or lower background rate than in the original study. Consequently, this enables the model-independent search for WIMPs to be freed from previous assumptions, and our results indicate that this can result in an up to three times more sensitive interpretation of the data. Future work could involve applying these variables to actual data and utilizing the increased sensitivity to set more stringent constraints on theoretical models, such as the Invariant Mass Distribution for specific event types. Additionally, incorporating these variables may aid in identifying physical signals in regions of the parameter space that were previously excluded due to background contamination. Our code and the generated data are publicly available for further use.

Their expert input can be effectively incorporated to enhance the assessment of driver behavior and improve traffic flow. Our research centers around developing a driver assessment system that incorporates expert feedback to identify aggressive driving behaviors based on a comprehensive driver model. Aggressive driving behaviors are categorized into three primary types: speed, lateral position, and following distance. To measure these aspects, a driver's spatial awareness of the surrounding environment and their ability to adjust to both road conditions and the actions of other drivers are taken into account. A questionnaire was designed to gather feedback from experienced drivers regarding specific driving scenarios, and the responses were analyzed to determine the effectiveness of the assessment system. Our results show that the evaluation of aggressive driving behaviors has been successfully improved, and the assessment of spatial awareness has been achieved. Moreover, the incorporation of expert feedback has been found to provide a more in-depth and accurate understanding of driver behavior compared to assessments based solely on objective driving data. The assessment system primarily consists of two key components: a driver model that incorporates aggressive driving behaviors as a key variable, and a feedback analysis model that gathers and processes expert feedback. The study provides valuable insights into the way experienced drivers behave while driving and offers practical advice on how to incorporate their feedback into the assessment of driver behavior in a more effective manner. Our results have the potential to be applied towards the development of more accurate driver-assistance systems in the future. To account for the distinct electronic properties of graphene and conventional materials, we employ a derived effective superconducting energy gap that varies according to the conductance of the junction. This new gap allows us to provide concrete conductance calculations for graphene-normal conductor and graphene-superconducting conductor junctions, and to explain experimentally observed conductance patterns in graphene-superconducting conductor junctions, ultimately demonstrating quantitive agreement with experimental results. Additionally, our theoretical model predicts zero-bias peaks of specific heights in graphene-superconducting conductor junctions, which can be verified through experimental validation. Moreover, we extend the developed theory to cover the case of a normal conductor connected to a superconducting nanoribbon, producing conductance predictions that can be validated experimentally. Lastly, we speculate on potential future research directions involving graphene, including the investigation of Caroli de Gennes Matricon conductance channels. For a given graph G, having an independence number ρ(G) and a chromatic number χ(G), G is classified as l-pancytic if it can be divided into l subgraphs, each having a chromatic number of χ(G). This research focuses on finding the smallest possible value of l for a graph with n vertices. It initially finds a upper bound of n/ρ(G), then proves the lower bound to be similar, leading to the conclusion that l is at most n/ρ(G) and at least n/ω(G), where ω(G) is the maximum degree of G and ω(G) ≥ ρ(G) ≥ n/n-1 for n ≥ 2. Extra conditions on the graph are required to achieve the lower bound of l. Specifically, if the graph is non-bipartite or has a chromatic number greater than 2, then l is guaranteed to be at least n/ρ(G). We then find the exact values of l for some specific graphs - n-queens problem graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and circular complete bipartite graphs. In these cases, the value of l is either n/ρ(G) or n/ω(G). Moreover, based on ρ(G) and χ(G), we propose an algorithm to construct n subgraphs, each having a chromatic number of χ(G), which can be used to solve the n-queens problem when the independence number and chromatic number of the queue graph converge to the same value. We conclude by providing insights for further research and potential applications in the fields of graph coloring and the n-queens problem. We have also conducted a study to develop a rapid method for obtaining a pancyclic coloring of a graph with a limited number of colors. We have found that a split and a bipartite graph can be colored in at most Δ(G) colors with a pancyclic structure, and this can also be applied to the class of semi-complete graphs. We have found a c_1(c_2(G)+1) upper bound for l in c_1-c_2 graphs. We have found a c_1(c_2(n/G) + n/G) upper bound for l in c_1-c_2 graphs. We have found a (χ(G)+1)(Δ(G)+1) upper bound for l in graphs with a maximum degree Δ(G) and chromatic number χ(G). We have found a n/2 upper bound for l in trees with n vertices.

In this paper, we introduce an innovative technique for generating specialized sparse indirect solvers for solving partial differential equations on uniform grids, specifically designed for stochastic inputs and outputs. Our proposed SASK method, combining static analysis with dynamic kernel inversion, efficiently handles such problems by initially applying a probabilistic relaxation to the given partial differential equation and utilizing it to determine the required matrix entries. By experimentally verifying the accuracy of the resulting approximations, we demonstrate that our SASK method significantly enhances the performance compared to traditional implicit solvers when applied to fundamental stochastic equations like the one-dimensional heat equation. Additionally, we showcase the inherent versatility of the SASK method to adapt to diverse problem specifications. Since its underlying approach is agnostic to the specific partial differential equation, the only prerequisites involve specifying the field of interest, the type of solver desired, and the desired error tolerance, resulting in the automatic selection of the appropriate solver. Furthermore, we also expand on the SASK method to incorporate an additional layer of safety by enabling it to enforce discrete conserved quantities even in the presence of numerical dissipation in the desired solver. By employing a conservative approximation of the given partial differential equation and modifying the probabilistic relaxation operator to incorporate the conservation constraints, we successfully extend the SASK method to ensure the enforcement of discrete conservation constraints on uniform grids, specifically in the context of FEM-based finite difference solvers for partial differential equations. Our proposed approach is specifically designed to augment existing solvers by incorporating conservative approximations that may introduce slight numerical dissipation, and our experimental findings validate the effectiveness of the conservative approximation in ensuring accurate results for both time-dependent and time-independent problems. Finally, we showcase the versatility of the SASK method on a variety of applications, including one-dimensional heat equations, Poisson's equations, and the advection-diffusion equation, thereby emphasizing the inherent generality and usability of the approach. The Sinkhorn algorithm, an efficient method for estimating a transport plan, has proven useful in various fields. It's a simplified version of a more complex approach to solve the Schrödinger problem, a fundamental concept in quantum physics. The Sinkhorn algorithm can be seen as a way to approximate Planckian gradients of a function that's consistent with given marginal laws. This paper explores how the Sinkhorn algorithm handles cases where no solution exists for the Schrödinger problem, finding that it converges towards a solution that's equivalent to a measure that's uniformly distributed over a set called the singular spectrum. We then derive an explicit formula to calculate this measure and provide additional examples to illustrate its applicability. The results derived provide an analytical basis for the Sinkhorn algorithm's behavior in scenarios where no solution exists for the Schrödinger problem. The derived solution is particularly useful when dealing with tasks that involve estimating a quantum state from partial information. We show that using a combination of entropic regularization, as implemented in the Sinkhorn algorithm, and quantum teleportation significantly improves the estimated fidelity of a quantum bit. This increase in fidelity is consistent with all possible measurements and is not limited to specific observables. We further demonstrate that the estimated quantum state achieves the maximum possible overlap with respect to a given subspace of possible states consistent with the given marginal laws, a result that holds both when the subspace is comprised of pure states and when it's a mixture of both pure and mixed states. Measurements obtained using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider have revealed precise measured cross-sections for pairs of top-quarks produced in proton-proton collisions. These collisions occurred at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy and involved 36 fb-1 of data collected during 2015 and 2016. Compared to theoretical quantum chromodynamics models, the measurement shows a 1.7 standard deviation discrepancy. Also measured was the top-quark pair differential distribution for the average momentum of tagged top-quark jets. This distribution showed a 2.9 standard deviation difference compared to quantum chromodynamics models. A parallelizable method, the Fully Implicit Multi-Scale Mixed Nutation Seismic tomography approach (FSMSN), has been developed for reconstructing 3D Earth's models. FSMSN aims to solve inverse and forward problems using a combined 'pre-post-processing' strategy to compute numerical derivatives, thereby reducing computational complexity and facilitating higher-resolution, multi-scale seismic tomography. With FSMSN, only the model where the objective function is maximized needs to be updated, and this occurs after data misfit and regularization gradients are calculated at multiple model points. A 'pre-processing' step iteratively updates a series of smaller multi-dimensional hyper-cubes, where FSMSN's complexity is determined by the size of these hyper-cubes. A 'post-processing' strategy is then applied to interpolate updated values from these hyper-cubes to create a fully updated model, with no need for re-computing forward or inverse problem solutions. One- and multi-dimensional numerical examples demonstrate that FSMSN is comparable to the Sequential Fully Implicit method but has the potential for significant speed-up in 3D Earth's model reconstruction using Multi-Scale seismic tomography. A 3D Extremes-based benchmark test demonstrated FSMSN can handle challenging problems such as maximizing Gaussian functions with ten million data points, with extremely efficient performance and memory usage. This was proven through experiments using ten million data points on a single graphics processing unit, with the ability to up-scale to multi-processors or CPUs. FSMSN has the potential to advance the development of Multi-Scale seismic tomography by providing an efficient and powerful algorithm for reconstructing 3D Earth's models. An implementation of FSMSN is available on the C++ language platform at https://git.unm.edu/unm-gg/FSMSN.git.

Current decision-supporting systems face significant difficulties in generating high-quality solutions when applied to large-scale, complex problems. There is an urgent need for more effective approaches to manage project timelines and interact with complex planning models efficiently. We showcase the effectiveness of this framework by developing and applying it to tackle challenging planning tasks related to underground storage tanks for water and sewage. The crystal's initial shape is mapped to ensure it doesn't distort key detection signals.  By analyzing time-correlated measurements of the crystal's dimensions, the effect of measurement noise on the frequency spectrum can be determined.  This is further utilized to derive equations for analyzing the spectral features related to the crystal's deformation caused by thermal motion.  By calculating the total number of ions in the crystal and applying the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the 2D temperature can be derived from the width of the low-frequency peak in the frequency spectrum.  The outcome is a straightforward method to monitor the ambient temperature using the capacitive sensing technology without it affecting the crystal's shape or required dimensions smaller than 2 mm. In order to isolate and compare the two effects, TERS experiments were conducted under two sets of conditions: one involving resonance Raman of p-systems and another using non-resonant Raman on ionic substances. For p-systems, the EM and CE intertwined due to resonance coupling, making it hard to distinguish between them. In contrast, for monolayer NaCl on Au, a clear distinction could be made, demonstrating a significantly greater EM contribution. Additionally, by employing a 2D autocorrelation technique, the EM and CE signal intensities could be compared directly, resulting in an approximate intensity ratio of 80 to 20. Furthermore, it is shown that lowering the tip-samples distance enhances the CE's contribution but reduces the EM's, suggesting a need to balance these competing influences when attempting to isolate either the EM or CE alone. Crucially, these results challenge prevailing assumptions about TERS, reviving debate about existing interpretations, and offering new insights into the underlying physics of the EMCE model. A widely observed tendency in probabilistic learning is 'probability-matching,' where people tend to choose the most frequently occurring outcome rather than optimizing for rewards. By extending the predictive accumulation framework to incorporate various types of losses, we've developed a model that explains probability-matching as a consequence of adjusted gain settings in low-outcome-probability ranges. Our model, however, does not require the high-outcome-probability range to be identical to the high-reward region. Moreover, the model predicts that probability-matching will occur more frequently under conditions of larger losses and intermixed high and low probability options, both of which are supported by experimental data. Additionally, separate studies have demonstrated the models' relevance to both the presence of negative rewards and the involvement of ventral striatum activity during probability-matching tasks. Since our model focuses primarily on the potential for damage or injury resulting from losses, it may also be applied to other contexts of negative valuation. Ultimately, our models offer a unified framework that explains how different types of losses (both financial and emotional) affect decision-making via varying levels of loss sensitivity. Moreover, the models also highlight the role of adjusted gain settings in contributing to probability-matching. The conceptual and experimental support provided by our models suggest their reliability and validity. The models' broad applicability to scenarios involving negative rewards, their reliance on theories supported by previous studies, and their alignment with self-report data in functional neuroimaging studies further confirm their validity. The models' explanatory power in the domain of probability-matching fails in rare scenarios however, as probability-matching has been observed more frequently in situations where all outcomes have a low probability, not just those below 0.5 as our model suggests. However, this distinction is shown to be an illusion stemming from an incomplete understanding of the logical structure of quantum theory, particularly in how different quantum states are associated. A revised framework is proposed that views all quantum states as variations of a single fundamental one, thereby eliminating the distinction between nonlocality and contextuality and providing a clearer understanding of when a system exhibits nonlocality. The new framework is based on a refinement of the PBR game originally designed to test contextuality, incorporating two key changes: allowing for mixed strategies and incorporating a reward for nonlocality. In contrast to its initial form, the revised game captures both nonlocality and contextuality equally well and develops a quantitative measure of nonlocality that makes contextuality a necessary condition. As a result, the PBR game's core goal of distinguishing local and classical states is rendered redundant, alongside the distinction between nonlocality and contextuality. To validate the new framework, the logical structure of quantum theory is used to derive a strict logical inequality among projectors corresponding to specific quantum states, thereby establishing the nonlocality of a wide range of quantum systems including entangled systems, the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, and the mermin s inequality. Moreover, it is shown that the nonlocality of a wide range of quantum systems follows logically. The revised game's equivalence of nonlocality and contextuality implies that contextuality undercuts nonlocality by making contextuality a necessary condition for nonlocality. Consequently, it is shown that a single context cannot give rise to nonlocality. More generally, it is shown that the classicality of a system follows logically when its contextuality and nonlocality are absent, thereby establishing a logical distinction between nonlocal and non-contextual systems. Furthermore, it is shown that the revised game's logic corresponds with a generalised Clifton-Fuchs inequality applicable across various contextuality scenarios. The new framework provides a logical reason for administering a reward for nonlocality in the PBR game, thereby addressing an earlier controversy about the PBR game's payoff matrix. In conclusion, the revised game's logical structure offers a comprehensive understanding and interpretation of nonlocality and contextuality in quantum theory, thereby advancing basic knowledge in quantum theory. When interacting with a robot that assigns its own meanings to specific task-related inputs, users' ability to complete tasks efficiently might be impacted. However, if the robot shares its mapping strategy with the user, it's likely that the user's performance will improve. This study examines how different levels of transparency about a robot's input mappings affect human performance when completing a series of tasks that involve executing a rotary endgame with a mobile manipulator. We found that revealing a robot's chosen input mappings had no significant impact on performance in tasks where specific inputs were constant across multiple interactions. On the other hand, revealing the robot's mappings for interactions with variable inputs notably improved performance. A key conclusion from this research is that the same level of transparency can have different effects on human performance depending on the characteristics of the task at hand. Furthermore, while revealing a robot's mappings might enhance human performance in some situations, it is not always necessary for task completion. In fact, our study demonstrates that in cases where the mappings need to adapt to changing task parameters, not revealing the robot's choices can actually lead to more efficient interactions in the long run. This study's findings suggest that the decision to share a robot's input mappings should be based on specific task requirements and considerations. What's more, these research findings are relevant not only to the field of human-robot collaboration but also to computer systems that interact with human users. We provide several design guidelines that system designers can use to determine the optimal level of transparency for specific tasks. Finally, this study has the potential to contribute to future research in other areas of interactive transparency. Researchers could build upon this work by investigating other aspects of transparency in human-robot interaction systems. One potential area for exploration is designing systems that reveal statistical patterns or correlations within robot input mappings. Another area that is worthy of further investigation is the design of systems that share user-centric goals rather than specific input mappings. To address these questions, we plan to conduct more comprehensive research in this area in the future. For now, our study offers several key takeaways that system designers can use when deciding on the level of transparency for their systems. First, system designers should consider the type of tasks that users will perform interactively. Second, revealing sensitive system information may not always lead to better performance. Third, system designers can improve human performance in some cases by sharing task-relevant information. Finally, the same level of transparency is not always beneficial across different tasks as demonstrated by our study which shows that revealing transparency in tasks where specific inputs are constant had no significant impact

Time-series data often provides valuable insights into systems or processes when their behavior over time is analyzed. However, individual time-series values are typically linked to relevant geographical, textual, or compositional attributes that offer additional insight into what the time-series represents. Current time-series visualizations usually isolate the time-series data from the broader context, making it difficult to draw connections between these dimensions. To address this issue, we introduce time-series driven visualization techniques that synchronize time-series data with other visual elements, such as maps, tables, and graphs, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the data. We outline best practices for creating comprehensive time-series visualizations, develop four concrete schemes, and evaluate their effectiveness on real-world datasets in a professional data analysis environment. Our work aims to provide a systematic approach to time-series data exploration that enhances domain experts' ability to extract meaningful information. Additionally, we believe that these techniques can be applied beyond domain experts by professionals in data visualization fields. We showcase 11 distinct time-series visualization cases, offering a foundation for further research in this area.
