The application of spin-orbit coupling to theoretical models of YSR states enables us to accurately account for certain experimental findings. In the case of magnetic monomers or dimers integrated into a metallic surface, spin-orbit coupling results in spin-dependent shifts to the YSR state peaks located at low and high energy spectrums. Such effects are characterized by a specific relationship where the positions of high energy peaks are equally affected but on the opposite end of the spectrum they are twice as far apart as would be expected in the absence of such coupling. Consequently, when considering a magnetic dimer rather than a monomer, spin-orbit coupling results in two distinct sets of shifted YSR state peaks instead of four as would be predicted in the absence of such coupling. Such predictions align with experimental evidence of YSR states as observed in the clean and covered (110) surface of Au. Furthermore, in the case of the clean (110) surface of Au, spin-orbit coupling results in the merging of two dominant YSR state peaks to three, as evidenced through magnetic umklapp processes. Such understanding is also applied to a recent study examining the variation in spin-polarization as a function of energy following the integration of Fe dimers onto a (110) surface of Au. Such integration results in the creation of four distinct peaks, each exhibiting opposite spin-polarization, as compared to the clean (110) surface of Au where only two peaks are observed. Such effects of spin-orbit coupling are considered non-existent in the absence of such coupling. This research introduces a novel downsampling strategy for LIDAR point clouds to streamline scene registration, including dynamic features. A thorough evaluation of existing downsampling methods was conducted to illustrate their impact on registration accuracy, including Monte Carlo simulations to isolate the influence of density. A new algorithm is proposed to downsample the point clouds generated during Monte Carlo iterations, specifically tailored for dynamic environments. By optimizing the downsampling strategy, a notable improvement in registration precision was observed, specifically a 25% increase in the 95% confidence interval for Monte Carlo simulations in contrast to random density sampling. Moreover, the proposed approach is versatile and compatible with various Monte Carlo-based registration techniques. While the method was conceived with Monte Carlo registrations in mind, its application is not limited to this specific use case. Rather, it can be used for any registration task that benefits from downsampling, such as computational efficiency or a decrease in noise-related issues, and is particularly suited for scenarios involving dense dynamic objects. To illustrate the utility of the method, a practical application on a real-world parking lot scenario is presented, showcasing its potential in real-world use cases. In order to facilitate the implementation of the proposed approach, a simple and efficient tool has been developed, which is compatible with popular software frameworks such as PCL and the AWS car segmentation toolkit. A detailed description of the implementation, along with the code base, can be found at https://github.com/JoaoBPL/dynamic-downsampling. A practical evaluation of the method was carried out using real-world datasets from the KITTI dataset and a parking lot video, revealing a notable decrease in processing time. A discussion on potential future directions is presented, focusing on exploiting dynamic information to enhance downsampling, which may not be readily available in most real-world datasets. A preliminary evaluation of dynamic information has been conducted to illustrate its potential. A final conclusion is provided along with potential future areas of research. In particular, the results demonstrate that dynamic information can be used not only to downsample but also to create a initial guess for registration, as well as to improve the overall performance in the absence of dense dynamic objects. A last point is made regarding the significance of incorporating dynamic elements to improve registration precision, which may not be readily available in some scenarios. A summary of the results is given at the end. Overall, the present work seeks to contribute meaningfully to the development of catadiagnostic systems for dynamic objects by addressing a basic, yet crucial, problem that has widespread relevance. The availability of satellite data has increased dramatically with the proliferation of low-cost, commercial satellites. The analysis of this data type has seen a significant shift from traditional methods, now largely being handled by deep learning techniques. These new methods have shown promise but come with a cost, necessitating substantial datasets and high-performance computing equipment. The following research explores ways to reduce the cost of conducting deep learning based satellite image analysis by using graphics processing units (GPUs) in a distributed setting. The investigation first evaluates the effectiveness of two popular deep learning architectures for enhancing image resolution, and it presents a novel approach for enhancing image bands. The study then presents methods for increasing the efficiency of these techniques' computation and discusses how to distribute GPU-based tasks effectively. The findings of this research of this are tested on actual scenarios: improving the illumination of low-quality images and enhancing the resolution of images captured under cloudy conditions. The investigation demonstrates that using multiple GPUs leads to significant cost reductions without compromising outcomes while using the novel approaches yields better performance than traditional methods. The total cost savings achieved in the experimental scenarios range from 66% to 87%. The research presents a new method for distributing complex computer tasks, which is generally applicable and can be utilized in various fields. A highly saturated and nonlinear change in reflectivity occurs at high fluences, and changes in the beam focus point reveal the absorption coefficient to be spatially non-uniform. Electron redistribution within the material is identified as the cause of this observed nonlinear change, and resulting surface plasmon frequency changes correlate with this phenomenon, occurring 14.5 femtoseconds after excitation. Notably, this time lag in the surface plasmon frequency change in relation to the electron temperature measurement supports the thermal contribution to the surface plasmon, and further clarifies the discrepancy between the electron and lattice temperatures observed in the study. A model describing the SPP frequency as a function of electron and lattice temperatures also accounts for the multiple-peak occurrence in the inverse nonlinear changes observed across different beam focus points. Focusing the beam to a central point results in two distinct peaks emerging, whereas at larger focus points, only a single peak dominates. Conversely, at lower focus points, the central peak dominates over the inverse nonlinear changes. In accordance with this phenomenon's origin from the material's inverse nonlinear changes, it is hypothesized that the inversion of the central peak occurs due to the reversal of the electron and lattice temperatures. Consequently, when the lattice temperature exceeds the electron temperature, the contribution to the surface plasmon from the lattice becomes predominant, and when the converse occurs, the contribution from the electron becomes predominant once more. Combining this phenomenon with the material's inverse nonlinear changes, and combining it with the model describing the SPP frequency as a function of electron and lattice temperatures, allows for accurate simulation of the material's picosecond time-resolved reflectivity measurement. Adversarial attacks on deep learning models have raised serious concerns within the security community. To counter these threats, experts have proposed various countermeasures. This study focuses on counteracting attacks through generative adversarial networks. Generative adversarial networks have garnered significant attention in both academic and industrial settings, and are widely employed in text, image, sound, and other types of generative tasks. This study aims to explore how GANs can be applied to counteract adversarial attacks. In contrast to traditional defense mechanisms that are often vulnerable to specific attack techniques, data-driven approaches like GANs can learn and adapt to counter a broader spectrum of adversarial attacks. The main challenges in using GANs for defense mechanisms involve training issues, particularly the need to balance generative quality and accuracy in the face of malicious inputs. The proposed approach uses a combination of adversarial examples and legitimate inputs during the training process to achieve a more accurate output. Additionally, this study highlights the potential effectiveness of GANs in counteracting attacks, particularly those using the black-box scenario. Based on the experimental results using the CIFAR-10 dataset, using GANs to enhance input quality can successfully prevent adversarial attacks in the black-box scenario, with a notable accuracy increase to 84.59%. In contrast, using GANs in the white-box scenario did not yield a significant defense benefit. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of GANs in counteracting adversarial attacks and sheds light on the underlying challenges and mechanisms. The simplicity and adaptability of GANs make them an attractive choice for defending against a broader range of adversarial attacks. Automated segmentation of multiple sclerosis lesions in magnetic resonance images (MRIs) across various hospitals is a complex task due to consistent labeling discrepancies among expert radiologists. Given that prior studies have primarily focused on universal lesion definition criteria from a single hospital source, this research employed a novel approach to segment MS lesions, achieving uniformity in annotations across a combined dataset from multiple hospitals. Although initial attempts without experience replay demonstrated annotation inconsistencies, achieving uniform consistency required annotating a combined dataset from three hospitals, requiring three times the effort. A modified experience replay strategy was developed by combining multiple transformed versions of a dataset from a single hospital, mimicking the annotation style of the multiple hospitals. This strategy allowed for consistent annotation of MS lesions in cases of reduced dataset availability. Additionally, the segmented MS lesions from multiple hospitals were combined to refine a multiple sclerosis lesion detection model, which demonstrated improved performance on a multiple sclerosis lesion detection dataset. A statistical multiple sclerosis lesion probability map was generated by combining the probability maps of multiple models, which also served as a metric to quantify the presence of MS lesions across different hospitals. This probability map showed improved performance compared to individual models, which was also validated as a biomarker for disease quantification. MS lesion segmentation across different hospitals was also evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient, showing significant improvement with the proposed approach. A similar approach was also developed to quantify the presence of cerebral atrophy using MRI scans from multiple hospitals. These findings demonstrate the potential of experience replay in reducing the challenges associated with annotating medical images, including labeling discrepancies and data scarcity. A comprehensive evaluation of the segmentation performance of the proposed MS lesion segmentation approach was not feasible due to contractual restrictions with multiple hospital sources, limiting the assessment of its generalization capabilities across different domains. A similar limitation applied to the evaluation of the AT segmentation approach. These concerns are the subject of a companion letter. A multiple responsibility framework was also proposed to ensure the accountability of the MS lesion segmentation model in the presence of data biases and inconsistencies. This research demonstrated the potential of the experience replay strategy in achieving uniform annotation consistency of MS lesions in MRI scans from multiple hospitals. Additionally, the incorporated multiple responsibility framework can be applied to other medical imaging applications, including data obtained from single hospitals. A converted MCML code to PyTORCH was included for enhanced model flexibility. The analysis was applied to idealized cores with uniform density and rotating, uniform molecular gas to represent different types of cores. The study covered a wide range of initial conditions, including various values of the core's central density, radius, mass, and rotational velocity. The results provided a comprehensive picture of core collapse and protostar formation, focusing on the effects of geometry, mass, and angular momentum. A comprehensive set of curves and tables were derived, offering a systematic understanding of core evolution in relation to standard core mass function and protostar formation. Additionally, the effect of the core's initial mass on protostar formation and formation efficiency was examined, as well as the efficiency of core collapse and protostar formation in relation to the core's initial mass. The study also enabled a comparison with typical values for the free parameters of the simulations, offering an efficient tool for quickly identifying which parameters influence core evolution and protostar formation. The exploration of supramolecular helical metals has been driven primarily by the ability to induce chirality in the lattice through external stimuli in previously non-chiral systems. In the field's rapid development, multiple systems have been discovered that exhibit chirality upon increasing pressure, but the influence of this pressure remains limited to the chemical bonds within the lattice structure. The discovery of supramolecular metal perovskites, where rare earth ions are surrounded by specific organic molecules, has led to the investigation of additional external influences. The rare earth ions can be arranged in an alternating pattern, resulting in the occurrence of polar crystal phases that are frustrated below a certain temperature, known as the N\'eel temperature. Through Monte Carlo simulations, researchers have now discovered that a phase transition in these polar crystal structures occurs in supramolecular metal perovskites when the packing density exceeds 0.5, resulting in the formation of twisted ice structures. Furthermore, at even higher packing densities, two new polar crystal phases emerge, characterized by a hexagonal structure with $p3m1$ symmetry and a structure with $p6/mmm$ symmetry, respectively. The former displays properties similar to hexagonal boron nitride, while the latter exhibits properties similar to herringbone materials. The use of optical spin-injection in supramolecular metal perovskites makes them suitable for the creation of novel spintronics devices and the observation of the twisted ice phenomenon, which has significant implications for quantum materials research. By incorporating magnetic ions with half-filled orbital configurations alongside specific rare earth ions, researchers have discovered that the resulting structure exhibits ferromagnetic ordering at or below the rare earth ordering temperature. Consequently, the possibility of creating a quantum state similar to a Bose-Einstein condensate using phonons or the magnetic lattice is also being explored. The phenomenon of spin-injection optical coupling has been discovered to have a significant impact on the thermal properties between certain rare earth ions, where it gives rise to the occurrence of a fourth-order phase transition and a lattice distortion in certain cases, including the possible emergence of a hexagonal structure. By strategically incorporating specific rare earth ions with specific magnetic properties, researchers have discovered that the resulting structure exhibits a phenomenon known as reverse Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling and the possible emergence of a hexagonal structure. Theoretical predictions have also been confirmed by experimental observations of the possible emergence of a hexagonal structure in an SrEuFe[PO$_2${}$\beta$-APSO}] multiple exchange metal perovskite

Pretrained language models have achieved remarkable success in diverse tasks and datasets. Leveraging these models requires breaking down input text into distinct tokens, but the impact of special tokens on their performance remains poorly understood. This study investigates and clarifies the significance of special tokens in Pretrained Language Models (PLMs), highlighting their adaptability and need to be tailored to specific tasks and datasets. In contrast to the prevalent practice of including special tokens, we propose an alternative method where tokens are segmented solely into basic types, including numeric, English, and non-English characters. By doing so, we eliminate unnecessary spacers and showcase improved results in PLM inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. The advantages of our approach are demonstrated in two scenarios: first, in task-agnostic models; and second, in task-specific models, where results are compared across different datasets, including GLUE benchmarks. Notably, the efficiency gain is particularly pronounced in models used in online applications with significant parameter counts, such as the XLSR-204k multi-language XLSR-104k models, leading to reduced inference time. The sources of this improved efficiency are examined through successive case studies. Specifically, the following gains are attributed to each scenario: 1) a 10% decrease in token access rate; 2) a 30% decrease in token neural network layer usage; and 3) a 2.5% decrease in token neural neural network layer usage. By quantifying these individual contributions, we offer a theoretical explanation for observed performance and efficiency effects when using pretrained language models. The research code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zeinon/gcokenization. This work represents a significant improvement over previous work, including Li et al. 2020 and Zhang et al. 2021. The research gaps addressed by this study include isolated token segmentation approaches in the past and combining efficiency and accuracy in the present. The new ideas introduced in the paper include special token clarification, automatic spacer removal, and the understanding of token utilization. Our findings demonstrate that this transformed ViT network not only surpasses the majority of existing methods but also outperforms its original form and a more complicated version on multiple benchmark datasets. Through careful analysis of NLI data, we identified three distinct forms of negation that necessitate consideration in NLI. I supplemented the existing RoBERTa-based NLI framework with three novel specialization modules for handling these forms of negation. Experimental results demonstrate that the enhanced framework outperforms the baseline in NLI tasks. Notably, our focus on contravening negation contributed significantly to the improvement. The findings also suggest that incorporating modules for negation poses minimal adverse effects on NLI performance overall, including when using NLI datasets with reduced negation content. The proposed model, which we term NegRoBERTa, is subsequently evaluated in relation to other prominent NLI models. Despite significant advancements by Transformer-based models in machine learning, they tend to be impractical for real-time processing due to their quadratic complexity in sequence length. This is costly in terms of computation and memory storage. To mitigate this issue, look-ahead attention was proposed, a method that enables predicting attention values based on future input tokens. Current implementations, however, rely on precomputed attention matrices and the inverse square root law for efficiency, which is very demanding in both memory and time. To resolve this issue, we present FastLookAheadAttention, an optimized look-ahead attention method that is highly parallelizable and thus suitable for fast training and efficient inference. Experiments demonstrate that our approach is superior to the original look-ahead attention in terms of speed and memory usage while providing strong base performance in translation quality. Notably, FastLookAheadAttention can be combined with sparse attention for even more significant performance improvements. Our final model achieved a new benchmark in efficiency with only 35% of the original 16GB GPU's memory while still achieving a high BLEU score of 41.16 on the en-fr WMT dataset. This breakthrough makes it possible to use look-ahead attention in the deep learning community at a cost comparable to contemporary state-of-the-art models. FastLookAheadAttention has also outperformed its competitors in terms of speed under limited GPU conditions, producing a latency of 50ms for generating one sentence with 15 tokens, which is significantly lower than the original look-ahead method. This exceptional performance makes it possible to utilize look-ahead attention in real-time applications. The code for this approach has been made available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/steffenwied/FastLookAheadAttention. Our model-free method also extends to powering the probability method, allowing us to derive exact solutions for a range of time-dependent options. To gain insight into what features convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are learning, we develop a generalized method called the Latent Visual Semantic Explainer (LaViSE). This method analyzes the complexity of a CNN's intermediate layers using separate, simpler networks that have been specifically designed to mimic the behavior of the original network. By making these new networks progressively more complex, LaViSE identifies the specific intermediate layers within a CNN that are responsible for extracting biologically relevant features, such as edges and color information, through the use of a search space defined by the architecture of the original network. By doing so, it generates text descriptions of these extracted features at an unprecedentedly later stage than previous methods, demonstrating that some networks are capable of naturally acquiring the principles of object recognition outlined in DiCarlo and Belhumeur 2000. LaViSE successfully reveals the internal workings of four state-of-the-art networks by identifying which features they use to generate their final outputs. Furthermore, it significantily enhances the state-of-the-art performance in visual recognition tasks when applied as a regularizer to ResNet-50, resulting in a robust 91.0 vs. 88.3 on the ImageNet benchmark for top-1 accuracy. Individuals' familiarity with travel time to HIV care facilities may influence their treatment adherence, but reliable travel time data is often limited in studies of patient behavior. We address this challenge using a unique single-hidden-layer feedforward neural network model to forecast the probability of patients initiating and continuing HIV treatment based on geographical factors and facility characteristics. Our approach employs a proprietary data set that bridges demographic information with discrete geographic data, marked by geographic facility codes and patient zip codes. We calculate various measures of travel time, such as driving distance and accessibility to facilities, to create diverse features for the model. With a binary classification framework, our model achieves high cross-validation accuracy in predicting new patients' initiation and continuation rates. The estimated probability outcomes can then be applied to enhance resource allocation by estimating treatment adherence for new facilities or those with unknown characteristics. Moreover, our model's output can inform policy decisions that minimize expected outcomes by adjusting specific resource variables, such as the number of HIV care facilities. This minimization problem was solved using the coordinate descent method with the help of the scipy library. The results indicate an optimal reduction in expected outcomes of approximately 8% in different scenarios. By leveraging geographical data and facility codes, our approach offers an efficient method for strategic planning in the public health domain. Furthermore, the model's ability to operate with limited data compared to traditional regression models increases its practicality and adaptability in real-world applications. As the availability and reliability of travel time estimates continue to improve, they may further influence patient behavior, presenting an opportunity for future research on the impact of travel time on HIV treatment adherence. With the ongoing advancements in automotive technology, future studies may also examine how self-driving vehicles can enhance travel time familiarity and the subsequent impact on patient behavior. The proposed model can be expanded to other fields, such as medical resource planning, by integrating various geocoded health data types, like cancer care and organ transplantation. The associated code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/adinwang/GeographicNeuralNetwork. Lastly, our model's output highlights a pressing policy issue: many new patients are still able to adhere to treatment at existing facilities, suggesting that further improvements in resource allocation may have limited effectiveness until more individuals become treatment-naive. To enable seamless navigation to these results, we have included an embedded interactive visualization in this document that demonstrates the model's predictions based on geographical factors and facility characteristics. A comprehensive study, employing neutron scattering, has been conducted to examine the interplay between the crystal structure and the magnetic ordering of a metastable skyrmion phase in a substance. Initially, we outline the underlying physical properties and provide a detailed description of a new type of skyrmion arrangements that are stable at lower temperatures and are induced by crystal structure changes. Using in-depth neutron scattering analysis, we successfully distinguish between the signature neutron scattering patterns created by the underlying crystal structure and those generated by the magnetic skyrmions. Our findings reveal that the metastable skyrmion phase in this substance is characterized by specific crystal structure transitions at low temperatures, leading to the breakdown of symmetry and the transformation of the skyrmion lattice into a more uniform magnetic phase. This study employs comparative analysis with a closely related substance to further illustrate the correlation between the metastable skyrmim phase and the breaking of crystal structure symmetries. Ultimately, our data illustrate how the collective behavior of the crystal structure and the magnetic ordering of the skyrmions in this substance are closely intertwined.

Deep learning models frequently incorporate assumptions that result in predictive distributions that fail to accurately capture uncertainty in real-world scenarios. In an attempt to overcome this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach that makes the most of the benefits of Bayesian methods and the efficiency of predictive uncertainty estimation. This proposed method, referred to as the generalized posterior expectation of the squared deviation (Gpesd), involves taking the expectation of a squared deviation measure between new data and the mean of samples generated by sampling from the predictive distribution. Bayesian methods allow for uncertainty quantification but often come with computational limitations due to the complexity of their approximated posterior distributions. In order to bypass this limitation, we develop an analytical expression for Gpesd based on the Laplace approximation for Gaussian mixture models, a common fit for the posterior distribution in practical applications. Through experimental evaluation, the predictive distributions generated via the Gpesd method demonstrate greater alignment with observed data than those generated via the predictive entropy method, and its computational requirements are significantly lower than those of the variational inference method, particularly in cases where the posterior distribution needs to be approximated. In addition to these results, the Gpesd method's versatility is further illustrated through its application in classification tasks with datasets like the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. In these cases, the classification accuracy is observed to be more robust in scenarios involving the Gpesd method than the predictive entropy method. In a final assessment of the method's worth, the empirical results suggest that the Gpesd method outperforms the predictive entropy method and variational inference in terms of balance between predictive accuracy and robustness. It is worth noting that the Gpesd method's main advantages reside in its ability to generate robust predictive distributions that accurately capture uncertainty and its computational efficiency as an alternative to Bayesian methods when the assumptions of these methods do not hold. In total, the contributions of this research consist of a new approach, the Gpesd method, for generating predictive distributions that accurately capture uncertainty, an analytical expression for the Gpesd based on the Laplace approximation for Gaussian mixture models, an experimental evaluation in classification tasks with results comparable to or superior to state-of-the-art methods, an assessment of the Gpesd method's robustness in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, and an empirical demonstration of the Gpesd method's effectiveness in scenarios where deep learning-based methods frequently fall short. characterized by intense, narrow emission lines, often associated with the breakout
regimes of supernovae and the emergence of hot stars. This research focuses on 88
Green Pea galaxies (out of a total of 399) within the redshift range of 0.5 to 1.0
found in the CANDELS survey, with the aim of studying their star-forming activities
and black hole activities using spectral and imaging data. By analyzing their star
formation rates and gas consumption rates from spectral data, we observed that
star-forming activities have ceased for the majority of galaxies, yet a smaller
group exhibits the presence of active, massive black holes. Our analysis further
revealed that rapid gas consumption and ceasing star-forming activities often occur
simultaneously. This study demonstrates that merging galaxies contribute significantly
to the formation of galaxies in the early universe, based on their gas consumption
rates and velocities of their outflowing gas. Additionally, we discovered a strong
correlation between outflow velocities and galaxy masses, which supports the idea
that merging galaxies can lead to the rapid infusion of gas into central regions. 
Utilizing advanced modeling techniques to analyze composite spectra, we found that
infusing gas into central regions does not fully explain the observed outflow
velocities; instead, we propose the existence of powerful, self-sustaining outflows
powered by massive black holes. Such outflows would remove obstacles, enabling the
infusion of gas into central regions and the exposure of central supermassive black
holes, as seen in active galactic nuclei. This research supports the idea that
infusing gas into central regions by merging galaxies plays an essential role in the
infusion of gas into central regions and the exposure of central supermassive black
holes, an idea consistent with the observed properties of merging galaxies in the
general universe. We calculated gas consumption times to be approximately 100

The task of extracting summaries automatically is now feasible due to the advancement of neural models, however, high-quality human fact-checking is necessary to validate these models' performance. To enable fast and accurate human involvement, we've created a qualification pipeline to filter and assign seasoned annotators to the task. We've also developed a comprehensive annotation guide and conducted two rounds of hiring, resulting in a team of experienced annotators capable of efficiently working on automatic summary quality evaluation. Furthermore, in response to the recent invasion of Ukraine, we organized a volunteer-driven effort to gather donations for the people affected by this conflict, with our project being an example of a collaborative initiative. This kind of community-driven approach can be applied to various social causes, as demonstrated by our own Donations Verification task. In which, annotators perform difficult tasks of collecting and verifying donations, with impressive results, as within one month of the Ukraine invasion, our team was able to verify over 0.9 million dollars in donations. Additionally, in this FLAME-2021 paper, we're making our qualification pipeline and annotation guide publicly available, so that the research community can easily replicate our results and improve the quality of automatic summary models. The pipeline and annotation guide can be accessed at https://forms.glasgow.ac.uk/annotation-work/2021/inv. KEY WORDS: automatic summary, annotation, verification, open-source pipeline, social impact.

Text-video retrieval has received significant interest in recent years, with researchers in the field pursuing easy-to-implement, effective models. This work proposes TS2-Net, a two-stream Transformer model designed to enhance text-video retrieval performance through the creation of accurate spatial-temporal video representations. By incorporating an effective motion template extraction mechanism, TS2-Net generates a concise video representation, thereby improving representation quality and reducing computation requirements. In particular, our findings indicate that representing 8 seconds of video content within 100 pixels requires only 200 dimensions, a substantial reduction from the 8000 dimensions required to represent 8 seconds of video content with length 224. Video representations produced by TS2-Net are then used in conjunction with a simple retrieval model consisting of an adaptive contrastive loss and Transformer-based video encoding for optimal results. Our model exhibits state-of-the-art performance on widely used video retrieval benchmarks, specifically top 1 recall @ 1 on VGSA-VT and top 1 recall @ 1 on ActivityNet Capts while also being more efficient than existing methods. We have made TS2-Net available on our team's website at this URL: https://sites.es.aau.at/ts2net/., where you can find additional information including our code and data used during model development. This contribution is significant as we have conducted a thorough analysis of spatial-temporal representations and provided insight into their characteristics in the process of developing TS2-Net. Our findings indicate that current video representations are dominated by texture rather than motion, a fact we utilized in the design of TS2-Net. This work is a first in its examination of spatial-temporal video representations and has paved the way for the development of more effective models in the text-video retrieval domain. Our model outperforms existing models when used in conjunction with vision-language pre-training models, a fact we utilized in our own training procedure. Our contributions are significant as we have provided a simple yet effective model design that offers better performance and efficiency, an area in need of improvement in the text-video retrieval domain. This work is a first in its examination of retrieval performance as a function of spatial and temporal locations in video content. Our findings suggest that model performance is significantly limited by temporal complexity, an insight we have provided in the development of TS2-Net. Our work is significant as it allows for the design of models tailored to specific application requirements, an insight we have provided in the development of TS2-Net. Our findings suggest that current video representations are best described as having a dominant texture

This investigation explores the influence of electromagnetic forces on the quantum mechanics of Klein-Gordon particles within the frameworks of globally hyperbolic spacetimes and their relation to an initial data set. The study reveals that a particle's quantum states can be linked to a pre-geometric, fundamental Hilbert space even when the gravitational field is considered to have an insignificant effect. The presence of a metric with varying geometric implications gives rise to novel phenomena - particle creation and transformation due to gravitational influences in certain spacetime conditions. The research also demonstrates that, in selected scenarios, such as globally hyperbolic spaces or a specific, asymptotically flat case (the Schwarzschild spacetime), the quantum states can be mapped to a phase space, followed by a focused analysis of the quantum mechanics of a single KG-particle in the Schwarzschild spacetime. The investigation concludes by deriving initial data definitions for a static, asymptotically flat spacetime and provides initial comparisons of QGKGe metrics with the Schwarzschild and Coulomb spacetimes through explicit calculations. The study ultimately enables a thorough analysis of QGKGe metrics by comparing them with known, exactly solved gravity-theoretic models. The research findings indicate that a particle's quantum mechanics can be described using a pre-geometric Hilbert space, and that a particle's evolution can be characterized within the framework of a phase space, underscoring the quantum implications for particles navigating a wide range of spacetimes, from Schwarzschild to cosmologically evolving spacetimes. Spartan bypasses traditional non-regularization methods, which can lead to overfitting, by balancing exploration and exploitation. It achieves this through a regularized objective function that diverges from the optimal solution, representing unproven hypotheses, and converges to a tighter, potentially better solution. Spartan leverages the one-standard-deviation rule, where it samples weights from the optimal distribution during training, enabling it to escape local minima and improve upon the original performance. Our experiments demonstrate that Spartan surpasses state-of-the-art compression methods across various benchmarks, achieving better performance. Our findings also illustrate that, in some cases, zero-shot improvement can be achieved and, more surprisingly, that improved results may become apparent before training is completed. Embedding dynamic graphs poses significant challenges compared to static graphs due to the inherent temporal patterns they exhibit. The conventional approach in unsupervised graph representation learning often disregards these temporal patterns, integrating temporal information as an afterthought. As a result, the performance of embedded graphs on downstream tasks is frequently inconsistent and dependent on task-specific designs. The causes of these issues include the failure to capture temporal patterns, the inadequate exploitation of temporal information, and the inability to adapt embedded graphs to temporal data. The proposed Temporal Dynamic Graph Neural Network offers a new understanding of temporal patterns in graph data and provides a universal solution to embedding graphs dynamically. The TDGNN computes temporal patterns as a product of orthogonal matrices, derived from Temporal Principal Component Analysis, and combines them with graph structure information using multiple instance learning. The model also adjusts embedded graphs to suit temporal data and demonstrates superior performance on real-world datasets compared to other state-of-the-art methods, achieving improved consistency and more efficient design in embedded graphs. The performance of TDGNN is further enhanced when applied to downstream tasks. The source code of TDGNN is available at https://github.com/sekilawie/TDGNN. The model's detailed architecture and implementation have been illustrated in Figure 1 and Table 1, respectively. The main contributions of TDGNN are its novel capture of temporal patterns in graph data and the development of a universal solution to embedding graphs dynamically. The model's key design elements include its utilization of Temporal Principal Component Analysis, the definition of the graph-temporal relation pair, and the design of the multiple instance learning loss function. The model's scalability has been increased by minimizing the memory usage of each agent and the use of sparse matrices. The model's performance has been demonstrated to be superior to other state-of-the-art methods, both on embedded graphs and downstream tasks. However, the data indicated the resonance's characteristics differ significantly - it had a much broader width, a significantly reduced height, and a distinctly different energy dependence compared to the observed $^{8}$He resonance. These new results raise substantial doubts about the validity of statistical models used in astrophysics and particle physics. Furthermore, they suggest that, under specific conditions, these models underestimate low-energy molecular states by a factor of tens of thousands. We identify a resonance problem with two distinct eigenvalues, one of which is positive, denoted as $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$. A function $F$ is then sought for a quotient elliptic equation on the sphere's upper half, such that the given eigenvalues become critical points in a functional with $F$ as its variable. This quotient problem shares similarities with its fully spherical counterpart but exhibits a divergence in their respective solution properties, marked by a shift in the pattern of their growth as the given parameters ($k,l$) change. Due to their capability to capture subtle differences in pose and other relevant features, large-scale person re-identification methods have seen success. However, their high memory requirements, making them unsuitable for devices with limited resources such as the GPU100, limit their practical application. This paper proposes a technique to reduce the embedded feature space's sensitivity to pose to learn a more discriminative representation. We employ a minimal number of parameters, equal to the number of classes, by introducing the Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), thereby achieving significant performance gains. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on standard person re-identification benchmarks, with a paired precision@1/recognition score of 98.22% / 98.95% on MSMT, outperforming the best available approach by 3% in terms of memory usage and 1% in accuracy. Moreover, we set a new benchmark for person re-identification on the challenging large-scale SOP and SystemuShanghaiTech benchmarks at precision@1: 98.95% and 99.15%, respectively. The code and model used in this research can be found at the provided GitHub repository. A Tier-2 component of England's Covid-19 Test and Trace program sought to understand the movement of the virus through contact tracing, particularly in areas experiencing high infection rates. This program included a public health aspect which involved sending staff to trace Covid-19 cases within local areas, in contrast to the primary, digital-based contact tracing method. A study examining the effectiveness of this local tracing effort found it had a very minor impact on reducing infections when considered in isolation, however, when paired with increased digital contact tracing efforts within the same region, it demonstrated some limited benefits in reducing infections. Furthermore, a subsequent analysis focused on specific time periods showed that the local tracing effort was most effective immediately after it was implemented, but that its effects tended to fade over time. Importantly, the study found that the local tracing effort was not successful in reducing infections within areas that were experiencing high infection rates, but rather it helped to slow the spread of the virus elsewhere, allowing these regions to prepare for the rollout of the primary, digital contact tracing method. Guidelines for conducting similar program evaluations are also offered in the study's conclusion. It suggests that the most effective approach may be a hybrid model which combines both local and digital contact tracing methods in regions experiencing high infection rates. Specifically, the study offers three potential strategies for implementing this hybrid model: pairing local tracing for high infection rate areas with distant tracing for areas with lower infection rates, or combining local and distant tracing methods within those areas, or finally implementing a hybrid model which combines all three methods - local, distant, and mixed - through a sliding scale approach that adjusts the proportion of each method based on infection rates. 

Keywords: Covid-19, Test and Trace, local tracing, program evaluation, mixed methods

The spectroscopic analysis provided by the TRES instrument at the Smithson Telescope has offered new insights into Melotte 72, a nearby star cluster located at 1,636 parsecs. By examining radial velocities, our research has determined that all 44 cluster members, spanning a broad range of spectral types from O to M, share a relatively high velocity of 39.85 km/s. The large sample size of these members has allowed us to set tight constraints on the cluster's origin, age, and solar composition. We discovered that Melotte 72, born approximately 1 million years ago, is a relatively young cluster. Its origin is also linked to the Perseus molecular cloud. The cluster's mass, spanning a broad range from 9 to 26 solar masses, exhibits a suppressed distribution above 10 solar masses and is consistent with recent star formation studies in the same region. The cluster's members will eventually leave the cluster as a result of adiabatic expansion, an outcome unique to low-mass star clusters such as this one. The cluster's relatively short lifespan means that Melotte 72 will likely disband within 1-2 million years. This, in combination with its already moderate age, makes it less likely to experience a core collapse and instead follow the conventional path of star cluster evolution. The TRES survey has contributed significantly to our understanding of the dynamics and evolution of this and other star clusters in similar dynamical environments. The dataset obtained will aid in the identification of potential young stellar members in other star clusters. The cluster's data on stellar masses, radii, luminosities, and radii have been made available for independent verification and to compare with theoretical models for pre-main-sequence stars. The data can be accessed at https://www2.cao.upm.es/TRESMelotte72. Directly regressing camera calibration parameters from images can lead to more accurate results than traditional methods, especially when using sufficient data. We explore two key aspects: the theoretical foundation of direct regression and the potential bias in classical calibration methods. To compare the effectiveness of direct regression, we develop a technique based on deep neural networks called DeepTR, which imitates the camera model's transformation to image coordinates and learns rotation, translation, focal lengths, and distortion parameters simultaneously. For comparison, we adapt GSOC, a classical calibration method to predict all parameters and evaluate both approaches using 31 datasets from the public calibration repository Jupyter-CALIBRATION. The results show that direct regression is more efficient and produces better results, specifically for distorsion parameters. Additionally, we find that the bias in classical methods grows with increasing distorsion. Therefore, direct regression is recommended for camera calibration. The Gaia space mission by the European Space Agency released its data on the Local Area of the Galaxy through a dataset known as the Gaia DR2. The data released contains precise measurements of stars near the Solar System, excluding those within the Solar System itself. The researchers at the National Astronomical Research and Study Center analyzed this data using their own methods, accounting for proper motion and interstellar absorption, to determine the positions and distances of 1.345 star members in the local cluster. The analysis identified hitherto unrecognized members of the local cluster, increasing the total count of stars in the cluster to 1.345. The researchers also found that the local cluster is a subset of the Perseus structure, a region of the galaxy founded on the common origin of stars. The distribution of stars in the local cluster across various Galactic coordinates changed after the Gaia data release, specifically with regards to the Shapley-Cesarsky radius and Galactocentric longitude. The researchers found that 75% of the local cluster members reside within 85% of the Shapley-Cesarsky radius of the original cluster, and 68% of the members are situated inside 75% of the original radius, indicating the cluster has expanded. The number of local cluster members also decreased as one moves further away from the Galactrocentric radius, specifically those at positive longitudes. The researchers discovered that 19% of the local cluster members reside within 25% of the original radius of the cluster on the other side, a region known as the anti-center. The remaining 85.5% of the local cluster members are found between the two reference points. The researchers found no correlation between the original and new distributions of local cluster members. The new distribution of local cluster members shows a significant overlap with various structures in the galaxy, specifically the Perseus stream and the Local Arm. The overlap of local cluster members with various galactic structures on both the center and anti-center sides indicates the local cluster is a part of the galactic disk. Classical graph problems such as Vertex Cover and MaxCut can be efficiently solved
for structured graphs by leveraging tree decomposition, which divides a graph into
nested subgraphs called trees. This decomposition can efficiently represent and
solve these problems, achieving a linear time complexity regardless of graph size
when using a optimal tree decomposition. Research has introduced a new
decomposition technique called SP-quasi-spanners, which sometimes offers better time
complexity performance in solving graph problems. In this study, we propose a new
method to apply SP-quasi-spanners to Vertex Cover and MaxCut, achieving a linear
time efficiency. Our technique uses a SP-quasi-spanner with a limited number of edges,
retaining a property useful for computing Vertex Cover. We demonstrate that our
method applies to other problems, such as Maximum Dissolving Set and -coloring, that
can be reduced to Vertex Cover. This new approach enhances the state-of-the-art by
offering a linear time complexity for solving these reduced problems. We further examine
how the performance of our technique depends on the characteristics of the graph
decomposition used. In particular, for specific types of Vertex Cover instances, we
can improve our time complexity to sub-linear performance by using a compact
tree decomposition. Similarly, for certain types of MaxCut instances with a simple
structure, we can achieve a linear time efficiency using a SP-quasi-spanner with a
limited number of edges. Our results contribute to the understanding of when tree-based
decomposition can yield efficient solvers for various graph problems. They also introduce
a new possibility for independent performance improvements in graph algorithms by
modifying the graph structure used for solving graph problems. To illustrate this, we
apply our technique to a specific type of social network and observe how it leads to
improved practice results for the Vertex Cover problem. All source code related to
this research has been made available publicly.

A new, sophisticated metric called the Continuous Clustering Coefficient (CCC) has been created for assessing network quality, with specific applications in MindSensors - a decentralized system for detecting deceptive activity within decentralized networks. This novel CCC value ranges between 0 and 1 and increases significantly as the network becomes more trustworthy. In order to further examine its effectiveness, two studies were conducted: one that compared the performance of the CCC to that of the well-established Zhang--Horvath Clustering (ZHC) in various scenarios, and another where the reliability of the CCC was evaluated under different levels of noise and malicious activity. These examinations demonstrated that the CCC is more sensitive to changes in network trustworthiness than the ZHC. They also revealed that the CCC based on spatial clustering tends to produce higher values than its counterpart when certain conditions occur. This may lead to overoptimistic security assessments. Consequently, a modified spatial CCC value has been suggested that combines its attributes with those of the ZHC, resulting in a more accurate and reliable security assessment. This novel method is then applied to a specific use case - decentralized sensors in MindSensors - to ensure that alerts are effectively verified by the decentralized system, thereby reducing false alarms. This, in turn, helps to enhance the system's overall accuracy and reliability. Consequently, a more efficient verification process followed by a modified CCC value allows for the production of more accurate warnings, thereby improving user experience. This novel method highlights the significance of accurate network quality assessment in decentralized systems. Decentralized systems that rely on spatial principles may benefit from using warning verification as a cost-effective solution to minimize user anxiety caused by unnecessary alarms. This, in turn, can lead to an improvement in the Decentralized System's (DS) overall performance, which in this case applies to MindSensors. Similarly, centralized systems that rely on cluster-based principles may benefit from using warning verification with a more robust clustering concept - the ZHC, which is less sensitive to certain conditions. This novel method highlights the potential for the application of clustering concepts in both centralized and decentralized systems to assess network quality and facilitate trust management processes. The zero-energy peak that appears in the conductance of an open quantum dot, resulting from non-Majorana effects, undergoes a transformation with the rise in temperature. At finite temperatures, the zero-energy peak shifts to a peak having g^2 approximately equal to 1, developing a broad width in the process. The observed behavior is particularly relevant in the context of a pair-hopping model that models the interactions between Majorana and non-Majorana isolated modes within a superconductor, mimicking the properties of an open quantum dot. It has been observed that even a relatively small temperature variation leads to a significant change in the g^2 conductance metric, thus distinguishing between the zero-energy peak and the peak occurring at finite energies. The distinguished behavior of the former is noteworthy as it persists in the situation where the hybridization strength, i.e., g, is relatively low, thus offering a promising new method for detecting and identifying non-Majorana isolated modes within a superconductor. The proposed technique is particularly valuable because it makes use of relatively weak binding between the nano-object and its surrounding environment, thus offering an appealing new method for detecting and identifying zero-energy states, which are otherwise difficult to resolve using standard techniques based on transport measurements. The resulting broad width of the zero-energy peak can potentially be utilized to estimate the average time spacing between Majorana modes occurring in a single quantum dot. The predicted conductance and local density of states have also been discussed in the context of different temperature variations using both real and imaginary components of the Green's function, based on quantum transport. The occurrence of zero-energy peak broadening has been demonstrated in numerical simulations involving discrete quantum levels and continuous quantum levels occurring in nano-objects, thus offering valuable new insights into environmental influence and the emergence of Majorana modes occurring within isolated environments. We offer spectral limits for model selection and clustering in linear bandit formulations using generalized linear models (GLMs), given that certain conditions are met. This encompasses common applications such as linear, logistic, Poisson, and matrix regression. Our outcomes are marked by two significant features: a robust performance in model selection despite little data; and a rigorous requirement for sufficient data. The spectral bounds we derive for model selection hold a 10% edge over existing choices. Additionally, we demonstrate that the models producing the top spectral values are the top model selections in many instances, making spectral analysis a valuable tool for model selection without the need for additional analysis. This model selection is also applicable to clustering, where the results are consistent with the model selection outcomes. Consequently, the methods we developed for model selection can also be employed for clustering, using only the first $d+1$ coordinates of the design matrix, thereby reducing computational demands. The theoretical findings translate into practical success as evidenced by our experiments. Based on these outcomes, we recommend the following: whenever working with bandit frameworks that involve linear GLMs, the model with dimension $d$ should always be the primary consideration, especially when the number of available samples exceeds the feature dimension; however, when the model fails to perform well, we propose a procedure for selecting the correct model dimension, based on the spectral properties of the target object, but this approach is associated with higher sample complexity requirements. In general, the model selection problem in bandit frameworks presents a challenging task, particularly under subgaussian sample limitations. Consequently, the methods we developed for model selection can also be employed for clustering, achieving an improved balance between performance and data efficiency. This reduced requirement for sufficient data marks a notable advancement, as previous methods required at least a similar number of data samples, in the order of the feature dimension, but often with significantly tighter error bars around these sample complexity estimates. Valley and orbital Hall effects are considered to be two-phased phenomena, where the former is typically measured, but the latter is measured after the valley Hall effect has subsided, leading to a misleading measurement.  A new phenomenon, the orbital Hall effect, is proposed to replace the valley Hall effect in the absence of a valley Hall effect.  This orbital Hall effect is characterized by electron rotation in a magnetic field, making it a clearer measurement than the valley Hall effect.  This distinction leads to an ordinal relationship among conductivity, resistivity, and permittivity in the case of a valley Hall effect, but a distinct case in the orbital Hall effect where conductivity, resistivity, and permittivity have varying powers of the magnetic field.  This distinct case reveals that Drude model predictions for conductivity, resistivity, and permittivity all have the same power of the magnetic field applies to the orbital Hall effect, an observation that is inconsistent with valley and orbital Hall effects in the thermal transport experiments.  This distinction also results in an absence of a valley Hall effect constraint on the dielectric effect in the orbital Hall effect, single crystal, and gossam microstructure, making it a clearer measurement than the valley Hall effect.  This distinction also leads to an applicability of the valley Hall effect in a dielectric phase and an absence of its relevance in a metallic phase, but the orbital Hall effect is applicable in both phases.  Finally, a connection between an orbital Hall effect in the absence of a valley Hall effect and an absence of a dielectric effect in a valley Hall effect is suggested with the two through a change from semiconductor to metal.  This suggests a new possibility with the orbital Hall effect in the absence of a valley Hall effect that may lead to an improved performance in an optoelectronic device.  This improvement may result in an absence of a valley Hall effect constraint on the optical Hall effect in a metal, an observation that can be confirmed by measuring conductivity, resistivity, and permittivity all have the same power of the magnetic field.  This improvement may lead to an improved performance in an optoelectronic device as well as in an absence of a valley Hall effect constraint on the optical Hall effect in a metal, an observation that can be confirmed by measuring conductivity, resistivity, and permittivity all have the same power of the magnetic field.  This development may also lead to an extended applicability of a metal orbital Hall effect in a dielectric phase and a valley Hall effect in a semiconductor phase

This study utilizes Reinforcement Learning to train neural networks in an adversarial setting, specifically in the context of Adversarial Robustness Challenge 2022's image classification task. By comparing the effectiveness of different training methods, including both direct gradient optimization and reinforcement learning approaches, the importance of explicit accounting for adversarial threats is underscored. Among the reinforcement learning methods examined, the utility of Reward via Parameter-based Adversarial Analysis as a criterion for generating adversarial examples is particularly demonstrated, leading to improved robust accuracy and reduced sensitivity to adversarial inputs when compared to more traditional approaches. Moreover, the value of combining reinforcement learning with multiple criteria to increase machine learning model reliability is illustrated. Ultimately, the findings of this study highlight the potential of reinforcement learning as a valuable framework for addressing adversarial machine learning challenges. They also serve as a foundation for further research in this area under exploration. They are even submitted as a entry to the ARCA 2022 competition. Visual aids are invaluable in understanding and managing ontologies, but their current implementation is limited to specific tasks and settings. We have developed OntoPlot, a versatile tool that enables the creation of in-depth, interactive 3D visualizations of ontologies. Its underlying structure is built around a concept of 'layers', allowing for the incorporation of diverse data and the exploration of various aspects of the ontology. From clauses and individuals to class hierarchies and relations, as well as external connections and external data, OntoPlot facilitates the customisation of 3D visualizations to suit individual requirements. The software also accommodates 'points of interest' to highlight specific parts of the ontology and to provide an in-depth analysis of particular aspects of the 3D image. A comprehensive, 3D image of the entire Biomedical Friend domain ontology can be generated with OntoPlot and displayed interactively using web-based client-server technology. The OntoPlot tool offers a unique solution for 3D visualisations of ontologies and provides a comprehensive, in-depth image of complex domains, which can be understood and explored interactively. This research demonstrates the application of CycleGAN to the challenge of generating X-ray images from Point Cloud data. By utilizing CycleGAN, the training process is facilitated without the need for paired images. As a result, the CycleGAN-generated images effectively retain the characteristics of input features, thereby enhancing the integrity of the three-dimensional (3D) input data in the generated X-ray images. In addition to promoting feature preservation, the CycleGAN results in more realistic data without fundamental inconsistencies, thereby enabling more efficient data augmentation. Furthermore, we utilize both CycleGAN-processed data and actual data for training X-Ray 3D object detectors, thereby significantly enhancing detection performance. Notably, the detection precision is substantially improved on processes with limited ground truth annotations. This research showcases the potential of using CycleGAN in various fields, including computer vision and geo-informatics. Furthermore, it also highlights the potential of using CycleGAN in other fields, such as machine learning. The objective of generative models is to produce new data points akin to those in our everyday environment. Deep learning has given generative models new life by equipping them with a robust capacity for learning complex patterns in real-world sensory data. New techniques have been developed to generate realistic raw sensor data, marking a significant shift towards raw data generation. Nevertheless, the influence of optimized data generation on actual applications remains unclear. This paper investigates the efficacy of raw visual data generation in real-world machine learning tasks through a comprehensive evaluation of a diverse range of tasks based on the benchmarks of CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Our experiments employ specific models, including a VGG-16, ResNet-18, Inception V3, and All-CNN, alongside various generative models, including GANs, their variants, and WGAN-GP. Our results indicate that generative models can indeed produce raw visual data with class information intact. Moreover, the efficacy of raw data generation in training convolutional neural networks was found to be comparable to that of using labeled data. The outcomes of our study demonstrate that the conventional practice of using pre-processed image features in computer vision machine learning tasks may be superseded by the direct utilization of raw sensory data, thereby offering potential to spearhead advancements in the field of machine learning. The research delves into the relationship between the thermal diffusion coefficient and the gravitational separation of gases consisting of rigid and flexible molecules, applying the reduced Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluid models. Evaluations are conducted to validate the suitability of the reduced models for describing gas mixtures under diverse thermal conditions. The findings also emphasize the importance of accounting for non-Newtonian behavior in gas mixtures, particularly at lower temperatures and microscopic length scales. Recent developments in pre-trained language models have led to significant breakthroughs in natural language processing tasks through a method called fine-tuning. Although earlier research indicated that smaller models are more efficient and perform well on a variety of tasks, the initial essay scorer was one exception, requiring larger models to achieve optimal results. This paper challenges this notion and presents an alternative perspective by assessing the performance of finely tuned models, including BERT, RoBERTa, and ELECTRA, in the context of the G3 ERS score. To evaluate the strength of each model, it was applied to a complex task: generating scores for unmarked essays. The findings indicate that models with fewer parameters, which are more compact and efficient, can achieve comparable or even superior results to their larger counterparts. Moreover, it was observed that models with a relatively modest number of parameters, such as BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, can perform nearly as well as more refined models with many more parameters, suggesting a reduced need for extensive models in the context of the G3 ERS score. These conclusions emphasize the importance of thoroughly evaluating multiple models before selecting the most suitable one and highlight the potential for improved efficiency in the design of these models. Training machine learning models without labels in information retrieval tasks has been largely unexplored. In this research, we focus on an aspect of retrieval known as false positive suppression, which involves preventing irrelevant documents from topping the list during query results ranking. A common approach to this challenge is to treat document ranking as a classification task for eliminating the top-1 document from consideration. However, this method has not been effectively explored in the context of unsupervised learning, primarily because laboratory datasets for FPS have been privately owned and not made public. In our work, we successfully reframe the FPS problem as a good document ranking challenge within a controlled environment, and also introduce a new lab dataset called Sustento, which is released under a permissive license. To address the unsupervised aspect, we develop a novel solution that relies on a contrastive learning approach, which involves combining it with the existing supervised approach using regularized weight updating, ultimately demonstrating superior performance on the Sustento and other existing datasets. Additionally, the source code and dataset for our research are publicly available for community use and improvement. Recent advancements in music restoration using deep learning have drawn significant interest. These techniques have shown considerable potential in enhancing the quality of music recordings compromised by noise, distortion, or other interference. This research focuses on improving the quality of low-quality music recordings contaminated with mixed noise, a common issue in the music domain. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative two-stage method grounded in a multi-exceptance deep neural network called ME-DNN. The first phase entails converting a single noisy music recording into multiple versions with differing noise patterns, facilitated by a policy network. The second phase involves generating a high-quality version of the original music signal from these modified versions. Through experimental evaluation on two music degradation datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses several competing approaches in noisy music signal reconstruction. Additionally, we visually verify the effectiveness of the policy network in generating diverse versions of a single noisy music recording. Furthermore, an analysis of the representative data from the generated versions reveals that the policy network learns critical musical characteristics during training. Creating hand-thrown object animations poses significant difficulties for animation techniques. A major challenge is devising an straightforward and intuitive method to provide animation parameters that yield visually acceptable results. This research presents a straightforward solution by dividing the throwing motion into three phases - pre-throw, throw, and catch - and associating each with distinct motion patterns. Specifically, pre-throw motions involving hand motion around 90% of the trajectory, throw motions covering 10% to 90%, and catch motions for the remaining 0% to 10%. An experimental evaluation using both expert and novice animators revealed that hand-thrown object animations generated via this simple setup were perceived as more realistic than those produced via a state-of-the-art approach. Moreover, incorporating 3D simulations via physically-based modeling enhanced the realism further, yet interestingly, it did not outdo the simple convolutional neural network-based method in terms of realism perception. A subsequent survey confirmed the simplicity of this approach by showing that users could easily grasp its parameters even without animation expertise. The proposed motion patterns also contributed to a 77% agreement among animators regarding the correct hand-thrown motion for simulated objects. The outcome suggests that this simple method offers an efficient solution for hand-thrown object animations in animation practices. The research is open-sourced at https://mrl.v6.io/. To improve the efficiency of NMT for low-resource languages, a proposed method
includes a new encoder-decoder attention model, which applies syntactic information
to NMT models via an existing tree-based model, originally designed for monolingual
purposes, on the fly during translation without requiring extra training. The role
of the syntax-aware attention model in enhancing target language syntax is investigated
through a parallel experiment with French, a high-resource language, which demonstrates
that incorporating syntax improves translation fluency and reduces motion in sentence
structure. The proposed method is subsequently validated on six language pairs, including
some with limited parallel texts, showing that combining syntax and increasing the amount
of parallel texts significantly boosts the quality of translations. The high performance
of the proposed method is attributed to its ability to efficiently transfer syntax knowledge
from the source to the target language, thus aiding in sentence translation. The outcomes
also demonstrate that incremental syntax can complement incremental memory to increase
translation quality when there is insufficient memory to process the entire input sentence. 
The findings provide evidence for the beneficial impact of syntax in high-quality NMT systems
even for expansive translation tasks, thus stressing the importance of carefully designed
attention mechanisms in NMT models. The proposed method is considered innovative due
to its on-the-fly incorporation of syntax in NMT systems without requiring extra training
and can be viewed as an extension of the existing work in machine translation, by utilizing
existing tree-based models, originally designed for monolingual purposes. The method
is viewed as a practical solution for low-resource languages, thus opening a new path
for further investigation in this area. The experiments conducted can be easily replicated
using the provided code, thus enabling other researchers to continue this line of research. 
A new multilingual NMT dataset is also introduced to facilitate comparisons of NMT systems
on various language pairs, thus enabling other researchers to perform similar experiments. 
The performance of the proposed method can be viewed via two video summaries available
at this link: https://youtu.be/2bG34gDjA0U, which demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed
method in translating target language sentences, thus highlighting its on-the-fly incorporation
of syntax in NMT systems without requiring extra training.

A protoplanetary disc's Snow Line serves as the boundary beyond which volatile compounds like water are trapped in solid ices in the outer disc regions, potentially inhibiting the growth of planets in those areas. However, recent investigations employing various model types have yielded disparate results for the Snow Line's location in the temperature-radius plane. The current study aims to evaluate how differences in binding energies, considered in the context of two distinct models, as well as Snow line computation methods, influence its variously determined locations. Initially, binding energy variations among H2O, CO, and CH4 are assessed in relation to Snow line calculations employing the transfer gap model, yielding an approximate 90 degree radius difference. Binding energy changes are also found to impact the diffusion model by nearly doubling the H2O Snow line location. Moreover, Snow line locations in diffuse discs are found to be significantly reduced compared to more typical discs with elevated gas densities. Ultimately, disc turbulence levels are identified as a critical factor in determining planet formation feasibility. Planet formation may be possible in cases with moderate turbulence but likely remains out of reach for those with elevated levels of gas turbulence. Nonetheless, in the event that gas density in the outer disc corners increases, the prospect of planet formation in those areas becomes enhanced, albeit slim. High-accuracy approximations of wave propagation are essential in geometrical optics, particularly for problems involving obstacles and in diffraction tomography. Recent research has yielded enhanced asymptotic relations for waves emitted by sources confined to a small region, enabling the refinement of the geometrical optics equation and the derivation of reliable estimates for their errors. We have discovered that, by applying the recently developed 'near-to-far field transformation', an accelerated convergence rate can be achieved, surpassing the order previously considered optimal. Specifically, for problems in two-dimensional spaces, solutions can be expressed as the sum of a potential-based term and an error term, which is proven to decay at an accelerated rate. Consequently, this allows the inclusion of additional terms in the geometrical optics equation, thereby increasing its accuracy. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in recovering potentials from synthetic data. Notably, for certain cases, the method yields explicit bounds on the potential reconstruction errors, providing insight into factors such as stochastic noise and data resolution. We have also found that, under certain conditions, the method yields a near-optimal estimate for the potential reconstruction errors. We intend to adapt this theory to address related problems, including electromagnetic scattering and diffraction tomography. Furthermore, there is potential for the application of this theory to other fields, including, for example, the analysis of linearized Einstein equations at the gravitional wave level.
